qs.q: The cell is best defined as which of the following?
c: The basic unit of a living organism
A collection of tissues that perform one function
The smallest organ in the body
An organelle that produces ATP
qs.e: The lecture opens with this definition: the cell is the basic unit of a living organism, and every nursing problem traces back to a part of it failing.

qs.q: Which organelle is the control center of the cell, holds DNA, and makes RNA?
c: Nucleus
Ribosome
Golgi complex
Mitochondria
qs.e: The nucleus holds DNA and makes RNA, which carries those instructions out to the cytoplasm where protein synthesis happens.

qs.q: A defect in the nucleus is most likely to produce which nursing problem?
c: Defective proteins or genetic disorders, because the recipe is wrong before the ribosome starts
Decreased ATP production so the cell cannot meet energy needs
Accumulation of worn-out cell parts and foreign material
Substances are not transported appropriately within the cell
qs.e: The nucleus holds the instructions for essential proteins, so a bad recipe gives defective proteins or genetic disorders. The energy answer belongs to mitochondria and the transport answer to the ER.

qs.q: If ribosomes are impaired, what result does the practice item expect?
c: Synthesis of defective proteins, or decreased protein synthesis
The cell cannot generate enough energy to maintain function
Worn-out parts and foreign material accumulate in the cell
Substances are not transported appropriately within the cell
qs.e: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis, so the problem is defective or decreased protein synthesis. That line about not making enough energy is the mitochondria answer.

qs.q: What does the endoplasmic reticulum do for the cell?
c: A tube system that transports substances throughout the cell and houses ribosomes and enzyme systems for metabolic work
Bags of enzymes that digest worn-out cell parts and bacteria
Modifies proteins and packages them into secretory granules
Breaks down ATP to release energy
qs.e: The ER is the internal transport tube, and it also houses ribosomes and the enzyme systems for the cell's metabolic work.

qs.q: If the endoplasmic reticulum fails, the nursing problem is:
c: Substances may not be transported appropriately within the cell
Material cannot enter the cell by endocytosis
Enzymes are never delivered into the lysosome
Hormones cannot be released outside the cell
qs.e: The ER moves substances through the cell, so failure is an internal transport problem. Endocytosis is a job of the membrane, not the ER.

qs.q: Which organelle transforms food energy into ATP and is the site of aerobic metabolism?
c: Mitochondria
Ribosome
Peroxisome
Lysosome
qs.e: Mitochondria turn food energy into ATP, which powers cell activities, and aerobic metabolism happens here.

qs.q: Worn-out cell parts and foreign material such as bacteria accumulate when which structure fails?
c: Lysosomes
Ribosomes
Nucleus
Golgi complex
qs.e: Lysosomes are bags of enzymes that digest worn-out parts and foreign material, so failure means that debris piles up.

qs.q: Which disorder does the recorded slide name as an example of a lysosomal storage disease?
c: Tay-Sachs
I-cell disease
Myasthenia gravis
Iron-deficiency anemia
qs.e: Tay-Sachs is the example given for lysosomal storage disease, where digestion in the lysosome cannot happen.

qs.q: I-cell disease is grouped with which problem?
c: A packaging problem: lysosomal enzymes are never delivered into the lysosome
An antibody against a receptor so the message does not land
A lysosome digesting its own membrane
Bad DNA instructions in the nucleus
qs.e: I-cell disease sits with the Golgi packaging problem because the enzymes are made but never get delivered into the lysosome.

qs.q: What is the main job of peroxisomes?
c: Hold enzymes that detoxify substances and help control free radicals
Synthesize proteins from RNA instructions
Package hormones into secretory granules
Pump sodium out of the cell and potassium into it
qs.e: Peroxisomes are similar to lysosomes but their enzymes detoxify substances and help control free radicals.

qs.q: The Golgi complex fails. What happens to what the ribosomes made?
c: It is made but not modified, packaged, or sent to the right place
It is digested by lysosomal enzymes and destroyed
It leaks out as proteins and RNA
It is never synthesized because the recipe is missing
qs.e: The Golgi modifies, packages into secretory granules or vesicles, and addresses the product. Hormones and lysosomal enzymes both depend on this step.

qs.q: In myasthenia gravis the membrane problem is:
c: An antibody against the receptor, so the message does not land
An antigen that no longer labels the cell self
A failure of carrier proteins and ion channels
A potential that cannot fire because potassium leaked out
qs.e: Myasthenia gravis is the receptor failure example: antibodies block receptors, so the chemical messenger cannot do its job.

qs.q: What do the antigens on the cell membrane do?
c: Label the cell self or nonself
Move substances in and out of the cell
Digest foreign material that enters the cell
Generate ATP for cell activities
qs.e: Membrane antigens are the cell's identity tag, labeling it self or nonself. Transport is the job of carrier proteins and ion channels.

qs.q: Where does aerobic metabolism take place?
c: Mitochondria
Cytoplasm
Lysosome
Golgi complex
qs.e: Aerobic metabolism requires oxygen and happens in the mitochondria, the efficient energy path.

qs.q: Which statement describes anaerobic metabolism?
c: No oxygen, occurs in the cytoplasm, and is less efficient; matters when oxygen delivery is low
Requires oxygen, occurs in the mitochondria, and is the efficient path
Requires oxygen but occurs in the cytoplasm
Happens in the Golgi complex, which packages the lactic acid
qs.e: Anaerobic metabolism runs without oxygen in the cytoplasm and makes less ATP, so it matters when oxygen delivery is low.

qs.q: Osmosis is best defined as:
c: Water moving down its gradient through a semi-permeable membrane until solute concentration is equal on both sides
Particles moving down the concentration gradient
A vesicle fusing with the membrane to release contents outside
Movement against the concentration gradient using ATP
qs.e: Diffusion moves particles; osmosis moves water. Which one happens depends on whether the membrane lets that particle through.

qs.q: In hypernatremia, what happens to the cell?
c: More water leaves and the cell shrinks
More sodium and water enter and the cell swells
The lysosomal membrane breaks and the cell digests itself
Proteins and RNA leak out and the cell grows larger
qs.e: With more sodium outside, water leaves the cell by osmosis and the cell shrinks. Pump failure causes the opposite picture, swelling.

qs.q: What is the purpose of active transport?
c: To let substances move in and out of the cell against the concentration gradient
To activate enzymes that protect against free radicals
To carry the electrical signal itself along the membrane
To spread water evenly across a semi-permeable membrane
qs.e: Active transport is the only transport that spends ATP and the only one that goes uphill against the gradient; the sodium-potassium pump is the classic example.

qs.q: Which type of endocytosis brings in fluid and dissolved particles?
c: Pinocytosis
Phagocytosis
Exocytosis
Diffusion
qs.e: Pinocytosis takes in fluid and dissolved particles, while phagocytosis engulfs microorganisms, damaged cells, and other particles.

qs.q: Which statement describes the resting membrane potential?
c: All body cells are electrically polarized and the inside is more negative than the outside
The inside is more positive because sodium is concentrated inside the cell
Only nerve and muscle cells are electrically polarized
The cell is polarized only after it fires an action potential
qs.e: All body cells are electrically polarized at rest, with the inside more negative; a change in that polarization can carry a message and trigger work.

qs.q: Why is oxygen necessary for a cell to repolarize?
c: The sodium-potassium pump is active transport, which needs ATP, and the efficient aerobic ATP path needs oxygen
Oxygen is converted directly into potassium during repolarization
Oxygen binds the receptor protein so the message can land
Oxygen is required to make the lactic acid that resets the membrane
qs.e: Repolarization ends with the sodium-potassium pump restoring sodium and potassium; that pump is active transport, which needs ATP, and aerobic ATP needs oxygen.

qs.q: Which comparison of reversible injury and cell death is correct?
c: Reversible injury means the cell is hurt and can still recover; necrosis means the injury is irreversible
Both are forms of cellular adaptation
Cell death is reversible if the cause is removed; reversible injury always ends in necrosis
Reversible injury is another name for dysplasia
qs.e: The handout lists three boxes: cellular adaptation, reversible injury, and cell death. Only adaptation and reversible injury leave room for survival.

qs.q: Select all the functions of the cell membrane listed in the handout.
c: Acts as a barrier against foreign organisms and toxic molecules
Contains proteins that move substances in and out, such as carrier proteins and ion channels
Carries receptors for hormones and other active substances
Produces ATP by aerobic metabolism
Maintains and transmits membrane potentials
qs.e: The membrane has five listed jobs: barrier, transport proteins, receptors, self/nonself antigens, and membrane potentials. ATP production is the mitochondria.

qs.q: Select all the predisposing factors listed for impaired cell communication.
c: Autoimmune disease
Congenital defects
Genetic predisposition
Degeneration from age or toxins
Electrolyte imbalances
qs.e: These four factors can leave the messenger or the receptor missing or not working. Electrolyte imbalances belong to the changes-in-membrane-permeability row.

qs.q: Select all the predisposing factors listed for altered energy production.
c: Less oxygen getting to the cell
Less food or fuel
Metabolic enzymes that are missing or not working
A receptor blocked by antibodies
Antigens that label the cell nonself
qs.e: Altered energy production comes from less oxygen, less fuel, or enzymes that are missing or not working. The last two options belong to membrane and signaling problems.

qs.q: Select all statements that describe passive transport.
c: No energy is required
It follows a chemical or electrical gradient
Substances move from high to low concentration
The goal is equilibrium
It is the only way substances move against the gradient
qs.e: Passive transport needs no energy and runs downhill to equilibrium. Moving against the gradient is active transport.

qs.q: Select all mechanisms of movement across the cell membrane named in lecture.
c: Passive transport (diffusion and osmosis)
Active transport
Endocytosis
Exocytosis
RNA transcription
qs.e: The notes name three categories: passive (diffusion and osmosis), active transport, and endocytosis and exocytosis. Transcription is nuclear work, not movement.

qs.q: Select all external sources of free radicals named by the instructor.
c: Tobacco smoke
Pollutants
Pesticides
Radiation
ATP breakdown
qs.e: Free radicals also come from normal work such as oxidative reactions in metabolism and inflammation, but ATP breakdown is not one of the named outside sources.

qs.q: Select all the ways free radicals damage the cell.
c: They damage membranes and proteins
They inactivate enzymes
They damage DNA
They detoxify substances in the peroxisome
They digest worn-out cell parts
qs.e: Free radicals are highly unstable atoms that react with key molecules; peroxisomes are what help control them, and lysosomes digest debris.

qs.q: Select all the intracellular enzymes the slide names as leaking out when membranes are damaged.
c: CK (creatine kinase)
LD (lactate dehydrogenase)
Troponin
DNA
Carrier proteins
qs.e: These three enzymes are the named leakage markers after membrane damage from acidosis. DNA and carrier proteins are not the enzymes on the slide.

qs.q: Select all consequences of sodium-potassium pump failure and other energy-dependent transport failure.
c: More sodium and water enter and the cell swells
Membrane permeability rises and proteins and RNA leak out
More calcium enters and turns on enzymes that damage the cell
The cell shrinks as water leaves
The cell returns to aerobic metabolism and recovers
qs.e: Pump failure lets sodium and water in, which swells the cell; the calcium entry is what switches on damaging enzymes. Shrinking is the hypernatremia picture.

qs.q: Select all the cellular adaptations listed on the handout.
c: Atrophy
Hypertrophy
Hyperplasia
Metaplasia
Necrosis
qs.e: The five adaptations are atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, metaplasia, and dysplasia. Necrosis sits in a separate box after reversible injury.

qs.q: Select all the predisposing factors for cell injury listed by the instructor.
c: Physical forces such as mechanical forces, temperature extremes, and electricity
Radiation
Chemicals such as drugs, environmental toxins, lead, and tobacco smoke
Biologic agents such as microorganisms and parasites
Excess potassium diffusing out at rest
qs.e: The list also includes nutrition in both directions (obesity with atherosclerosis, iron-deficiency anemia), genetic derangements, and autoimmune disorders.

qs.q: Name the cellular adaptation in which the cell becomes smaller and drops to a lower level of function.
qs.e: Atrophy lowers oxygen and energy needs, which makes survival more likely.

qs.q: At rest, the inside of the cell is more ______ than the outside.
qs.e: All body cells are electrically polarized at rest, and the inside holds mostly negatively charged ions after potassium diffuses out.

qs.q: Which ion diffuses out of the resting cell, down its gradient?
qs.e: The resting membrane is more permeable to potassium than sodium, so potassium leaves and leaves negative charges behind. Sodium cannot get in, so water moves instead.

qs.q: Hypernatremia causes the cell to ______.
qs.e: More sodium outside draws water out of the cell by osmosis. Pump failure is the opposite: sodium and water enter and the cell swells.

qs.q: Which acid builds up when the cell switches to anaerobic metabolism?
qs.e: Without oxygen the cell runs anaerobic metabolism, lactic acid accumulates, pH falls, and the result is metabolic acidosis with membrane damage.

qs.q: Which type of endocytosis engulfs microorganisms, damaged cells, and other particles?
qs.e: Phagocytosis takes in whole particles and then kills or breaks them down; pinocytosis takes in fluid and dissolved particles.

qs.q: What are the direct cell-to-cell channels in nerve and muscle that let an action potential spread fast?
qs.e: Gap junctions let small ions and molecules pass straight from cell to cell, so the impulse moves quickly through muscle or nerve.

qs.q: What is the name for the highly unstable compounds that can damage cytoplasm?
qs.e: Free radicals react with membranes, proteins, enzymes, and DNA. Peroxisomes hold enzymes that help control them.

qs.q: Which adaptation is deranged growth in which cells vary in size, shape, and appearance?
qs.e: Dysplasia usually follows chronic irritation or inflammation and is the one adaptation that looks abnormal; metaplasia is a change of type, not deranged growth.

qs.q: The cell is described as the basic unit of a:
c: Tissue
Living organism
Organ system
Membrane
qs.e: The cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of all living organisms. Understanding the cell is foundational to understanding how tissues, organs, and body systems work.

qs.q: The nucleus is described as the cell's:
c: Powerhouse
Transport system
Control center
Protective barrier
qs.e: The nucleus is the control center of the cell. It contains the genetic material (DNA) that directs all cellular activities.

qs.q: What does DNA provide instructions for?
c: Synthesis of essential proteins
Production of ATP
Detoxification of free radicals
Transport of ions
qs.e: DNA provides instructions for the synthesis of essential proteins and carries genetic information passed down through generations. Protein synthesis is a key function directed by the DNA in the nucleus.

qs.q: RNA transmits instructions from DNA to:
c: The cell membrane
Mitochondria
Cytoplasm (where protein synthesis occurs)
The Golgi complex
qs.e: RNA transmits instructions from DNA in the nucleus to the cytoplasm, where protein synthesis takes place. It also facilitates protein production.

qs.q: Ribosomes are the sites of:
c: ATP production
Protein synthesis
Free radical detoxification
Waste digestion
qs.e: Ribosomes are the specific sites of protein synthesis within the cell. They read the instructions carried by RNA to build proteins.

qs.q: The endoplasmic reticulum is described as the cell's:
c: Control center
Powerhouse
Transport system
Protective barrier
qs.e: The endoplasmic reticulum is the cell's transport system. It transports substances throughout the cell and also houses ribosomes and enzyme systems that carry out metabolic functions.

qs.q: Mitochondria transform food energy into which molecule used to power cell activities?
c: RNA
DNA
ATP
Lactic acid
qs.e: Mitochondria transform food energy into ATP (adenosine triphosphate), which is used to power cell activities. This is why mitochondria are called the 'powerhouse' of the cell.

qs.q: Lysosomes are described as:
c: 'Powerhouse of the cell'
'Bags of enzymes' that digest worn-out cell parts and foreign material
'Transport system' for the cell
'Control center' of the cell
qs.e: Lysosomes are 'bags of enzymes' that digest worn-out cell parts and foreign material, such as bacteria, that have gotten into the cell. This digestion function is critical for cellular housekeeping and defense.

qs.q: Which organelle contains special enzymes that detoxify substances and help control free radicals?
c: Lysosomes
Golgi complex
Peroxisomes
Endoplasmic reticulum
qs.e: Peroxisomes are similar to lysosomes but contain special enzymes that detoxify substances and help control free radicals—highly unstable compounds that can damage the cytoplasm. This protective function is essential for cell survival.

qs.q: The Golgi complex modifies substances synthesized by ribosomes and packages them into:
c: Ribosomes
Lysosomes
Secretory granules/vesicles
ATP molecules
qs.e: The Golgi complex modifies substances synthesized by ribosomes, packages them into secretory granules or vesicles, and directs them to where they are supposed to go. It acts as the cell's 'shipping and receiving' center.

qs.q: Aerobic metabolism requires oxygen and occurs in:
c: Cytoplasm
Mitochondria
Endoplasmic reticulum
Ribosomes
qs.e: Aerobic metabolism is the more efficient pathway for energy production and occurs in the mitochondria. It requires oxygen to produce ATP.

qs.q: Anaerobic metabolism occurs in the:
c: Mitochondria
Nucleus
Cytoplasm
Golgi complex
qs.e: Anaerobic metabolism occurs in the cytoplasm without oxygen. It is less efficient than aerobic metabolism but is important during periods of low oxygen delivery.

qs.q: Which type of molecular movement across the cell membrane requires no expenditure of energy?
c: Active transport
Endocytosis
Passive movement
Exocytosis
qs.e: Passive movement requires no energy expenditure and occurs related to chemical or electrical gradients. Diffusion and osmosis are examples of passive movement.

qs.q: Diffusion is the process by which substances move from areas of greater to lesser:
c: Voltage
Temperature
Concentration
Molecular weight
qs.e: Diffusion moves substances from areas of greater to lesser concentration in an attempt to reach uniform distribution. It is a passive process driven by concentration gradients.

qs.q: Osmosis is the diffusion of ____ through a semi-permeable membrane along a concentration gradient:
c: Sodium
Potassium
Glucose
Water
qs.e: Osmosis is specifically the diffusion of water through a semi-permeable membrane. Water moves until the concentration of solute particles is equal on both sides of the membrane.

qs.q: Active transport is necessary when substances need to move:
c: Along the concentration gradient
Against the concentration gradient
Only through gap junctions
Only within the cytoplasm
qs.e: Active transport requires energy and is needed when substances must move against (opposite to) their concentration gradient. The sodium-potassium pump is a key example of active transport.

qs.q: Pinocytosis involves the cell engulfing:
c: Bacteria and microorganisms
Solid particles only
Fluid and dissolved particles
Worn-out cell parts
qs.e: Pinocytosis is a type of endocytosis that specifically involves the uptake of fluid and dissolved particles into the cell. It is sometimes called 'cell drinking.'

qs.q: Exocytosis is described as the:
c: Reverse of endocytosis
Same as pinocytosis
Process of water movement
Formation of gap junctions
qs.e: Exocytosis is the reverse of endocytosis—a secretory granule fuses to the cell membrane and opens to the outside of the cell. It is a mechanism for releasing hormones and getting rid of cellular debris.

qs.q: Free radicals are described as:
c: Stable compounds that repair DNA
Highly unstable compounds that can damage cytoplasm
Enzymes that digest bacteria
Ions that maintain membrane potential
qs.e: Free radicals are highly unstable atoms or compounds that react with key molecules in the cell. They can damage cell membranes and proteins, inactivate enzymes, and damage DNA.

qs.q: The sodium-potassium pump causes which ion to be more concentrated outside the cell?
c: Potassium
Sodium
Calcium
ATP
qs.e: The sodium-potassium pump actively pumps sodium out of the cell and potassium into the cell, resulting in sodium being more concentrated outside and potassium more concentrated inside. This creates the electrochemical gradient essential for cell function.

qs.q: At rest, the cell membrane is more permeable to which ion, causing it to diffuse out of the cell?
c: Sodium
Calcium
Potassium
Chloride
qs.e: The resting membrane is more permeable to potassium than sodium, so potassium diffuses out of the cell down its concentration gradient. This leaves mostly negatively charged ions inside, making the inside of the cell negative at rest.

qs.q: If cell injury is irreversible, it results in:
c: Atrophy
Metaplasia
Cell death/necrosis
Hypertrophy
qs.e: If cell injury progresses to the point where it is irreversible, the cell dies—a process called necrosis. Reversible injury can potentially be corrected, but irreversible injury leads to cell death.

qs.q: Select ALL functions of the cell membrane/plasma membrane:
c: Keeps cell together and acts as a protective barrier against foreign organisms and toxic molecules
Produces ATP to power cell activities
Contains proteins (carrier proteins, ion channels) that assist transport of substances in/out of the cell
Contains antigens that label cells as self or nonself
Contains DNA that directs all cellular activities
qs.e: The cell membrane keeps the cell together, provides a protective barrier, contains transport proteins and ion channels, contains hormone receptors, contains self/nonself antigens, and maintains/transmits membrane potentials. ATP production occurs in the mitochondria and DNA is in the nucleus.

qs.q: Select ALL functions of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER):
c: Transports substances throughout the cell
Digests worn-out cell parts and foreign material
Houses ribosomes
Houses enzyme systems that carry out metabolic functions
Modifies and packages substances for secretion
qs.e: The ER is the cell's transport system, houses ribosomes, and contains enzyme systems for metabolic functions. Digesting worn-out parts is the role of lysosomes, and modifying/packaging substances is the role of the Golgi complex.

qs.q: Select ALL effects that occur during power failure (hypoxia and ATP depletion) within the cell:
c: Switch to anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid production → decrease in pH
Lysosomal membranes may be damaged → leakage of lysosomal enzymes → self-digestion
Cell undergoes hypertrophy to compensate
Failure of sodium-potassium pump → more Na and water enter cells → cellular swelling
Increase in calcium entry → abnormal activation of enzymes → cell damage
qs.e: Hypoxia and ATP depletion cause a switch to anaerobic metabolism (lactic acid, ↓ pH), lysosomal membrane damage and self-digestion, Na⁺/K⁺ pump failure with cellular swelling, and calcium influx with abnormal enzyme activation. Hypertrophy is an adaptive response, not a consequence of power failure.

qs.q: Select ALL adaptive responses to cell injury:
c: Atrophy – cell reverts to a smaller size and lower level of functioning
Necrosis – cell death from irreversible injury
Hypertrophy – increase in cell size and functional components
Hyperplasia – increase in number of cells
Metaplasia – change from one cell type to another
qs.e: Adaptive responses include atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, metaplasia, and dysplasia. Necrosis (cell death) is not an adaptive response—it is the outcome of irreversible injury.

qs.q: Select ALL exogenous (external) sources of free radicals mentioned in lecture:
c: Oxidative reactions during metabolic processes
Tobacco smoke
Pollutants
Pesticides
Inflammatory process
qs.e: Exogenous sources of free radicals include tobacco smoke, pollutants, pesticides, and radiation. Oxidative reactions during metabolic processes and the inflammatory process are byproducts of normal body processes (endogenous sources).

qs.q: Select ALL predisposing factors (PF) for alterations in the availability/function of chemical messengers or receptor sites (cellular communication):
c: Autoimmune disease
Electrolyte imbalances
Congenital defects
Genetic predisposition
Nutritional excess (obesity)
qs.e: Predisposing factors for communication problems include autoimmune disease, congenital defects, genetic predisposition, and degeneration related to age or toxin exposure. Electrolyte imbalances are a PF for changes in membrane permeability, not cellular communication.

qs.q: Select ALL steps that occur during repolarization of a cell:
c: Sodium moves into the cell down its concentration gradient
Membrane becomes less permeable to sodium and more permeable to potassium
Sodium-potassium pump restores membrane to resting potential by pumping sodium out and potassium in
Current-carrying ions pass through gap junctions to other cells
Inside of the cell becomes negatively charged again
qs.e: During repolarization, the membrane becomes less permeable to Na⁺ and more permeable to K⁺, the Na⁺/K⁺ pump restores resting potential, and the inside of the cell becomes negative again. Sodium entering the cell and ions passing through gap junctions occur during depolarization, not repolarization.

qs.q: Select ALL general categories of predisposing factors/agents that can cause cell injury:
c: Physical agents (mechanical forces, temperature extremes, electricity)
Radiation
Chemicals (drugs, environmental toxins like lead, tobacco smoke)
Biologic agents (microorganisms, parasites)
Positive reinforcement
qs.e: General PF for cell injury include physical agents, radiation, chemicals, biologic agents, nutritional imbalances (excesses and deficiencies), genetic derangements, and autoimmune disorders. Positive reinforcement is a behavioral concept, not a cell injury factor.

qs.q: Select ALL events that occur during depolarization of a cell:
c: An initial stimulus causes the cell membrane to become more permeable to sodium
Sodium moves into the cell down its concentration gradient
The inside of the cell is no longer more negative than outside
Membrane becomes more permeable to potassium
Current-carrying ions pass through gap junctions to other cells, conducting the impulse
qs.e: Depolarization involves the membrane becoming more permeable to Na⁺, Na⁺ rushing in, the inside losing its negative charge, and ions spreading through gap junctions to conduct the impulse. Increased potassium permeability occurs during repolarization, not depolarization.

qs.q: Select ALL methods of cellular communication described in lecture:
c: Chemical messengers that interact with receptor proteins of other cells
Gap junctions in nerve and muscle cells allowing ions/molecules to pass directly from cell to cell
Active transport of sodium through the cell membrane
Phagocytosis of signaling molecules
Formation of action potentials through membrane polarization changes
qs.e: Cellular communication occurs through (1) chemical messengers interacting with receptor proteins and (2) gap junctions that allow direct passage of small ions/molecules between nerve and muscle cells. Active transport, phagocytosis, and action potentials are other cell processes, not communication methods per se.

qs.q: The organelle known as the 'powerhouse of the cell' is the ____.
qs.e: Mitochondria are called the powerhouse because they transform food energy into ATP, which powers all cell activities.

qs.q: Lysosomes are described as '____' that digest worn-out cell parts and foreign material.
qs.e: The phrase 'bags of enzymes' is the key description of lysosomes in the course material. They digest worn-out cell parts and foreign material like bacteria.

qs.q: A change from one cell type to another, usually triggered by chronic irritation/inflammation, is called ____.
qs.e: Metaplasia is an adaptive response where one cell type changes to another that is better able to survive under adverse conditions, typically from chronic irritation or inflammation.

qs.q: Gap junctions are channels found in nerve and ____ cells.
qs.e: Gap junctions are found in nerve and muscle cells and allow small ions and molecules to pass directly from cell to cell, enabling action potentials to spread rapidly.

qs.q: An increase in the number of cells is called ____.
qs.e: Hyperplasia is an adaptive response involving an increase in the number of cells. It is distinct from hypertrophy, which is an increase in cell size.

qs.q: If cell injury is irreversible, it results in cell death or ____.
qs.e: Necrosis is the term for cell death resulting from irreversible injury. This is distinguished from reversible injury where the cell can potentially recover.

qs.q: The organelle that serves as the cell's transport system and houses ribosomes is the ____.
qs.e: The endoplasmic reticulum is described as the cell's transport system that houses ribosomes and enzyme systems for metabolic functions.

qs.q: Deranged cell growth in which cells vary in size, shape, and appearance is called ____.
qs.e: Dysplasia is an adaptive response involving deranged cell growth, with cells that vary in size, shape, and appearance. It is usually related to chronic irritation or inflammation.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe the nucleus and ribosomes? Select all that apply.
c: The nucleus serves as the cell's control center.
The nucleus contains DNA and makes RNA.
Ribosomes are sites of protein synthesis.
Impaired ribosomes may cause defective or decreased protein synthesis.
Ribosomes primarily digest worn-out cell parts.
qs.e: The nucleus contains genetic material and makes RNA, while ribosomes synthesize proteins. Digesting worn-out cell parts is a lysosomal function.
qs.src: [Doc: Cell Part 1 notes; Deck A Slide 6]

qs.q: An organelle that houses ribosomes and metabolic enzyme systems is impaired, causing inappropriate transport within the cell. Which organelle is affected?
c: Lysosome
Endoplasmic reticulum
Cell membrane
Nucleus
qs.e: The endoplasmic reticulum is the cell's internal transport system and houses ribosomes and metabolic enzyme systems. Its impairment can disrupt transport within the cell.
qs.src: [Doc: Cell Part 1 notes; Deck A Slide 7]

qs.q: Which organelle is the cell's 'powerhouse,' making its dysfunction most directly concerning for inadequate energy production?
c: Golgi complex
Lysosome
Mitochondrion
Ribosome
qs.e: Mitochondria are described as the cell's powerhouse. They are also the location of aerobic energy production.

qs.q: Worn-out cell parts and foreign material accumulate because the cell's 'bags of enzymes' are not functioning. Which organelle is impaired?
c: Lysosome
Nucleus
Golgi apparatus
Endoplasmic reticulum
qs.e: Lysosomes contain enzymes that digest worn-out cell parts and foreign material. Impaired digestion would allow these materials to accumulate.

qs.q: Which organelles contain enzymes that help detoxify free radicals?
qs.e: Peroxisomal enzymes help detoxify free radicals. This distinguishes them from lysosomes, which digest cell parts and foreign material.

qs.q: Which organelle packages substances made by ribosomes into vesicles for release?
qs.e: The Golgi complex packages substances into vesicles for release. Ribosomes make proteins, while the Golgi performs the packaging role.

qs.q: Which are functions of the cell membrane, also called the plasma membrane? Select all that apply.
c: Keeping the cell together and providing a protective barrier
Providing carrier proteins for transport across the membrane
Providing receptors for hormones and antigens identifying self or nonself
Maintaining and transmitting membrane potentials
Serving as the primary site of RNA production
qs.e: The membrane has structural, transport, recognition, receptor, and electrical functions. The notes assign RNA production to the nucleus.

qs.q: Cells use oxygen and food to produce energy stored in which molecule?
qs.e: Energy is stored as ATP. When the cell needs energy, ATP is broken down and energy is released.

qs.q: Which comparison of the two energy-production pathways is correct?
c: Aerobic metabolism occurs in the cytoplasm without oxygen; anaerobic metabolism occurs in mitochondria.
Aerobic metabolism requires oxygen and occurs in mitochondria; anaerobic metabolism occurs without oxygen in the cytoplasm.
Both pathways require oxygen, but only anaerobic metabolism occurs in mitochondria.
Anaerobic metabolism is more efficient than aerobic metabolism and is unimportant during low oxygen delivery.
qs.e: Aerobic metabolism requires oxygen and occurs in mitochondria. Anaerobic metabolism occurs in the cytoplasm without oxygen; it is less efficient but important when oxygen delivery is low.

qs.q: Which factors are identified as relevant to altered cellular metabolism or energy production? Select all that apply.
c: Oxygen available to the cell
Food or fuel available to the cell
Metabolic enzyme availability
Metabolic enzyme function
The particular label used for the Golgi apparatus

qs.q: Movement across the membrane is needed to maintain cell function. What characterizes passive movement?

qs.q: What process moves substances from greater to lesser concentration in an attempt to achieve uniform distribution?

Engulfment of microorganisms into a vesicle

Osmosis
Passive movement

Osmosis

qs.q: What channels in nerve and muscle cells allow small ions and molecules to pass directly between cells, rapidly spreading electrical signals?

qs.q: Which statement describes resting membrane potential and its functional significance?

qs.q: Which sequence explains the negative cell interior at rest?
c: The pump concentrates sodium inside; sodium diffuses out and leaves potassium behind.
The pump concentrates potassium outside; potassium diffuses inward through an impermeable membrane.
The pump concentrates sodium outside and potassium inside; greater resting permeability to potassium allows potassium to diffuse out, leaving mostly negative ions inside.
The pump removes all sodium and potassium, leaving no concentration gradients.
qs.e: The sodium-potassium pump establishes higher sodium outside and higher potassium inside. The resting membrane is more permeable to potassium, so its outward diffusion leaves the interior relatively negative.

qs.q: Which sequence describes depolarization and impulse spread?
c: A stimulus increases sodium permeability, sodium enters down its gradient, and current-carrying ions pass through gap junctions to neighboring cells.
A stimulus decreases sodium permeability, sodium leaves, and the cell becomes more negative.
Potassium enters through lysosomes, causing hormones to exit through gap junctions.
The cell loses all receptor proteins, causing an impulse to spread through its nucleus.
qs.e: During depolarization, increased sodium permeability allows sodium to enter and the inside is no longer more negative than the outside. Current-carrying ions then pass through gap junctions, conducting the impulse through muscle or nerve tissue.

qs.q: Which changes restore the cell toward its resting state during repolarization?
c: Greater sodium permeability and pumping potassium out
Permanent closure of all ion pathways and cessation of ATP use
Pumping sodium in and potassium out while sodium permeability rises
Lower sodium permeability, greater potassium permeability, and pumping sodium out and potassium back in
qs.e: The interior becomes negative again as the membrane becomes less permeable to sodium and more permeable to potassium. The sodium-potassium pump restores the resting state by moving sodium out and potassium back in.

qs.q: Why does impaired oxygen delivery threaten the cell's ability to restore resting membrane potential?
c: Oxygen directly substitutes for potassium inside the cell.
Hypoxia can reduce energy production needed for active transport by the sodium-potassium pump.
Oxygen is the receptor protein used by every chemical messenger.
Hypoxia makes active transport independent of ATP.
qs.e: Oxygen supports aerobic energy production, and active transport requires energy. Hypoxia or impaired metabolism can therefore compromise the pump's ability to maintain or restore resting membrane potential.

Normal packaging of substances by the Golgi apparatus

Normal vesicle packaging alone

qs.q: Which description of free radicals and their effects matches the notes?

The word 'hyperplasia' itself

qs.q: Which injury sequence is described when hypoxia and ATP depletion cause cellular 'power failure'?

qs.q: Why can damage to lysosomal membranes cause cellular self-digestion?

qs.q: Which consequences of ATP depletion and failure of energy-dependent transport are described in lecture? Select all that apply.

qs.e: Energy depletion disrupts transport and membrane integrity, allowing loss of cell contents and abnormal ion entry. Sodium and water entry cause swelling, while calcium entry can abnormally activate enzymes.

qs.q: What adaptation involves a cell becoming smaller and functioning at a lower level to reduce oxygen and energy needs and support survival?

Hypertrophy
Hyperplasia

Pinocytosis
Reversible injury

qs.q: Which study strategy best addresses how teachers write questions and choose distractors?

Avoid comparisons between diseases with more than one type.
Assume an opposite of a correct statement must also be correct.
Review similar vocabulary and easily confused diseases, comparing similarities, differences, types, and opposites.

Memorize the disease name without examining causes or outcomes.
Wait for complications before deciding whether the original problem mattered.

qs.q: Which are listed steps in logical thinking for nurses? Select all that apply.

Compare easily confused concepts and identify patterns through clustering and linking.
Prioritize problems or interventions and individualize decisions.
Defend conclusions and decisions.
Apply the same intervention to everyone without considering differences.

qs.q: Which statement best summarizes the slides' reasons for group work?

qs.q: Which approach correctly applies the vocabulary prompts for a body part and a normal finding or process?

qs.e: Studying an abnormal finding involves defining it and connecting its causes and predisposing factors to patient problems. This supports understanding rather than isolated memorization.

Na+ rushes into the cell to restore the negative charge
Anions are pumped out of the cell by the lysosome
qs.e: Slides 62-64: membrane reverts first, then the pump restores K+ inside and Na+ outside so the cell is ready to start all over again.

qs.q: In which direction does the sodium-potassium pump move each ion?
c: Na+ out of the cell, K+ into the cell
Na+ into the cell, K+ out of the cell
Both ions out of the cell
Both ions into the cell
qs.e: The pump diagram shows sodium ions pumped out and potassium ions pumped into the cell.

qs.q: Sodium ions (Na+) are pumped ______ of the cell by the sodium-potassium pump.
qs.e: The pump moves Na+ out of the cell and K+ into the cell, maintaining the resting gradient.

qs.q: Which two mechanisms of cell injury are named in this lecture segment?
c: Free radicals and hypoxia
Free radicals and hyperthermia
Hypoxia and radiation
Infection and inflammation
qs.e: Slides 68/71/77 list only two mechanisms of cell injury: free radicals and hypoxia.

qs.q: Select ALL mechanisms of cell injury listed in these slides.
c: Free radicals
Hypoxia
Dehydration
Ionizing radiation
Chemical burns
qs.e: Only free radicals and hypoxia are given as mechanisms of cell injury in this chunk.

qs.q: When oxygen is inadequate, the cell must rely on which type of metabolism?
c: Anaerobic metabolism
Aerobic metabolism
Lipid metabolism
Protein synthesis
qs.e: The flow chart shows inadequate oxygen leads to anaerobic metabolism.

qs.q: Anaerobic metabolism results in the production of ______.
qs.e: Slide 72: anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid production.

qs.q: Lactic acid production from anaerobic metabolism leads directly to which problem?
c: Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Depolarization
qs.e: The diagram shows lactic acid production leading to metabolic acidosis.

qs.q: According to the inadequate oxygen flow chart, metabolic failure ultimately results in:
c: Cell death
Cell adaptation
Hypertrophy
Reversible injury only
qs.e: The sequence ends in metabolic failure and cell death.

qs.q: Select ALL events shown in the 'Inadequate Oxygen' flow chart.
c: Inadequate energy
Anaerobic metabolism and lactic acid production
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic failure leading to cell death
Increased aerobic metabolism
qs.e: The chart traces inadequate oxygen → inadequate energy/anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid → metabolic acidosis → metabolic failure → cell death.

qs.q: Which substances are named as markers released when cells are injured or die?
c: CK (creatine kinase), LD (lactate dehydrogenase), and troponin
Insulin, glucagon, and hemoglobin
Sodium, potassium, and chloride
Antibodies, antigens, and histamine
qs.e: Slide 74 lists CK, LD, and troponin in the context of cell injury/death.

qs.q: Select ALL markers listed in this lecture segment.
c: CK (creatine kinase)
LD (lactate dehydrogenase)
Troponin
Hemoglobin
Amylase
qs.e: Only CK, LD, and troponin are named on the slide.

qs.q: CK stands for ______.
qs.e: Slide 74 gives the abbreviation CK = creatine kinase.

qs.q: LD stands for ______.
qs.e: Slide 74 gives the abbreviation LD = lactate dehydrogenase.

qs.q: Which of the following is the correct list of 'cellular responses' given in the lecture?
c: Cellular adaptation, reversible injury, cell death
Hypertrophy, hyperplasia, cancer
Depolarization, repolarization, action potential
Free radicals, hypoxia, acidosis
qs.e: Slides 78/92 list three cellular responses: cellular adaptation, reversible injury, and cell death.

qs.q: Select ALL cellular responses listed in the lecture.
c: Cellular adaptation
Reversible injury
Cell death
Metastasis
Fibrosis
qs.e: Only cellular adaptation, reversible injury, and cell death are given as cellular responses.

qs.q: A photo of wasted/thinning legs was used in lecture to illustrate which adaptation?
c: Atrophy
Hypertrophy
Hyperplasia
Metaplasia
qs.e: The leg muscle photo demonstrates atrophy (decrease in cell/tissue size).

qs.q: A flexed muscular arm was shown in lecture to illustrate which adaptation?
c: Hypertrophy
Atrophy
Hyperplasia
Dysplasia
qs.e: The enlarged, flexed muscle arm represents hypertrophy.

qs.q: Left ventricular hypertrophy, shown in a heart cross-section, is an example of:
c: Hypertrophy — enlargement of cells/organ
Hyperplasia — increase in cell number
Metaplasia — change in cell type
Atrophy — shrinkage of cells
qs.e: The enlarged heart wall shown is an example of hypertrophy of the left ventricle.

qs.q: An enlarged prostate compressing the urethra, shown in the diagram, is an example of:
c: Hyperplasia
Hypertrophy
Metaplasia
Atrophy
qs.e: The normal vs. enlarged prostate diagram is used to illustrate hyperplasia.

qs.q: A change from normal columnar epithelium to squamous epithelium is an example of:
c: Metaplasia
Hypertrophy
Hyperplasia
Atrophy
qs.e: The diagram shows normal columnar epithelium converting to squamous metaplasia.

qs.q: Select ALL examples of cellular adaptation types shown in these slides.
c: Atrophy
Hypertrophy
Hyperplasia
Metaplasia
Dysplasia
Cancer
qs.e: The adaptation diagram on Slide 79 lists atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, metaplasia, and dysplasia as adaptation types; cancer appears on Slide 100 only as a later progression, not as an adaptation.

qs.q: According to the diagram of ciliated epithelium, dysplasia results from:
c: Persistent severe injury or irritation
A single brief episode of irritation
Normal aging
Increased ATP production
qs.e: The sequence shows chronic injury/irritation causing metaplasia and persistent severe injury/irritation causing dysplasia.

qs.q: In the progression diagram, the abnormal change that can advance to cancer is ______.
qs.e: Slide 100 shows normal cell → hypertrophy/hyperplasia → dysplasia → cancer.

qs.q: Per the definition shown in the slide, osmosis is:
c: Diffusion of molecules from a place of higher concentration to a place of lower concentration until concentration on both sides is equal
Active transport of molecules using ATP against a gradient
Movement of only water molecules through a pump
Random movement of ions with no concentration difference
qs.e: The slide defines osmosis as diffusion from higher to lower concentration until equilibrium is reached.

qs.q: Select ALL statements consistent with the concentration gradient/diffusion slides.
c: Molecules move from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration
Movement continues until concentration on both sides is equal
Molecules move from lower to higher concentration without energy
Diffusion is described as moving down the concentration gradient
Diffusion requires the sodium-potassium pump
qs.e: The slides describe movement from higher to lower concentration until equal — i.e., down the concentration gradient; no pump is required.

qs.q: Figure 3-31 is titled 'Methods used for ______ communication.'
qs.e: The figure caption on Slide 61 reads 'Methods used for intercellular communication.'

qs.q: In the cell membrane diagram, the water-insoluble portion of the phospholipid is the:
c: Tails
Heads
Cholesterol layer
Carbohydrate receptor sites
qs.e: The membrane figure labels water-insoluble tails and water-soluble heads.

qs.q: Select ALL structures labeled in the composite cell diagram shown in the lecture.
c: Mitochondrion
Lysosome
Ribosomes
Golgi apparatus
Chloroplast
qs.e: The labeled cell diagram includes mitochondrion, lysosome, ribosomes, Golgi apparatus, nucleus, nucleolus, chromatin, endoplasmic reticulum, centrioles, and pinocytic vessel — no chloroplasts.

qs.q: Why is ongoing cellular replication necessary even in a healthy person?
c: Healthy cells never die but must become larger
New cells replace cells that continually die
Replication prevents all genetic mutations
Replication eliminates the need for differentiation
qs.e: Cells continually die even in healthy people. Ongoing cellular replication supplies replacement cells.

qs.q: What step of cellular replication increases the number of cells?
qs.e: Proliferation increases cell number. It is distinct from differentiation, in which newly formed cells develop specialized capabilities.

qs.q: What step of cellular replication allows new cells to develop unique, specialized capabilities?
qs.e: Differentiation produces more specialized cells. The lecture visual shows newly formed cells passing through levels of differentiation to become mature cells with unique characteristics.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes mitosis in lecture?
c: One somatic parent produces two daughters, each with 46 chromosomes
One germ cell produces gametes with 46 chromosomes each
One somatic parent produces two daughters, each with 23 chromosomes
One germ cell produces regular body cells with 23 pairs of chromosomes
qs.e: Somatic cells are regular body cells and reproduce by mitosis. One parent produces two daughter cells, each intended to match the parent with 46 chromosomes, or 23 pairs.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains meiosis and the chromosome number in fertilization?
c: Derm cells undergo meiosis, producing gametes with 23 pairs each
Germ cells undergo meiosis, producing eggs or sperm with 23 chromosomes each; together they supply 46
Somatic cells undergo meiosis so each gamete can contribute 46 chromosomes
Germ cells undergo mitosis so the zygote will contain 23 chromosomes
qs.e: Germ cells form gametes by meiosis; each gamete supplies 23 chromosomes, not 23 pairs. The notes explicitly correct the instructor's spoken 'derm cells' to 'germ cells.'

qs.q: Which order matches the lecture's ranking of influences on proliferation?
c: Situational factors → genetic programming → cell density–dependent inhibition
Cell density–dependent inhibition → situational factors → genetic programming
Genetic programming → cell density–dependent inhibition → situational factors
Genetic programming → situational factors → cell density–dependent inhibition
qs.e: Genetic programming is the primary influence on how often a cell divides. The lecture lists cell density–dependent inhibition second and situational factors third.

qs.q: Which comparison matches the normal division rates given in lecture?
c: Liver cells: twice daily; GI epithelial cells: once every 1–2 years
Liver cells: once every 1–2 years; GI epithelial cells: two or more times daily
Liver cells and GI epithelial cells: once every 1–2 years
Liver cells and GI epithelial cells: two or more times daily
qs.e: Different cell types have genetically programmed division rates. The lecture contrasts slowly dividing liver cells with rapidly dividing GI-tract epithelial cells.

qs.q: Cells proliferate to close an arm wound, then slow their proliferation when the wound edges meet. What best explains this response?
c: Crowding activates cell density–dependent inhibition
Crowding causes every cell to undergo meiosis
Contact eliminates the cells' need for oxygen
Contact permanently turns all cells into nerve cells
qs.e: Contact with many surrounding cells signals crowding and slows normal proliferation. Cancer cells lose this cell density–dependent inhibition.

qs.q: Which are situational influences or signals for proliferation listed in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Amount of growth factor present
Availability of hormones
Availability of nutrients
Blood loss or tissue injury
The cell's inherited division schedule, classified as a situational factor
qs.e: Growth factors, hormones, nutrients, and events such as blood loss or injury can influence proliferation. The inherited division schedule belongs to genetic programming, the primary influence, rather than situational factors.

qs.q: Excluding G0, how many main phases does the lecture count in the cell cycle?
qs.e: The four main phases are G1, S, G2, and M. G0 is described as resting outside the cycle.

qs.q: Which description correctly pairs G1 and G2 with their roles?
c: G1 divides the chromosomes; G2 produces gametes
G1 synthesizes only DNA; G2 stops all cell activity
G1 makes proteins, RNA, and organelles; G2 repeats similar preparation
G1 is outside the cycle; G2 is the only preparation phase
qs.e: G1 means Gap 1 and prepares the parent to supply two daughter cells by increasing proteins, RNA, and organelles. G2, or Gap 2, involves similar preparation.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly links cell-cycle errors with their consequences?
c: S-phase errors: unequal chromosome division; M-phase errors: incorrect DNA synthesis
S-phase errors: incorrect DNA replication and certain genetic disorders; M-phase errors: unequal chromosome division and chromosomal disorders
G0 errors: DNA synthesis disorders; G1 errors: all chromosomal disorders
G2 errors: gametes with no DNA; G0 errors: excess organelles
qs.e: S is the synthesis phase, when DNA is replicated. M is mitosis, when the cell divides into two; unequal chromosome distribution during this phase can cause chromosomal disorders.

qs.q: A cell is in G0. Which statement is accurate?
c: It is dead and no longer makes ATP
It is actively preparing to divide
It is resting from replication but remains alive and metabolically active
It is replicating DNA before division
qs.e: G0 means resting from replication, not resting from all cellular activity. The cell remains alive and can make ATP, but it is neither preparing to divide nor dividing.

qs.q: What does the lecture require students to understand about meiosis and the cell cycle at this point?
c: Meiosis has no cell-cycle-like process
Meiosis has a cell-cycle-like process with differing events, but detailed phases are not being tested yet
All meiosis phases are identical to mitosis phases
Meiosis produces cells with 46 chromosomes, so its phases need no study
qs.e: The notes say meiosis has a cell-cycle-like process whose exact events differ from mitosis. The required focus here is the general concept and the 46-versus-23 chromosome distinction.

qs.q: Which changes contribute to abnormal proliferation in cancer? Select all that apply.
c: A higher percentage of cells actively cycling
Fewer cells in G0 than expected
Loss of cell density–dependent inhibition
Failure to die within the normal genetically programmed time frame
Greater sensitivity to crowding that stops tumor growth
qs.e: Cancer combines increased active replication, fewer resting cells, loss of crowding-related inhibition, and prolonged cell survival. Together these promote uncontrolled growth.

qs.q: Which pairing accurately describes cell-cycle-specific chemotherapy?
c: S-phase drugs prevent DNA replication; M-phase drugs prevent division into two cells
S-phase drugs promote DNA replication; M-phase drugs place all cells in G0
S-phase drugs prevent crowding; M-phase drugs create new blood vessels
S-phase drugs only affect resting cells; M-phase drugs prevent RNA synthesis in G1
qs.e: Cell-cycle-specific drugs interfere with events in a particular phase. S-phase drugs often interfere with enzymes needed for DNA replication, while M-phase drugs prevent actual cell division.

qs.q: Which statements explain combination chemotherapy and prolonged treatment in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: An S-phase drug and an M-phase drug can target cancer cells during different phases
Using more than one drug can eliminate more cancer cells than one drug alone
Treatment must last long enough for cancer cells to pass through the targeted phase
A phase-specific drug works equally well in every phase
Long treatment is needed because cancer cells never enter the cell cycle
qs.e: Different phase-specific drugs broaden the opportunities to interrupt replication. Treatment continues long enough to allow, ideally, all cancer cells to cycle through the susceptible phase.

qs.q: Which statements about highly differentiated cells match the lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Nerve, skeletal muscle, and brain cells are examples
They have specialized capabilities, such as conducting action potentials
They are much less able to reproduce than less differentiated cells
Brain cells can reproduce, but at a much slower rate
They are more valuable than stem cells because specialized function is all the body needs
qs.e: Highly differentiated cells perform unique functions but have limited reproductive capacity. The notes reject the old belief that brain cells never reproduce and emphasize that both specialized cells and stem cells are necessary.

qs.q: Which description fits the lecture's mid-level parent/progenitor cells?
c: Skin and liver cells that reproduce more readily but produce only cells of their own type
Nerve cells that normally make RBCs and platelets
Bone-marrow stem cells that can produce only more stem cells
Brain cells that divide faster than skin cells
qs.e: Skin and liver cells are the lecture's parent/progenitor examples; skin cells reproduce especially often. These cells lack the more specialized capabilities of nerve cells, such as conducting action potentials, and produce only their own cell type.

qs.q: Which statements describe fairly undifferentiated bone-marrow stem cells? Select all that apply.
c: They have relatively few specialized capabilities
They can enter the cell cycle and produce large numbers of cells when needed
They can produce RBCs and platelets
They can produce the different types of WBCs
Their only possible product is another stem cell
qs.e: Stem cells are strong replicators despite having few specialized functions. Bone-marrow stem cells can produce multiple kinds of blood cells rather than just another stem cell.

qs.q: If body cells originate from the same zygote and receive essentially the same genes, why do they differ in function and replication rate?
c: Each daughter is supposed to lose most of the parent's chromosomes
Different genes are switched on or off in different cells
Only stem cells contain genes
Differentiation is independent of genetic programming
qs.e: Daughter cells are supposed to receive the same DNA and chromosomes as their parent. Which genes are expressed determines both how often a cell proliferates and how differentiated it becomes.

qs.q: Which situational factors affecting differentiation are specifically listed in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Growth factors
Nutrient availability
Oxygen availability
Cell crowding
Whether somatic cells switch to having 23 chromosomes
qs.e: Growth factors, nutrients, oxygen, and crowding can influence differentiation. These remain secondary to genetic programming and which genes are expressed.

qs.q: Which description best matches the lecture's definition and general nature of cancer?
c: A single disease involving useful growth and normal differentiation
Excessive, inappropriate tissue growth that serves no useful purpose, harms the host, and continues
Any temporary increase in cells needed to heal a wound
An increase in specialized cells with no change in proliferation
qs.e: Cancer involves abnormal proliferation and abnormal differentiation. It includes many diseases, such as skin, lung, and bone cancers, with unique features as well as shared characteristics.

qs.q: What term means a change in a person's genes?
qs.e: A mutation is a change; a genetic mutation is a change in genes. The lecture identifies genetic mutations as the current explanation for the origin of cancer cells.

qs.q: Which sequence matches the lecture's explanation of how cancer develops?
c: Gene mutation → altered genetic programming → abnormal proliferation and differentiation → cancer
Cell crowding → stronger inhibition → normal wound closure → cancer
Normal differentiation → loss of all genes → cancer
G0 entry → no cellular activity → cancer
qs.e: Genetic programming controls both proliferation and differentiation. A mutation can change that programming and disrupt both processes, resulting in cancer.

qs.q: Which statement best summarizes the lecture's approach to cancer risk?
c: Most cancers arise from exactly one risk factor
Additional risk factors do not affect likelihood once one is present
Most cancers reflect a combination of factors, and more factors increase likelihood
Every cancer type is linked to exactly the same factors to the same degree
qs.e: Most cancers are associated with a combination of risk factors rather than one factor alone. Different cancer types may be more closely related to different factors.

qs.q: What term means something that can cause cancer?
qs.e: A carcinogen is something that can cause cancer. The notes list environmental and chemical exposures as examples.

qs.q: Which carcinogen examples are listed in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Radiation, including radiation from the sun
Tobacco smoke
Asbestos
Toxic chemicals
The common cold
qs.e: Radiation, tobacco smoke, asbestos, and toxic chemicals are the listed examples. The notes specifically state that a cold does not increase cancer risk.

qs.q: How do the notes link environmental carcinogens, free radicals, and cancer risk?
c: Free radicals donate genes that always restore normal growth
Carcinogens generate free radicals that steal electrons; damage to DNA can cause mutations that predispose to cancer
Free radicals stop all cell division without affecting DNA
Carcinogens cause cancer only by increasing normal negative feedback
qs.e: Free radicals steal electrons from cellular components and cause damage. If genes or DNA are affected, a resulting mutation may predispose the person to cancer, depending on the mutation.

qs.q: What exposure-to-diagnosis latency range, in years, is often given for cancer in the lecture?
qs.e: The notes give a latency of often 5–30 years, which can make the original exposure difficult to trace. The instructor's example describes an uncle who smoked for about two decades and was diagnosed roughly 30 years after quitting.

qs.q: Which virus–cancer associations match the notes? Select all that apply.
c: HPV → cervical cancer in women
Hepatitis B → liver cancer
Hepatitis C → liver cancer
Epstein–Barr virus → certain lymphomas
Influenza → increased cancer risk
qs.e: The lecture links specific viruses to specific cancers: HPV to cervical cancer, hepatitis B and C to liver cancer, and Epstein–Barr virus to certain lymphomas. It explicitly excludes ordinary colds and flu as cancer-risk examples.

qs.q: What replication difference between viruses and bacteria is emphasized in lecture?
c: Both must incorporate DNA into a host cell before any replication
Bacteria can replicate on their own outside body cells, whereas viruses must use a host cell's machinery
Viruses replicate independently, whereas bacteria cannot
Neither can replicate in or outside body cells
qs.e: The lecture contrasts bacteria's ability to replicate independently outside body cells with viruses' dependence on a host. Viruses must enter cells and use their machinery to reproduce.

qs.q: In the lecture's viral life-cycle model, how can a cancer-causing virus alter the host cell?
c: Viral DNA enters host DNA, producing combined DNA that directs viral production and changes host genetic programming
The virus removes every host chromosome and prevents all protein production
The virus remains outside the cell and directly creates daughter cells
Viral DNA strengthens cell density–dependent inhibition without changing host genes
qs.e: The illustrated sequence is viral entry, incorporation of viral DNA into host DNA, and use of DNA instructions to produce more virus. The notes treat this insertion as a genetic mutation that can alter proliferation and differentiation.

qs.q: What hypothesis proposes that the immune system normally recognizes and eliminates developing cancer cells before they establish themselves?
qs.e: This hypothesis proposes that cancer cells probably arise continually in everyone's body. An impaired immune system may fail to recognize or eliminate them before they grow and cause problems.

qs.q: Which observations support the immune surveillance hypothesis in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: People with immunodeficiency disorders such as AIDS have higher cancer incidence
People taking immunosuppressive drugs have higher cancer incidence
Older people have higher cancer incidence as immune efficiency declines
A common cold is described as a cancer-causing virus
Immune defects guarantee that every abnormal cell will be eliminated
qs.e: The lecture cites higher cancer incidence with immunodeficiency, immunosuppressive therapy, and aging. Each is consistent with reduced immune recognition or elimination of abnormal cells.

qs.q: Which cancer-related mutation can be inherited by a child according to lecture?
c: A mutation confined to the parent's liver cells
A mutation confined to the parent's skin cells
A mutation in an egg or sperm that contributes to the child
Any mutation anywhere in a parent's body
qs.e: A mutation in a germ cell can be passed to a child and increase cancer risk. A mutation confined to somatic cells may harm that person but is not passed to children.

qs.q: Which clinical example illustrates the lecture's discussion of highly hereditary cancer risk?
c: Women carrying a mutation for a particular breast cancer may choose preventive mastectomies
All women with any mutation must wait for cancer before acting
Somatic skin mutations are routinely passed to every child
Preventive surgery eliminates the need to consider inherited mutations
qs.e: The lecture describes a particular breast cancer with such strong hereditary risk that carriers may undergo preventive mastectomies. This illustrates a preventive response to an inherited cancer-causing mutation.

qs.q: Why are extra cancer cells harmful rather than useful backup cells?
c: They improve the normal cells' access to blood
They crowd out normal cells and take blood supply, oxygen, and nutrients needed for normal function
They always become fully functional replacement cells
They restore normal tissue architecture by increasing cohesiveness
qs.e: Uncontrolled growth crowds out normal cells and diverts their blood supply. Deprived of oxygen and nutrients, normal cells can no longer function properly.

qs.q: Why can abnormal differentiation in liver or renal cancer eventually lead to organ failure?
c: Cancer cells specialize more effectively than normal cells
Cancer cells fail to perform the normal functions of the tissue they arise in
All cancer cells become normal liver cells regardless of location
Organ failure occurs only when cancer cells stop proliferating
qs.e: Cancer cells do not specialize properly and cannot perform the tissue's usual functions. The lecture gives liver failure and renal failure as examples and says to expect dysfunction in the affected organ.

qs.q: What term describes cancer cells spreading to other body sites and establishing cancers there?
qs.e: Normal cells tend to stick together, but cancer cells lose cell-to-cell cohesiveness. They can break away, travel through blood or lymph, and establish cancers elsewhere.

qs.q: What abbreviation identifies the tumor-produced factor called vascular endothelial cell growth factor in lecture?
qs.e: VEGF promotes the growth of new blood vessels. In the lecture's word breakdown, vascular means blood vessel, endothelial cells line blood vessels, and a growth factor promotes growth.

qs.q: How does VEGF help a tumor continue to grow?
c: It eliminates the tumor's need for oxygen and nutrients
It promotes new blood vessels, increasing supply as the tumor would otherwise outgrow its blood supply
It restores normal cell-to-cell cohesiveness
It prevents every cancer cell from entering S phase
qs.e: A tumor's growth is limited if it outgrows its blood supply. By promoting new vessels, VEGF increases access to oxygen and nutrients and supports continued growth.

qs.q: What does 'ectopic' mean, as illustrated by the lecture's pregnancy example?
c: In an abnormal location, such as an embryo in a fallopian tube rather than the uterus
Growing at a normal genetically programmed rate
Producing only cells identical to the parent
Regulated by normal negative feedback
qs.e: Ectopic means in an abnormal location. The notes use an embryo outside the uterus, such as in a fallopian tube, to illustrate the term.

qs.q: What are ectopic hormones in the lecture's cancer discussion?
c: Hormones produced only by their usual endocrine glands
Hormones produced by cancer cells rather than by the endocrine glands that should produce them
Growth factors that always stop blood vessel growth
Hormones that cancer cells make only when negative feedback permits
qs.e: Ectopic hormone production occurs at an abnormal source: cancer cells rather than the appropriate endocrine gland. This production can disrupt hormone balance.

qs.q: Which statements explain the hormone imbalance caused by ectopic hormone production? Select all that apply.
c: Normal endocrine glands are regulated by negative feedback
Negative feedback helps prevent normal endocrine glands from overproducing
Cancer cells producing ectopic hormones are not regulated by this feedback
Cancer cells may continue producing hormone despite an already high amount
Ectopic hormone production always stops as soon as the body's needs are met
qs.e: Normal negative feedback limits endocrine hormone production. Cancer cells disregard that regulation, so continued ectopic production can cause hormone imbalance.

qs.q: What term means “in an abnormal location,” as when an embryo is in a fallopian tube rather than the uterus?
qs.e: Ectopic describes an abnormal location. In ectopic hormone production, cancer cells rather than the usual endocrine glands produce hormones.

qs.q: Why can ectopic hormone production make a cancer patient appear to have an endocrine disease?
c: Cancer cells follow negative feedback more closely than endocrine glands.
Cancer cells produce hormones without feedback regulation, usually causing excess.
Cancer cells stop all hormone production by endocrine glands.
Cancer cells produce hormones only when existing levels are low.
qs.e: Normal endocrine glands are regulated by negative feedback. Cancer cells are not regulated by that feedback and can continue producing hormones despite already high levels.

qs.q: Which hormone-like substances do many lung cancers produce in the lecture examples? Select all that apply.
c: ACTH
ADH
PSA
PTH
CEA
qs.e: The notes identify ACTH, antidiuretic hormone (ADH), and parathyroid hormone (PTH) as classic examples. PSA and CEA are discussed as cancer markers instead.

qs.q: Why is a sore that does not heal included among cancer warning signs?
c: Cancer-associated enzymes or toxins can damage tissue that then fails to heal normally.
All nonhealing sores prove that cancer is present.
Cancer cells always form a protective capsule around wounds.
Ectopic hormones always prevent skin growth.
qs.e: Enzymes or toxins released by cancer cells can damage tissue and interfere with normal healing. The notes associate these nonhealing sores with various skin cancers, not with a definitive diagnosis from the sore alone.

qs.q: What does PSA stand for?
qs.e: PSA is prostate-specific antigen. The notes locate it on the cell membrane of some prostate-cancer cells and describe measuring it in blood to follow an established cancer.

qs.q: Which statements about abnormal cancer antigens match the lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Many poorly differentiated cancer cells have abnormal membrane antigens.
CEA stands for carcinoembryonic antigen.
CEA occurs in certain colon, gastric, pancreatic, and breast cancers.
PSA occurs on every cancer cell regardless of its origin.
These markers help monitor progression and evaluate treatment.
qs.e: Abnormal membrane antigens can serve as clinical markers for following cancer. CEA is associated with the listed GI cancers and certain breast cancers, while PSA is associated with some prostate-cancer cells.

qs.q: According to this lecture, why should PSA and CEA NOT be used to diagnose or screen for cancer?
c: They are always absent in advanced cancers.
They cannot be measured more than once.
They are unreliable for those purposes, may occur in noncancerous conditions, and may appear only when cancer is advanced.
They identify only the patient's chromosome count.
qs.e: The lecture explicitly reserves these markers for monitoring progression, evaluating treatment, and detecting possible recurrence. Their occurrence in noncancerous conditions and possible late appearance make them unsuitable for diagnosis or screening in this course's framework.

qs.q: A man has biopsy-confirmed prostate cancer. PSA remains high or rises after one chemotherapy drug, then drops after a replacement drug. What is the lecture's interpretation?
c: The first drug is working; stop the replacement.
Neither PSA result provides information about treatment response.
The falling PSA establishes the original diagnosis.
The first drug is not working; continue the replacement because the falling PSA suggests it is working.
qs.e: The notes use serial PSA measurements to evaluate treatment after biopsy has established the diagnosis. Persistently high or rising PSA prompts a drug change, while falling PSA supports continuing the new drug.

qs.q: Which actions or interpretations fit the lecture's PSA follow-up example after remission? Select all that apply.
c: Obtain periodic blood measurements.
Every 6 months for the first couple of years is the example schedule.
A rise about 5 years later raises concern for recurrence and calls for evaluation.
A later PSA rise alone definitively diagnoses recurrent cancer.
Monitoring can help detect possible recurrence.
qs.e: The notes give these intervals as examples, not universal schedules. A later PSA rise suggests that cancer may have returned and warrants checking it out rather than declaring a diagnosis from the marker alone.

qs.q: What term means the weight loss or wasting commonly seen in advanced cancer?
qs.e: Cachexia refers to weight loss and wasting, with advanced-cancer patients often becoming very thin. Anorexia instead means loss of appetite.

qs.q: Which explanation correctly connects the two taught mechanisms of cancer-related wasting?
c: Cancer steals nutrients and blood supply, while immune cytokines can reduce appetite.
Cachexia causes cancer cells to stop taking nutrients, while cytokines increase appetite.
Anorexia means low RBCs, while cachexia means loss of appetite.
Cancer-related wasting results only from chemotherapy.
qs.e: Cancer cells take blood supply and nutrients from surrounding normal cells. WBC-made cytokines help the immune response but can also cause anorexia, so the patient may be unable to eat even favorite foods.

qs.q: Which mechanisms are taught as possible causes of cancer pain? Select all that apply.
c: Tumor pressure on nerve endings
Pressure on vessels reducing tissue blood and oxygen supply
Tissue damage from cancer-associated enzymes or toxins
Possible direct release of chemical mediators of pain associated with cancer
Normal differentiation of a benign tumor necessarily causing generalized pain
qs.e: Pressure, reduced perfusion, and tissue damage can all produce pain. The notes also describe a view held by some experts that cancer directly promotes release of chemical pain mediators.

qs.q: What nursing challenge does the lecture emphasize when controlling pain near the end of life?
c: Pain medication always restores alertness.
Adequate pain relief may require medication amounts that cause sedation, conflicting with desired awake time with family.
End-stage patients never want pain medication.
Pain control is unnecessary when treatment cannot cure cancer.
qs.e: Cancer pain can be difficult to control without sedation. Patients may not want to sleep through their remaining time with family, creating a challenging care balance.

qs.q: What term means lower-than-normal RBCs or hemoglobin?
qs.e: Anemia is a reduction below normal in RBCs or hemoglobin. In cancer, it can result from the disease itself or its treatment.

qs.q: Which sequence correctly explains cancer-associated anemia from nutrition and blood loss?
c: Anorexia improves nutrition; tumor erosion prevents bleeding.
Poor nutrition causes only appetite loss, never anemia.
Anorexia can cause iron or B-vitamin deficiencies; toxin-damaged tissue and tumors eroding vessels can bleed.
Cancer anemia requires bone marrow metastasis in every case.
qs.e: The notes identify iron and B-vitamin deficiencies from poor intake as causes of anemia. They also identify bleeding from damaged tissue and larger blood losses when growing tumors erode blood vessels.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe marrow-related anemia and the distinction between benign and malignant growths? Select all that apply.
c: Bone marrow metastasis can prevent adequate RBC production.
Chemotherapy or radiation can suppress marrow and cause anemia.
Benign growths have abnormal proliferation but normal differentiation.
Malignant growths have abnormalities of both proliferation and differentiation.
A benign growth is cancerous if its proliferation is abnormal.
qs.e: Both cancer in marrow and treatment-related marrow suppression can cause anemia. Benign tumors are noncancerous and have normal differentiation; malignant tumors have abnormalities in both processes.

qs.q: Which growth pattern and image description best distinguish benign from malignant tumors in lecture?
c: Benign tumors metastasize; malignant tumors remain encapsulated.
Both always have capsules and grow only by expansion.
Benign tumors lack capsules and send tentacles into normal tissue.
Benign tumors expand and are frequently encapsulated; malignant tumors lack a capsule, infiltrate with tentacle-like extensions, and can metastasize.
qs.e: The benign image shows a contained lighter mass against reddish tissue, while the malignant image shows extensions into yellowish normal tissue. Malignant tumors may also expand, but invasion and metastasis distinguish them from benign expansion.

qs.q: Why is surgery generally easier to complete confidently for a benign tumor than for a malignant tumor?
c: A benign tumor's frequent capsule helps contain it; malignant extensions can leave cells behind that multiply and cause recurrence.
Benign tumors always disappear without removal.
Malignant cells cannot replicate after surgery.
A malignant tumor's thick capsule makes its boundary clearer.
qs.e: A contained benign tumor is easier to shell out completely. Malignant tumors infiltrate surrounding tissue, making it harder to know whether every cell has been removed.

qs.q: Which comparison of tumor products and effects matches the lecture?
c: Benign tumors routinely produce ectopic hormones and cause cachexia.
Benign problems are local and they do not make the listed VEGF, ectopic hormones, or damaging enzymes/toxins; malignant tumors can make these and cause systemic effects.
Malignant tumors cause only local pressure, never organ failure.
Benign and malignant tumors have identical effects because differentiation is normal in both.
qs.e: Benign problems arise from the growing mass rather than failed differentiation. Malignancy can involve cachexia, anemia, pain, organ failure, and metastasis, as well as the abnormal substances listed.

qs.q: Which statements about tumor lethality and surgical treatment match the notes? Select all that apply.
c: Uncontrolled malignant cancer will kill.
Benign tumors usually do not kill unless their size or location interferes with vital functions.
A benign brain tumor can compress tissue involved in breathing, heart rate, or blood pressure regulation.
Cancer surgery is almost always combined with radiation and/or chemotherapy because residual cells may remain.
Removing a cancer leaves its ability to steal local nutrients and blood unchanged.
qs.e: Benign does not mean harmless in every location, particularly within the brain. Removing cancer removes its local harmful effects, but the possibility of residual malignant cells explains combined treatment.
