qs.q: How does radiation treat cancer, and why can it still be useful despite harming nearby normal cells?
c: It creates a capsule, affecting only slowly dividing cells.
It blocks all hormone receptors without damaging cells.
It generates free radicals that kill cells or prevent replication, with rapidly proliferating cells usually most affected.
It repairs malignant DNA and never affects normal tissue.
qs.e: Radiation-generated free radicals can kill cancer cells outright or damage them so they cannot replicate. Nearby normal cells may also be exposed, but rapidly proliferating cells—usually the cancer cells—are most affected.

qs.q: Which description of chemotherapy matches the lecture?
c: It works only on tumor capsules and has no systemic effects.
Many drugs block events in a specific cell-cycle phase; usual oral or IV delivery exposes noncancer cells as well.
All drugs work by supplying intact chromosomes.
It preferentially affects the least proliferative cells.
qs.e: Chemotherapy may interfere with enzymes, DNA, protein, or the actual division into two cells during particular phases. Because exposure is not limited to cancer cells, side effects are almost always expected, though rapidly proliferating cancer cells are usually most affected.

qs.q: What treatment irony and decision tradeoff does the instructor emphasize?
c: Radiation and toxic drugs can predispose to a different cancer later, but treating an otherwise fatal cancer may buy additional time.
Radiation prevents all future cancers, so no risk discussion is needed.
Chemotherapy has no relationship to cancer-causing exposures.
Patients always reject treatment after hearing about later cancer risk.
qs.e: Radiation and toxic chemicals are both treatments and items on the list of possible cancer causes. The notes emphasize explaining the later risk while recognizing that most people still choose the potential additional time treatment offers.

qs.q: Which descriptions of newer cancer treatments match the awareness-level material? Select all that apply.
c: A biologic response modifier changes a biologic response, mostly an immune response, to improve cancer removal.
An immunomodulator changes the immune system and is essentially the same idea as a biologic response modifier.
A monoclonal antibody is a man-made, cloned antibody aimed at a specific disease-causing substance.
Synthetic cytokines are man-made versions of WBC-produced substances intended to improve immune responses.
Synthetic cytokines are tightly wound DNA molecules containing many genes.
qs.e: These therapies aim to modify immune responses or target a specific culprit substance. The lecture introduces the terms for awareness rather than as a full drug list.

qs.q: What is the full name of DNA?
qs.e: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It is a complex molecule that stores genetic information.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes DNA's structure and genetic code?
c: DNA contains chains of proteins, with genetic information only in their length.
DNA consists of chromosomes that each contain exactly one base.
DNA, genes, and chromosomes are identical-size structures.
DNA contains chains of nucleotides with four possible nitrogenous bases; the bases' identity, order, and quantity form the code.
qs.e: The four bases are represented by A, C, G, and T. DNA, genes, and chromosomes are closely related but refer to different-sized chunks of genetic material.

qs.q: Which statements match the notes' account of the route from genetic information to protein? Select all that apply.
c: RNA carries the genetic code into the cytoplasm.
Ribosomes use the code to make proteins.
The code is read in groups of three.
Proteins consist of amino acids arranged according to the instructions.
Each codon represents an entire chromosome.
qs.e: The notes describe a DNA-to-RNA step followed by RNA carrying the code to cytoplasmic ribosomes. Ordered codons specify which amino acids are needed, their order, and their quantity in a protein.

qs.q: What is the name for a three-base unit of genetic code that represents one specific amino acid?
qs.e: The genetic code is a triplet code: three bases form a codon. Each codon represents one specific amino acid in lecture' description.

qs.q: Which description of a gene is most consistent with this class?
c: It is one nitrogenous base with no protein instructions.
It is instructions for a particular protein, although the notes acknowledge that some complex proteins require more than one gene.
It always contains exactly 46 chromosomes.
It is an antibody designed to attack a protein.
qs.e: The course's useful shorthand is that a gene supplies instructions for making a particular protein. The notes qualify the older one-gene/one-protein idea by stating that some large or complicated proteins need more than one gene.

qs.q: How do genes, DNA molecules, and chromosomes relate structurally in lecture?
c: Genes joined end to end make a long DNA molecule, which winds tightly around a protein core to form a chromosome containing many genes.
Each chromosome is a single free nucleotide.
DNA is formed by attaching 46 protein cores to one codon.
Chromosomes contain no DNA once they are tightly wound.
qs.e: Genes joined end to end form a large DNA molecule. Repeated tight winding of that molecule around a protein core produces a chromosome with many genes.

qs.q: Which chromosome arrangement is typical of most body cells in these notes?
c: 23 chromosomes total, all from one parent
46 pairs, one pair per protein
46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, with one member of each pair from each parent
22 chromosomes plus 23 sex chromosomes
qs.e: Most body cells contain 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs. One chromosome in each pair comes from the mother and the other from the father.

qs.q: What are the 22 chromosome pairs that are alike in males and females called?
qs.e: Twenty-two of the 23 pairs are autosomes. The 23rd pair consists of sex chromosomes: XY for males and XX for females in lecture.

qs.q: A karyotype shows XY sex chromosomes. Which interpretation matches the notes?
c: Female genotype; sex is determined by the autosomes alone.
Male genotype; the 23 chromosome pairs collectively contain the protein instructions for one unique person.
Male genotype; only the Y chromosome carries protein instructions.
Female genotype; all 46 chromosomes are sex chromosomes.
qs.e: The notes identify XY as a male genotype and XX as female. All genes across the full chromosome set together provide the genetic information for one unique person.

qs.q: Which pairings correctly reproduce the lecture's letter-and-book analogy? Select all that apply.
c: Alphabet letters → nitrogenous bases A, C, G, T
Words → codons of three bases representing amino acids
Sentences → genes providing protein instructions
Wound-up paragraph/story → chromosome; whole book → the 46 chromosomes in a cell
Whole book → a single nitrogenous base
qs.e: The analogy builds from bases to codons to genes to chromosomes. The complete set of 46 chromosomes represents the whole book of genetic information for one person.

qs.q: Which pair of roles does the lecture assign to genes?
c: Only determining visible traits and producing tumor capsules
Only storing blood and controlling appetite
Directly carrying oxygen and removing free radicals
Regulating protein synthesis to control cell function and determining inheritance of physical, biochemical, and physiologic traits
qs.e: Proteins form cell parts and perform functions such as enzyme activity, so instructions for proteins control cell function. Inherited traits include hair and eye color, metabolic rate, and predisposition to diseases such as cancer.

qs.q: Who proposed the basic inheritance laws published around 1865 that are still taught under his name?
qs.e: Mendel's laws were published around 1865, approximately the time of the Civil War. The notes say the basic patterns are still taught essentially as he proposed them.

qs.q: In the lecture's basic Mendelian model, why does a zygote have two genes for each trait, and what are the members of a gene pair called?
c: It receives both from the father; they are codons.
It receives neither from its parents; they are cytokines.
Egg and sperm contribute one member of each chromosome pair, giving a maternal and paternal gene; the pair's members are alleles.
It has 46 chromosome pairs; their members are antigens.
qs.e: Egg and sperm unite to form a zygote with 23 chromosome pairs. In this introductory model, traits such as eye or hair color have two genes, one from each parent, called alleles.

qs.q: Using the lecture's simplified eye-color example, what happens when one brown-eye dominant allele is paired with one blue-eye recessive allele?
c: Brown eyes result because the dominant allele is more influential and is expressed.
Blue eyes result because a recessive allele overrides a dominant allele.
Neither allele can be expressed unless they match.
The person has no eye-color alleles to pass on.
qs.e: A dominant allele is the more influential member of the pair for determining the trait. In the lecture's example, brown is expressed when brown and blue alleles occur together.

qs.q: With uppercase A representing dominant and lowercase a representing recessive, which classification and expression rule are correct?
c: AA is heterozygous; recessive traits appear whenever A is present.
Aa is homozygous; dominant traits appear only in AA.
aa is heterozygous; neither allele is expressed.
AA and aa are homozygous; Aa is heterozygous; dominant traits appear in AA or Aa, while recessive traits appear only in aa.
qs.e: Homozygous means the two alleles are the same, and heterozygous means they differ. A recessive trait is expressed only without a dominant allele, so the lecture's blue-eye example requires two recessive alleles.

qs.q: What term describes a person who can pass on a disease-associated allele without having symptoms themselves?
qs.e: The lecture's formal carrier definition is someone who can pass on a disease but has no symptoms. Its introductory analogy is a brown-eyed heterozygous person who carries and can pass on the blue-eye allele.

qs.q: Why does a chromosome disorder usually cause a larger number of kinds of problems than a gene disorder?
c: Chromosomes contain fewer instructions than genes.
A chromosome is a larger chunk of genetic material containing many genes; more kinds of problems does not necessarily mean greater severity.
A gene disorder always affects every chromosome.
Chromosome disorders are never genetic.
qs.e: Genes and chromosomes are both genetic material, but a chromosome contains many genes. The notes distinguish a greater number of kinds of problems from necessarily more serious or severe problems.

qs.q: Which statements describe the origin of gene disorders as taught in this lecture? Select all that apply.
c: They result from mutations, meaning changes in genes.
Inaccurate DNA replication during meiosis can produce a mutation.
Radiation, toxic chemicals, or other environmental factors can sometimes contribute.
A mutation may arise spontaneously with no known cause, described as a “metabolic accident.”
Every mutation has an identifiable environmental cause.
qs.e: The notes describe mutations arising when DNA is not copied accurately during meiosis. Some have environmental contributors, but many have no known cause and may occur spontaneously.

qs.q: Which mutation is called a gene disorder under the lecture's specific definition?
c: Any mutation in a regular body cell, whether inherited or not
Only a mutation caused by radiation
A mutation in a germ cell that can be passed to the next generation
Only a mutation affecting every chromosome
qs.e: For this lecture, gene disorders involve germ-cell mutations that can be passed on. A regular body-cell mutation can cause problems but is not called a gene disorder in this discussion.

qs.q: What defines a single-gene disorder in the material covered by this class?
c: A mutation in one gene in a germ cell that is then passed on
A mutation in every gene on one chromosome
A change in all chromosomes of a regular body cell
A normal protein made by several unaltered genes
qs.e: A single-gene disorder involves one faulty gene among all the genes in all the chromosomes. Multigene mistakes also exist, but their inheritance is more complicated and is outside this class's stated coverage.

qs.q: Which conclusions follow from the lecture's explanation of single-gene disorders? Select all that apply.
c: The protein specified by the affected gene may be missing.
The specified protein may be defective or nonworking.
Assessment findings depend on which protein the gene codes for.
There is no blanket symptom list for all single-gene disorders.
All single-gene disorders necessarily cause the same clinical findings.
qs.e: A gene provides instructions for a particular protein, so a faulty gene can lead to an absent or defective protein. The clinical findings depend on that protein rather than following one universal symptom pattern.

qs.q: What defines the inherited single-gene disorders covered in this class?
c: A mutation in one gene in a germ cell that is passed to the next generation
Errors in every gene on one chromosome
A mutation affecting only a somatic cell and never passed on
A disorder that always requires mutations in several genes
qs.e: These disorders involve one defective gene passed on through a germ cell. Multigene disorders exist, but their more complicated inheritance is outside this class's focus.

qs.q: Which statements about single-gene disorders match the notes? Select all that apply.
c: The encoded protein may be missing or nonfunctional.
Every disorder has the same assessment findings.
Severity may range from very mild to fatal.
Interventions target the particular disorder's symptoms.
Current treatment routinely fixes the underlying mutation.
qs.e: Findings depend on which protein is affected and how crucial it is to normal function. The notes describe symptom-directed care, not an available method for fixing the mutation.

qs.q: The three primary Mendelian inheritance patterns in lecture are distinguished by which two features?
c: Protein size and age at diagnosis
Sex chromosome versus autosome, and dominant versus recessive trait
Number of symptoms and treatment duration
Chromosome length and cell division speed
qs.e: Single-gene disorders closely follow Mendelian patterns. Gene location and dominance distinguish X-linked, autosomal dominant, and autosomal recessive inheritance.

qs.q: Which explanation for the distribution of sex-linked disorders is given in lecture?
c: They are more common because there are 22 pairs of sex chromosomes.
They usually involve Y because everyone has a Y.
They are less common than autosomal disorders because there are 22 autosomal pairs but only one sex-chromosome pair; sex-linked defects usually involve X.
They are equally likely to involve X and Y because both contain identical genes.
qs.e: The notes explain that a random gene error is more likely to involve an autosome. They call sex-linked disorders X-linked because everyone has an X, whereas only males have a Y.

qs.q: Which statements explain the usual X-linked recessive pattern? Select all that apply.
c: Most sex-linked disorders are recessive.
A recessive defect is expressed when no normal dominant gene overrides it.
A female with one normal X and one defective X is usually an asymptomatic carrier.
A male with a defective X usually has the disease because he lacks a second X.
The smaller Y always supplies a normal matching gene for every X gene.
qs.e: Males usually have the disease and females are usually carriers. X has more than a thousand additional genes absent from the smaller Y; a female with two defective X chromosomes is described as rare and excluded from the instructor's test.

qs.q: Hemophilia A, identified in lecture as the most common X-linked disorder, involves a defective gene for which clotting factor?
qs.e: The affected gene provides instructions for Factor VIII. Associated findings include bruising, bleeding into muscles, and bleeding into joints with joint swelling.

qs.q: Which description of autosomal dominant inheritance is correct?
c: Sex determines expression, and two defective genes are required.
One defective dominant gene on an autosome is enough for disease, regardless of sex.
A person with one defective dominant gene is always an asymptomatic carrier.
Only aa individuals have the disease.
qs.e: The defective gene is on an autosome and is dominant, so one copy produces disease. There are no carriers in the pattern described: a carrier passes a defect without symptoms, whereas an affected person has symptoms.

qs.q: On this instructor's test, how should you diagram an affected autosomal dominant parent and an unaffected parent, respectively?
c: AA and Aa
aa and AA
Aa and aa
Aa and AA
qs.e: Use Aa for an affected parent unless two defective genes are specifically stated; aa represents two normal recessive genes. AA is theoretically affected but uncommon, requires both parents to pass the defect, and produces a more severe form; the notes say most such couples choose not to have children.

qs.q: Which findings are associated with Marfan syndrome in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Long, thin limbs and fingers with chest or spinal deformities
Detached retinas and dislocated lenses associated with weak ligaments
Heart valve prolapse and a tendency toward aneurysms
A defect involving connective-tissue instructions, producing multisystem findings
Factor VIII deficiency as the underlying defect
qs.e: Connective tissue is distributed throughout the body, so Marfan syndrome affects multiple systems. The notes include scoliosis or a hunchback appearance among the skeletal findings.

qs.q: Which genotype mapping is correct for an autosomal recessive disorder?
c: aa = disease; Aa = asymptomatic carrier; AA = unaffected noncarrier
AA = disease; Aa = disease; aa = unaffected noncarrier
Aa = disease; aa = carrier; AA = unaffected noncarrier
aa = disease; AA = carrier; Aa = unaffected noncarrier
qs.e: Disease requires two defective recessive genes, one inherited from each parent. A normal dominant gene prevents expression in Aa carriers, while AA contains no defective recessive gene.

qs.q: In sickle cell anemia, the defective gene codes for which protein?
qs.e: The notes emphasize that only one amino acid is coded incorrectly, while the others are correct. That single error creates defective hemoglobin.

qs.q: Which sequence explains the pain associated with sickle cell disease in lecture?
c: Defective hemoglobin → sickling under certain conditions → clumping and clots → blood-flow obstruction → pain
Factor VIII deficiency → excess clotting → long thin fingers → pain
Normal hemoglobin → extra chromosomes → muscle bleeding → pain
Sickling → improved blood flow → increased oxygen delivery → pain
qs.e: Under certain conditions, defective hemoglobin makes RBCs sickle-shaped. These cells clump, form clots, and occlude blood flow, causing substantial pain.

qs.q: Anemia caused by the body breaking down its own RBCs is called _____ anemia.
qs.e: The body destroys sickled RBCs because they are not considered normal, and the extra destruction causes anemia. The notes define hemo as blood or hemoglobin and lysis as breaking apart.

qs.q: A person with one defective sickle cell gene has sickle cell _____ rather than sickle cell disease.
qs.e: One defective gene indicates carrier status, called sickle cell trait. Two defective genes produce sickle cell anemia, also called sickle cell disease.

qs.q: Which practices match the instructor's Punnett-square approach? Select all that apply.
c: Use squares in genetic counseling to visualize disease or carrier risk.
Put parental genes on the sides, fill possible child combinations, and calculate risk.
Determine the correct letters, denominator, dominance, and number of defects needed for disease.
Identify which genotypes represent disease, carrier status, and normal status before diagramming parents.
Use uppercase and lowercase A to identify whether an autosomal outcome is a son or daughter.
qs.e: Correctly representing the parents is a common trouble spot, and some nurses perform genetic counseling. X and Y distinguish sex; uppercase and lowercase A do not.

qs.q: Which denominator rule applies to the instructor's test questions?
c: X-linked son or daughter questions: out of 4; autosomal child questions: out of 2
X-linked son or daughter questions: out of 2; autosomal child questions: out of 4
All inheritance questions: out of 2
All inheritance questions: out of 4
qs.e: For X-linked questions, the instructor asks about a specified sex, so consider only its two outcomes: 0/2, 1/2, or 2/2. Autosomal questions use four outcomes, giving possible risks of 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100%.

qs.q: An X-linked carrier mother and a father with normal genes have what risks for a son with disease and a daughter who is a carrier?
c: Son: 100%; daughter: 0%
Son: 0%; daughter: 100%
Son: 50%; daughter: 50%
Son: 25%; daughter: 25%
qs.e: The mother has one defective X and one normal X; the father has a normal X and Y. Half the sons receive the defective maternal X, and half the daughters receive it along with the father's normal X.

qs.q: A mother has two normal X chromosomes, and the father has an X-linked disease. What are the risks for their sons and daughters?
c: All sons affected; no daughters carriers
Half the sons affected; half the daughters carriers
No sons affected; all daughters carriers
All sons affected; all daughters affected
qs.e: The affected father has a defective X and a Y: sons receive his Y, so none are affected in this cross. Every daughter receives his defective X plus a normal maternal X, making carrier risk 2/2, or 100%.

qs.q: For an autosomal dominant cross of Aa × aa, what is the risk that a child has the disease?
c: 0/4, with all children carriers
1/4, with the remainder carriers
2/4, with no carrier category
4/4, with no unaffected children
qs.e: Two of the four combinations are Aa and affected; two are aa and unaffected. For further practice, the notes direct students to “Help with Punnett Squares” in the Class Two, Cell Part Two module, in-class practice, and specific questions on the pre-class exercise.

qs.q: Which statements about chromosome disorders match the notes? Select all that apply.
c: A chromosome is a long DNA molecule containing many genes.
Chromosome disorders usually create more kinds of problems than a single-gene disorder.
Every present gene may be coded correctly, yet missing material or an incorrect chromosome number can still cause disease.
A piece that breaks off and is lost during meiosis removes all genes on that piece.
A chromosome disorder necessarily involves an incorrect amino acid in every protein.
qs.e: Chromosome disorders can involve the amount of genetic material rather than incorrect coding in individual genes. Loss of a chromosome piece eliminates multiple genes at once.

qs.q: What term describes failure of chromosomes to separate equally, leaving one daughter cell with both copies and the other with none?
qs.e: Disjunction is normal equal separation; nondisjunction means that separation did not occur. A normal germ cell receives one copy of each chromosome, which combines with another germ cell's copy to make a pair in the zygote.

qs.q: A germ cell with zero copies of a chromosome combines with a normal germ cell. Which result and usual outcome are described in lecture?
c: Trisomy; usually no abnormalities
Monosomy; severe defects often incompatible with life and resulting in miscarriage
Monosomy; three chromosome copies
Trisomy; one chromosome copy
qs.e: Zero copies plus one normal copy produces a zygote with only one copy, called monosomy. The notes state that these defects are usually severe and the fetus usually does not survive.

qs.q: A germ cell with both copies of chromosome 18 combines with a normal germ cell. What results?
c: Monosomy 18, meaning 18 chromosomes are missing
Trisomy 18, meaning three copies of chromosome 18
Trisomy 3, meaning three different chromosomes are involved
Normal chromosome pairing
qs.e: Two copies plus one normal copy produces trisomy. The number identifies the chromosome with the extra copy; the notes also list trisomy 13 and trisomy 22.

qs.q: Which statements about Down syndrome and the instructor's slide are supported? Select all that apply.
c: Down syndrome is trisomy 21, identified as the most common trisomy.
The illustrated karyotype had three copies of chromosome 21 and pairs of the other chromosomes.
Possible findings include characteristic facial features, intellectual impairment, congenital heart problems, and GI malformations.
The karyotype was XY despite a girl's photograph, illustrating that Y is much smaller than X.
Down syndrome is described as an isolated Factor VIII problem.
qs.e: The extra chromosome produces a constellation of physical and mental abnormalities rather than one isolated protein defect. The instructor specifically noted the mismatch between the photograph and the male karyotype.

qs.q: Which care approach fits chromosomal disorders as described in lecture?
c: Use one universal assessment checklist and repair the chromosome.
Assess according to the chromosome involved, treat symptoms, and support quality of life and development.
Avoid symptom treatment because only mutation correction helps.
Expect all conditions to begin only in adulthood.
qs.e: There are no blanket findings or interventions, and the notes say the chromosome problem cannot currently be fixed. These conditions receive more attention in pediatrics because babies are born with them and families learn how to support care and development.

qs.q: What are the two steps of cellular replication?
qs.e: The notes identify proliferation and differentiation as the two steps. Their primary control is genetic programming—determining which genes are on or off.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly matches division type, cell type, and chromosome number?
c: Mitosis: germ cells, 23; meiosis: somatic cells, 46
Mitosis: somatic cells, 46; meiosis: germ cells, 23
Mitosis: somatic cells, 23 pairs; meiosis: germ cells, 23 pairs
Mitosis: germ cells, 46 pairs; meiosis: somatic cells, 23
qs.e: Mitosis applies to somatic or body cells with 46 chromosomes. Meiosis produces germ cells with 23 chromosomes, not 23 pairs.

qs.q: A normal zygote has how many chromosomes after two germ cells combine?
qs.e: The chromosome math is 23 + 23 = 46, or 23 pairs. Germ cells carry 23 so fertilization does not overload the zygote with chromosomes.

qs.q: Which cell-division timing matches the notes?
c: Liver: twice daily; GI epithelium: every 1–2 years
Liver: every 1–2 years; GI epithelium: two or more times daily
Liver and GI epithelium: every 1–2 years
Liver and GI epithelium: once per month
qs.e: The notes contrast relatively infrequent liver division with frequent GI epithelial division. Liver timing is 1–2 years, while GI epithelium divides 2+ times per day.

qs.q: What does cell density–dependent inhibition mean?
c: Crowding stimulates unlimited division.
Contact or crowding slows division; this restraint is lost in cancer.
Cells stop producing ATP whenever they touch.
Only germ cells respond to neighboring cells.
qs.e: Contact and crowding normally slow cell division. The notes associate this concept with the wound-edge example and emphasize its loss in cancer.

qs.q: Which cell-cycle phase descriptions are correct? Select all that apply.
c: G1: production of proteins, RNA, and organelles
S: DNA synthesis
G2: activities similar to G1
M: cell splitting
G0: DNA synthesis inside the active cycle
qs.e: The notes summarize G1 and G2 as preparatory phases, S as DNA synthesis, and M as splitting. G0 is outside the cycle and represents rest from replication.

qs.q: Which statement about G0 and cancer is correct?
c: G0 cells stop all activity, including ATP production.
Cancer has fewer cells cycling and more in G0.
G0 is rest from replication, not ATP production; cancer has more cycling cells and fewer in G0.
G0 is the phase in which chromosomes split.
qs.e: A cell in G0 remains active enough to make ATP even though it is not replicating. Cancer shifts the distribution toward more cells in the cycle.

qs.q: Which feature of chemotherapy does the rapid-fire bank connect with combination drugs and long treatment courses?
c: Chemotherapy often targets specific cycle phases, such as S versus M.
All chemotherapy works only in G0.
Chemotherapy repairs every defective gene immediately.
All cells remain permanently in the same cycle phase.
qs.e: The notes emphasize that chemotherapy is often cell-cycle specific, including S-phase versus M-phase targeting. They flag this concept as relevant to understanding combination drugs and long courses.

qs.q: Which error-to-disorder pairing matches the notes?
c: S-phase errors → chromosomal disorders; M-phase unequal splitting → gene disorders
S-phase errors → gene disorders; M-phase unequal splitting → chromosomal disorders
G0 ATP production → gene disorders; G1 protein production → trisomy
All replication errors produce only single-gene disorders
qs.e: S is the DNA synthesis phase, so the notes associate its errors with gene disorders. Unequal splitting during M is associated with chromosomal disorders.

qs.q: Which statement best describes reproduction by highly specialized cells in lecture?
c: They reproduce especially well and make all cell types.
They reproduce poorly; brain-cell reproduction is slow, not zero.
They all divide at least twice per day.
They are identical to marrow stem cells in reproductive capacity.
qs.e: The notes caution against saying that brain cells never reproduce. Highly specialized cells reproduce poorly, with brain-cell reproduction described as slow rather than absent.

qs.q: Which statements correctly compare progenitor and stem cells? Select all that apply.
c: Skin and liver are examples associated with progenitor cells.
Progenitor cells reproduce well but make only their own type.
Marrow stem cells can make multiple lineages.
Marrow stem-cell lineages include RBCs, platelets, and all WBCs.
Progenitor cells are described as unable to reproduce.
qs.e: The distinction is breadth of output, not simply whether division occurs. Progenitor cells make their own type, whereas marrow stem cells make many lineages.

qs.q: Nearly every cell has the same genome; differences arise from gene _____, meaning which genes are on or off.
qs.e: Different patterns of gene expression create differences among cells despite their nearly identical genomes. Genetic programming also primarily controls proliferation and differentiation.

qs.q: Which descriptions of cancer match the rapid-fire bank? Select all that apply.
c: Both proliferation and differentiation are abnormal.
Cancer is not one single disease.
Growth exceeds normal, is inappropriate, and continues.
Growth serves no useful purpose, harms the host, and results from mutations.
Only differentiation is abnormal; proliferation remains normal.
qs.e: The notes describe cancer as mutation-related abnormalities of both replication steps. Its growth is excessive, inappropriate, persistent, and harmful rather than useful.

qs.q: Which exposures are listed as carcinogens? Select all that apply.
c: Sun radiation
Tobacco
Asbestos
Toxic chemicals
Normal cell-to-cell contact
qs.e: The notes list all four exposures as carcinogens. They connect carcinogens with free radicals and DNA damage leading to mutation.

qs.q: Which carcinogen-to-mutation sequence is given in lecture?
c: Carcinogens → free radicals → electron theft from DNA → mutation
Carcinogens → normal chromosome pairing → mutation prevention
Carcinogens → increased contact inhibition → mutation
Carcinogens → Factor VIII replacement → mutation
qs.e: The notes describe free radicals stealing electrons from DNA as the link between carcinogen exposure and mutation. This sequence connects an exposure with altered genetic material.

qs.q: What cancer latency range, in years, is listed in lecture?
qs.e: The rapid-fire bank gives a latency of 5–30 years. This is the listed interval associated with the carcinogen and mutation discussion.

qs.q: Which virus–cancer associations are listed? Select all that apply.
c: HPV–cervical cancer
HBV–liver cancer
HCV–liver cancer
EBV–lymphoma
HPV–sickle cell anemia
qs.e: The listed associations are HPV with cervical cancer, HBV and HCV with liver cancer, and EBV with lymphoma. Sickle cell anemia is described separately as a single-gene hemoglobin disorder.

qs.q: What viral mechanism for mutation is stated in lecture?
c: Viral DNA enters host DNA.
Viruses replace both sex chromosomes with autosomes.
Viruses convert every cell to a germ cell.
Viral proteins always correct host gene errors.
qs.e: The notes summarize insertion of viral DNA into host DNA as a mutation mechanism. This appears in the discussion of virus-associated cancers.

qs.q: Which comparison of viruses and bacteria matches the notes?
c: Neither needs host machinery.
Both require host machinery in the same way.
Viruses need host machinery; bacteria do not.
Bacteria need host machinery; viruses do not.
qs.e: The notes explicitly contrast viruses' need for host machinery with bacteria. This point accompanies the viral DNA and cancer discussion.

qs.q: What is the central idea of immune surveillance in the supplied notes?
c: Cancer cells never arise unless a person has an infection.
Cancers arise often, and the immune system should clear them.
The immune system creates all inherited gene defects.
Immune surveillance is another name for nondisjunction.
qs.e: The notes state that cancers arise often and should be cleared by the immune system. The supplied text then names AIDS and immunosuppressants but ends before completing that discussion.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes normal proliferation and mitosis?
c: The number of actively dividing cells equals the number dying; mitosis divides somatic cells capable of reproducing.
The number of dividing cells always exceeds the number dying; mitosis produces gametes.
Proliferation means development of specialized functions; mitosis occurs only in germ cells.
Normal proliferation requires all somatic cells to divide continuously.
qs.e: The study guide defines normal proliferation as a balance between actively dividing and dying cells. Somatic cells are body cells other than germ cells.

qs.q: Which factors are listed as regulators of mitosis? Select all that apply.
c: Genetic programming
Contact inhibition or cell density-dependent inhibition
Growth factors and nutrients
Tissue injury
Inheritance of an extra chromosome as a normal requirement
qs.e: Mitosis is regulated by genetic programming, contact inhibition, growth factors, nutrients, and tissue injury. An extra chromosome is not listed as a normal requirement for division.

qs.q: Which sequence correctly matches the four cell-cycle phases with their activities?
c: G1: DNA synthesis; S: resting; G2: cell division; M: organelle synthesis
G1: preparation with protein, RNA, and organelle synthesis; S: DNA synthesis; G2: continued protein and RNA synthesis; M: division
G1: resting; S: division; G2: gamete formation; M: DNA synthesis
G1: division; S: protein synthesis only; G2: resting; M: differentiation
qs.e: The four phases are G1, S, G2, and M. During S phase, DNA synthesis produces two separate chromosome sets, with 46 chromosomes in each set for the daughter cells.

qs.q: What designation identifies the resting phase of the cell cycle?
qs.e: G0 is identified as the resting phase. It is listed separately from the four phases G1, S, G2, and M.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes meiosis?
c: It divides somatic cells into gametes with 46 chromosomes each.
It produces only sperm, each with 22 chromosomes.
It reproduces germ cells to form ova and sperm, each with 23 chromosomes.
It produces two chromosome pairs in each body cell.
qs.e: Meiosis is the reproduction of germ cells and produces gametes: ova and sperm. Each gamete contains only 23 chromosomes.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe differentiation and cell types? Select all that apply.
c: Differentiation develops specialized cell structures and functions.
Genetic programming, growth factors, and nutrients regulate differentiation.
Highly differentiated cells have limited ability to reproduce.
Progenitors usually reproduce within a single cell type; undifferentiated stem cells can produce progenitors, and some can produce more than one cell type.
Highly differentiated cells have greater reproductive ability than all undifferentiated stem cells.
qs.e: Differentiation involves specialization rather than simply increasing cell numbers. The notes distinguish limited division in highly differentiated cells from the reproductive potential of progenitor and undifferentiated stem cells.

qs.q: Which description best captures cancer in these sources?
c: One disease involving useful, self-limited growth
A normal response in which differentiation alone increases
Abnormal proliferation with normal differentiation in every case
A group of diseases involving mutations, abnormal proliferation and differentiation, and persistent growth that is excessive, inappropriate, purposeless, and harmful
qs.e: Cancer is not one disease, and its growth exceeds normal needs and continues to harm the host. CANVAS connects mutations in regulatory genes to both abnormal proliferation and abnormal differentiation.

qs.q: Which pathway and examples match the DOC explanation of carcinogenesis?
c: Sun radiation, tobacco, asbestos, and toxic chemicals → free radicals → electron theft from DNA → mutation
Sun radiation and tobacco → normal gamete formation → mutation repair
Asbestos and toxic chemicals → contact inhibition → permanent tumor suppression
Carcinogens → normal differentiation → elimination of all mutations
qs.e: The DOC links these carcinogens to free radicals that steal electrons from DNA and cause mutation. CANVAS also identifies drugs, radiation, and cigarette smoke as carcinogen exposures.

qs.q: What latency range, in years, is given for carcinogenesis in the DOC?
qs.e: The DOC gives a latency of 5–30 years. This indicates that cancer may appear long after the initiating exposure.

qs.q: Which statements about viruses and cancer agree with the DOC? Select all that apply.
c: HPV is associated with cervical cancer.
HBV and HCV are associated with liver cancer.
EBV is associated with lymphoma.
Insertion of viral DNA into host DNA can cause mutation; viruses need host machinery, whereas bacteria do not.
Bacteria require host machinery in the same way as viruses.
qs.e: The DOC provides these three virus–cancer associations and links viral DNA insertion to mutation. It also distinguishes viruses' dependence on host machinery from bacteria.

qs.q: Why do AIDS, immunosuppressant use, and aging increase cancer risk according to the DOC?
c: They convert every somatic mutation into a hereditary mutation.
They impair immune surveillance that should clear frequently arising cancers.
They prevent all abnormal antigens from forming.
They increase normal contact inhibition.
qs.e: The DOC states that cancers arise often and should be cleared by the immune system. Impaired immune surveillance allows more cancers to persist.

qs.q: Which statement correctly connects hereditary cancer risk with prevention?
c: All tumor mutations are inherited, so every cancer requires preventive surgery.
Only mutations caused by radiation are hereditary.
Only germ-line mutations are hereditary; highly hereditary breast cancer is an example in which preventive mastectomy may be used.
Hereditary cancer risk is unrelated to mutations.
qs.e: The DOC limits hereditary mutations to the germ-cell line. It gives highly hereditary breast cancer and preventive mastectomy as a clinical example.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly distinguishes consequences of abnormal proliferation from abnormal differentiation?
c: Proliferation: crowding normal cells and taking blood, oxygen, and nutrients; differentiation: altered characteristics and loss of normal organ function
Proliferation: specialized organ function; differentiation: balanced cell replacement
Proliferation: only ectopic hormones; differentiation: only increased cell number
Proliferation: improved nutrient delivery to normal cells; differentiation: preserved organ function
qs.e: Abnormal proliferation crowds out normal cells and competes for essential resources. Abnormal differentiation changes cell characteristics and prevents tissues or organs from performing their jobs.

qs.q: Loss of tumor-cell cohesiveness permits spread through blood or lymph. What is this spread called?
qs.e: The DOC links loss of cohesiveness to metastasis through blood or lymph. This differs from infiltration into nearby tissues.

qs.q: Which abbreviated tumor product promotes new vessels so a tumor can grow beyond its existing blood-supply limit?
qs.e: VEGF is the vascular endothelial cell growth factor identified in CANVAS. The DOC explains that new vessels allow further tumor growth beyond the prior blood-supply limit.

qs.q: Which abnormal tumor products or effects are described in lectures? Select all that apply.
c: Ectopic hormone production without negative feedback
ACTH, ADH, or PTH production by lung cancer
Enzymes or toxins associated with non-healing sores
Abnormal antigens
Ectopic hormones that always remain under normal negative feedback
qs.e: The DOC lists ectopic hormones, enzymes or toxins, and abnormal antigens as consequences of abnormal differentiation. Its lung-cancer examples are ACTH, ADH, and PTH, with no negative feedback.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes PSA and CEA as taught in the DOC?
c: Both are used to diagnose and screen for cancer, but not to assess treatment.
CEA is associated only with cervical cancer.
PSA and CEA directly eliminate residual tumor cells.
They monitor disease, judge treatment, and watch for recurrence—not diagnose or screen; CEA is associated with colon, gastric, pancreatic, and some breast cancers.
qs.e: The DOC explicitly limits PSA and CEA to monitoring, treatment assessment, and recurrence surveillance. It lists colon, gastric, pancreatic, and some breast cancers for CEA.

qs.q: What term means cancer-associated wasting?
qs.e: Cachexia means wasting. The DOC gives two mechanisms: the tumor steals nutrients, and cytokines cause anorexia, meaning loss of appetite.

qs.q: Which mechanisms contribute to cancer pain in the DOC? Select all that apply.
c: Nerve involvement
Ischemia from vessel compression
Tissue damage
Possible release of pain mediators
Restoration of normal contact inhibition
qs.e: Cancer pain may involve nerves, ischemia, tissue damage, and possibly pain-mediator release. The DOC presents several mechanisms rather than one universal cause.

qs.q: Which nursing tension related to cancer pain management is explicitly described?
c: Whether pain proves that a tumor is benign
Balancing medication dose and pain relief against sedation and time with family
Whether family time eliminates the need to assess pain
Avoiding all pain medication because sedation is always unacceptable
qs.e: The DOC highlights the tension between dose, sedation, and family time. This frames pain management as a balance of symptom relief and the patient's ability to interact.

qs.q: Which causes of anemia in cancer are listed in the DOC? Select all that apply.
c: Nutritional problems
Bleeding from toxins or vessel erosion
Bone marrow metastases
Marrow suppression from chemotherapy or radiation
Normal differentiation alone
qs.e: Cancer-associated anemia can involve nutrition, blood loss, marrow metastases, or treatment-related marrow suppression. These are distinct mechanisms that may contribute to the same problem.

qs.q: Which comparison of benign and malignant neoplasms matches the sources?
c: Benign tumors always metastasize; malignant tumors are always encapsulated.
Both always have abnormal proliferation and abnormal differentiation.
Benign tumors have abnormal proliferation only, expand, and often have a fibrous capsule; malignant tumors have both abnormalities, infiltrate, metastasize, and lack a capsule.
Benign tumors cannot cause local problems; malignant tumors cause only local problems.
qs.e: Benign neoplasms retain normal differentiation and generally expand locally, often within a fibrous capsule. Malignancy involves both abnormal proliferation and differentiation, with infiltration and metastasis.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the usual effects and danger of benign tumors?
c: They generally cause local problems and typically lack VEGF, ectopic hormones, toxins, cachexia, and anemia, but location such as the brain can make them fatal.
They always cause cachexia and anemia but never local damage.
They are always harmless regardless of location.
They usually cause widespread metastases rather than expansion.
qs.e: The DOC describes benign tumors as typically lacking the listed systemic effects. They are rarely fatal, but a critical location such as the brain is an important exception.

qs.q: Why is cancer surgery almost always combined with radiation and/or chemotherapy according to the DOC?
c: Surgery makes all remaining cells incapable of dividing.
Radiation is needed only to create a capsule.
Chemotherapy restores the original inherited gene in every cell.
Cells left behind after surgery can regrow.
qs.e: The DOC explains combined treatment in terms of residual cells. Removing the visible tumor does not prevent leftover cells from growing again.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes radiation treatment and the treatment irony noted in the DOC?
c: Radiation only affects resting cells and cannot cause mutations.
Radiation produces free radicals that kill cells or stop replication, hits fast dividers hardest, and—like toxic drugs—is itself carcinogenic but is used because the alternative may be death.
Radiation works by replacing defective genes and has no carcinogenic potential.
Toxic drugs are carcinogens, so the DOC says they must never be used.
qs.e: Radiation uses free-radical injury to kill cells or stop replication, particularly affecting fast-dividing cells. The DOC emphasizes accepting carcinogenic treatment risks when the untreated alternative is death.

qs.q: Biologics, immunomodulators, monoclonal antibodies, and synthetic cytokines are described as which kind of newer treatment?
c: Mechanical tumor-removal procedures
Normal gamete-production methods
Immune-modifying drugs
Tumor-marker screening tests
qs.e: The DOC groups these newer therapies as immune-modifying drugs. It does not provide more specific mechanisms for individual agents.

qs.q: Which four letters identify the DNA bases listed in the DOC?
qs.e: DNA consists of chains of nucleotides containing one of four possible bases. The DOC identifies these bases with the letters A, C, G, and T.

qs.q: According to the more explicit CANVAS wording, when is a triplet called a codon, and what does it specify?
c: After transcription into RNA; it specifies a particular amino acid.
After formation of a chromosome; it specifies an entire organ.
Only before transcription; it specifies 23 chromosomes.
After mitosis; it specifies all proteins in the cell.
qs.e: ⚠ Conflict: The DOC labels the triplet in its DNA sequence summary a codon, whereas the CANVAS handout specifies that the triplet is called a codon after transcription into RNA. Both associate a triplet/codon with one amino acid.

qs.q: Which statement correctly connects genes, chromosomes, and normal body-cell chromosome numbers?
c: A gene is an entire chromosome; body cells have 23 chromosomes total.
Chromosomes consist only of proteins, and genes do not contain DNA.
Body cells have 46 autosome pairs plus two sex-chromosome pairs.
A gene is a DNA segment usually specifying one protein; genes lie end-to-end in DNA wound around a protein core, forming 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: 22 autosome pairs plus XX or XY.
qs.e: CANVAS defines genes as DNA segments providing protein-synthesis instructions and chromosomes as DNA wound around a protein core. The normal body-cell complement is 23 pairs, including one sex-chromosome pair.

qs.q: Which statements about gene function and inheritance are supported? Select all that apply.
c: Genes control cell function through protein synthesis.
Inheritance includes physical and biochemical or physiologic characteristics.
Gametes transmit chromosomes, and the zygote receives a paired set from its parents.
The paired genes for a trait are called alleles; the DOC places Mendel around 1865, during the Civil War era.
Genes influence inheritance but not cell function.
qs.e: The sources assign genes roles in both protein synthesis and inheritance. CANVAS describes parental contributions and alleles, while the DOC supplies the historical reference to Mendel.

qs.q: Which set of definitions is correct?
c: Homozygous: different alleles; heterozygous: identical alleles; dominant: expressed only when homozygous
Homozygous: identical alleles; heterozygous: different alleles; dominant: expressed in either pairing; recessive: expressed only when homozygous
Homozygous and heterozygous both mean identical alleles.
Recessive traits are expressed in every heterozygous person, while dominant traits are never expressed.
qs.e: Homozygous means the alleles are the same, and heterozygous means they differ. Dominant traits can be expressed with either pairing; recessive traits require a homozygous pairing.

qs.q: What term describes an asymptomatic heterozygous person who can transmit a recessive disease allele?
qs.e: A carrier has the recessive allele without manifesting the recessive trait. The DOC emphasizes that the person can still transmit it.

qs.q: Which statement summarizes gene mutation and single-gene disorders as presented?
c: A single-gene disorder always changes chromosome number and has one universal treatment.
Single-gene disorders always result from abnormal contact inhibition without a code change.

Replication errors can change the genetic code; the DOC describes inherited gene disorders as germ-cell mutations or 'metabolic accidents,' often leaving one protein missing or defective, with no universal symptoms or treatment and no current mutation fix in these notes.
Chemicals, radiation, and environmental agents are excluded as predisposing factors for gene mutation.
qs.e: CANVAS links gene mutation to DNA replication errors and lists chemicals, radiation, and other environmental agents as predisposing factors. The DOC emphasizes the protein-specific effects and variable manifestations and treatment of single-gene disorders.

qs.q: Why are males usually affected and females usually carriers in the X-linked recessive pattern described?
c: Males have one X, so one defective X-linked gene can cause disease; females have two X chromosomes, and the DOC describes the Y as much smaller, with over 1,000 fewer genes.
Males have two X chromosomes, while females have only one.
Most sex-linked disorders are dominant and located on autosomes.
The Y chromosome contains every gene found on both X chromosomes.
qs.e: The sources describe most sex-linked disorders as recessive and usually X-linked. One defective X-linked gene can therefore affect a male, while females usually are carriers in the pattern taught.

qs.q: Hemophilia A involves deficiency or nonfunction of which clotting factor?
qs.e: Hemophilia A is the sex-linked example involving factor VIII deficiency or nonfunction. The DOC highlights bleeding into muscles and joints.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes autosomal dominant disorders and the instructor's test convention?
c: Two defective genes are required, and affected parents are always aa.
Unaffected carriers always have the disease allele in this pattern.
The defective gene must be on an X chromosome.
One defective dominant gene on an autosome causes disease; there are no carriers, and an affected parent is represented as Aa on the test.
qs.e: Autosomal dominant disease requires only one disease allele. The DOC specifically instructs students to treat an affected parent as Aa on the test.

qs.q: Which findings are associated with Marfan syndrome in the DOC? Select all that apply.
c: Connective tissue abnormalities with long limbs and fingers
Chest and spine deformities
Lens dislocation or retinal detachment
Valve prolapse and aneurysms
Factor VIII deficiency as its defining defect
qs.e: Marfan syndrome is the autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder example. The DOC lists skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular manifestations; factor VIII deficiency belongs to hemophilia A.

qs.q: Which genotype mapping correctly describes an autosomal recessive disorder?
c: AA: disease; Aa: disease; aa: normal
aa: disease; Aa: carrier; AA: normal
aa: carrier; Aa: normal; AA: disease
Every genotype produces disease.
qs.e: Autosomal recessive disease requires two recessive alleles, aa. Aa indicates carrier status rather than disease, while AA is normal in the notation used.

qs.q: Which mechanism and distinction match the sickle cell example?
c: A missing chromosome causes factor VIII deficiency; trait and disease are identical.
A connective tissue defect causes sickling without anemia.
One wrong amino acid in the hemoglobin gene leads to defective hemoglobin and sickled RBCs, causing clots, pain, and hemolytic anemia; disease is distinguished from carrier trait.
Sickling occurs because every gene on chromosome 21 is misspelled.
qs.e: The DOC links the hemoglobin amino-acid error to sickling, clots, pain, and hemolytic anemia. Sickle cell is the autosomal recessive example, so disease and carrier trait are distinct.

qs.q: Which conditions are listed in CANVAS as circumstances under which defective-hemoglobin RBCs may become sickle-shaped? Select all that apply.
c: Hypoxia
Infection
Exposure to cold
Stress
Normal contact inhibition
qs.e: CANVAS lists hypoxia, infection, cold exposure, and stress as sickling conditions. These are triggers associated with the defective hemoglobin molecule.

qs.q: Which approach matches the instructor's Punnett-square instructions?
c: Use X/Y for X-linked inheritance and calculate risk out of two by sex; use A/a for autosomal inheritance and calculate risk out of four.
Use A/a for every sex-linked problem and ignore offspring sex.
Use X/Y for autosomal inheritance and calculate all risks out of 23.
Use chromosome numbers instead of alleles for every single-gene problem.
qs.e: The DOC directs sex-specific X-linked calculations using X/Y and a denominator of two. Autosomal problems use A/a and a denominator of four.

qs.q: For an affected father with an X-linked recessive disorder and a normal, noncarrier mother, what outcomes does the DOC give?
c: 100% affected sons and 0% carrier daughters
50% affected sons and 50% affected daughters
100% affected sons and 100% affected daughters
0% affected sons and 100% carrier daughters
qs.e: The DOC's stated cross produces no affected sons and all carrier daughters. The percentages are calculated separately by sex.

qs.q: What chromosome-separation error can produce monosomy or trisomy?
qs.e: Nondisjunction can produce monosomy or trisomy. The DOC describes monosomy as usually incompatible with life or resulting in miscarriage.

qs.q: Which statements about chromosomal disorders are supported by the sources? Select all that apply.
c: Errors during meiosis can change chromosome structure or number; listed predisposing factors include chemicals, radiation, and viral infections.
Trisomy 21 means three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two and is called Down syndrome.
Down syndrome findings include facial features, intellectual disability, congenital heart problems, and GI malformations.

An extra chromosome can cause many problems even when individual genes are 'spelled' correctly; care targets symptoms and quality of life, with nursing problems depending on the chromosome and change.
Chromosomal disorders always have identical nursing problems and are treated by correcting every mutation.
qs.e: Chromosomal disorders involve changes in chromosome number or structure, not necessarily an incorrect code within each gene. The sources emphasize variable manifestations and symptom-focused, quality-of-life care.

qs.q: Using the DOC's autosomal recessive notation, what is the disease risk in an Aa × Aa cross?
c: 0 of 4
1 of 4
2 of 4
4 of 4
qs.e: The four combinations are AA, Aa, Aa, and aa. Only aa represents autosomal recessive disease, so the disease risk is 1 of 4.

qs.q: Which examples of chemical products appear in the opening notes fragment? Select all that apply.
c: Vascular endothelial cell growth factor (VEGF)
Ectopic hormone production
Toxins
Factor VIII replacement
Normal hemoglobin production
qs.e: The fragment lists VEGF, ectopic hormone production, and toxins as examples of chemical products. It also mentions abnormal antigens and generalized effects without further explanation.

qs.q: Which disorder category is explicitly named in the opening notes fragment?
c: Benign neoplasms
Trisomy 21
Hemophilia A
Marfan’s syndrome
qs.e: The opening fragment names benign neoplasms as an example of a disorder. Its nursing-problem and intervention fields are blank, so no specific findings or interventions can be learned from those fields.

qs.q: Which strategies match the slide’s advice for finding information at an appropriate professional level? Select all that apply.
c: Include “pathophysiology” in the search.
Consider Medscape.com and its free account.
Recognize “the doctor will ask you…” as language aimed at lay people.
Seek professional information that is not excessively technical.
Assume “you will have this diagnostic test…” identifies professional-level content.
qs.e: Slide 3 recommends using “pathophysiology” and Medscape while seeking professional material that is not too technical. Direct-to-patient wording is a clue that the resource is aimed at lay people.

qs.q: Which description of DNA matches the notes?
c: Chains of nucleotides containing one of four possible bases
Chains of amino acids containing one of two possible bases
A protein core without nucleotides
A collection of chromosomes without genes
qs.e: DNA consists of nucleotide chains, and each nucleotide contains one of four possible bases. The bases are arranged in a triplet code.

qs.q: After transcription into RNA, a triplet is called a(n) ______.
qs.e: The notes distinguish the DNA triplet code from the RNA codon. Each codon codes for a specific amino acid.

qs.q: Each codon is a code for a specific what?
c: Amino acid
Chromosome pair
Environmental agent
Sex chromosome
qs.e: A codon specifies an amino acid. This connects the genetic code to protein synthesis.

qs.q: A segment of DNA that provides instructions for synthesis of a protein is a(n) ______.
qs.e: A gene is a DNA segment containing protein-synthesis instructions. The notes describe genes as attached end-to-end in long DNA molecules.

qs.q: What is the structure of a chromosome in lecture?
c: A DNA molecule wound around a protein core
An amino acid wound around an RNA core
A free-standing codon without DNA
A pair of proteins without genetic material
qs.e: A chromosome consists of a DNA molecule wound around a protein core. Genes are segments within DNA.

qs.q: Body cells, except gametes, normally contain how many pairs of chromosomes?
qs.e: The notes specify 23 chromosome pairs in body cells other than gametes. These consist of 22 autosomal pairs and one sex-chromosome pair.

qs.q: Which chromosome composition matches the notes for body cells other than gametes?
c: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes
23 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes
21 pairs of autosomes and 2 pairs of sex chromosomes
1 pair of autosomes and 22 pairs of sex chromosomes
qs.e: The 23 pairs include 22 autosomal pairs, described as alike in males and females, plus one sex-chromosome pair.

qs.q: Which statements describe genetic functions and inheritance in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: DNA directs protein synthesis.
Inheritance is transmitted through gametes following Mendel’s laws.
The zygote receives chromosomes from each parent.
The paired genes for a trait are called alleles.
The zygote receives its entire chromosome set from only one parent.
qs.e: The notes link DNA to protein synthesis and describe inheritance through gametes. Chromosomes from both parents form paired sets, with two genes for each trait termed alleles.

qs.q: When the two alleles in a pair are the same, the pairing is described as ______.
qs.e: Homozygous means the alleles are the same. Heterozygous means they are different.

qs.q: When the two alleles in a pair are different, the pairing is described as ______.
qs.e: Heterozygous describes two different alleles. In the inheritance model presented, the dominant trait is expressed while the recessive allele can be carried without manifestation.

qs.q: Which comparison of dominant and recessive traits matches the notes?
c: Dominant traits can be expressed in homozygous or heterozygous pairings; recessive traits require homozygous pairings.
Dominant traits require homozygous pairings; recessive traits require heterozygous pairings.
Both traits are expressed only in heterozygous pairings.
Neither trait can be expressed in a homozygous pairing.
qs.e: The notes state that dominant traits are expressed with either pairing, whereas recessive traits require a homozygous pairing. The slides separately explain the single-X situation in males with X-linked recessive disorders.

qs.q: A heterozygous person who does not manifest the recessive trait but has its allele is a(n) ______.
qs.e: A carrier has the recessive allele without manifesting the recessive trait. The dominant allele determines the expressed trait in this pairing.

qs.q: Which sequence describes a gene mutation in lecture?
c: Error in DNA replication → change in genetic code
Error in meiosis → exclusively normal chromosome numbers
Normal protein synthesis → loss of all alleles
Dominant inheritance → automatic chromosome duplication
qs.e: The notes associate gene mutation with an error in DNA replication that changes the genetic code. They separately associate errors during meiosis with changes in chromosome structure or number.

qs.q: Which exposures are listed as predisposing factors for gene mutation? Select all that apply.
c: Chemicals
Radiation
Other environmental agents
Having identical alleles
Having 23 chromosome pairs
qs.e: Chemicals, radiation, and other environmental agents are listed as predisposing factors for gene mutation. Normal chromosome number and homozygosity are not listed as such exposures.

qs.q: According to the notes, an error during meiosis can lead to which change?
c: A change in chromosome structure or number
Only a change in protein-core color
The automatic correction of every mutation
The elimination of all inherited traits
qs.e: The notes link errors during meiosis to altered chromosome structure or number. This is presented separately from replication-related changes in the genetic code.

qs.q: Which factors are explicitly listed as predisposing factors for errors during meiosis? Select all that apply.
c: Chemical exposure
Radiation exposure
Viral infections
Normal autosomal pairing
Carrier status alone
qs.e: The notes list chemicals, radiation, and viral infections under predisposing factors for meiotic errors. These errors may change chromosome structure or number.

qs.q: What determines the nursing problem associated with a chromosomal disorder in these notes?
c: Which chromosome is affected and what change occurred
Only whether the patient is male
Only whether the patient is a carrier
The same fixed nursing problem for every chromosome change
qs.e: The notes explicitly state that the nursing problem depends on the chromosome affected and the change that occurred. No single universal nursing problem is supplied.

qs.q: Which statements describe sex-linked disorders in the supplied material? Select all that apply.
c: The defective gene is on a sex chromosome, usually the X.
Most have a recessive inheritance pattern.
A recessive defective gene is expressed if no dominant normal gene is present.
The defective gene must be on an autosome.
All sex-linked disorders have dominant inheritance.
qs.e: Sex-linked disorders involve a gene on a sex chromosome, usually the X. Most are recessive, so a dominant normal allele can prevent manifestation.

qs.q: Why can a single defective X-linked recessive gene cause disease in a male while a female with one defective copy is usually a carrier?
c: Males have only one X chromosome, while females have two.
Males have two X chromosomes, while females have one.
Females do not inherit sex chromosomes.
X-linked genes are always dominant in males.
qs.e: The notes explain that males have only one X chromosome, so one defective X-linked gene can cause disease. Females have two X chromosomes and are usually carriers when only one has the defective recessive gene.

qs.q: Which combination matches the slides’ normal sex-chromosome patterns?
c: Male: XY; female: XX
Male: XX; female: XY
Male: YY; female: XX
Male: XY; female: YY
qs.e: The slides use XY for males and XX for females. This difference underlies the presented explanation of X-linked recessive expression.

qs.q: Hemophilia A is associated with deficiency or nonfunction of which clotting factor?
qs.e: The notes identify hemophilia A as a sex-linked disorder involving deficient or nonfunctional factor VIII.

qs.q: Which statement best describes an autosomal dominant disorder?
c: A dominant defective gene is on an autosome, and one defective copy can cause disease.
A recessive defective gene is on an X chromosome, and two copies are always required.
A defective gene is on an autosome, but it can affect only males.
Two recessive defective copies are required, and heterozygotes have normal genes only.
qs.e: Autosomal dominant disorders involve a dominant defective allele on an autosome. One defective copy is sufficient, and the slides state that male versus female does not matter.

qs.q: For an autosomal dominant disorder in which A is defective, how should Aa and aa be classified?
c: Aa: disease; aa: normal genes
Aa: carrier; aa: disease
Aa: normal genes; aa: carrier
Aa: carrier; aa: normal genes
qs.e: With dominant defective allele A, Aa manifests disease, while aa has normal genes. The slides specify that this model has no carriers.

qs.q: Which example is correctly matched to autosomal dominant inheritance and its disorder description?
c: Marfan’s syndrome — connective tissue disorder
Hemophilia A — defective hemoglobin
Sickle cell anemia — factor VIII deficiency
Down syndrome — dominant single-gene connective tissue disorder
qs.e: The notes list Marfan’s syndrome as an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder. The other examples belong to different disorder categories.

qs.q: Which statements describe autosomal recessive disorders? Select all that apply.
c: The defective gene is on an autosome.
Male versus female does not matter for this inheritance classification.
Two defective recessive genes are needed to cause disease.
A heterozygous person can be a carrier.
One defective recessive allele always causes disease.
qs.e: Autosomal recessive disease requires two defective recessive alleles. A heterozygous person carries one defective allele without having the disease in this model.

qs.q: For an autosomal recessive disorder in which a is defective, which classification is correct?
c: aa: disease; Aa: carrier; AA: normal genes
aa: normal genes; Aa: disease; AA: carrier
aa: carrier; Aa: normal genes; AA: disease
aa: disease; Aa: disease; AA: carrier
qs.e: Two defective alleles produce disease in aa. Aa is a carrier, and AA contains normal alleles.

qs.q: Which mechanism and inheritance pattern are linked to sickle cell anemia in lecture?
c: Autosomal recessive inheritance with defective hemoglobin and conditional RBC sickling
Autosomal dominant inheritance with factor VIII deficiency
Sex-linked inheritance with excess normal hemoglobin
An extra chromosome 21 causing a connective tissue disorder
qs.e: Sickle cell anemia is listed as an autosomal recessive disorder involving a defective hemoglobin molecule. RBCs become sickle-shaped under certain conditions.

qs.q: Which conditions are listed as triggers for RBC sickling in sickle cell anemia? Select all that apply.
c: Hypoxia
Infection
Exposure to cold
Stress
Having normal genes only
qs.e: The notes specifically list hypoxia, infection, cold exposure, and stress as conditions associated with sickling. The underlying abnormality is defective hemoglobin.

qs.q: The chromosomal disorder with three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two is called ______.
qs.e: Trisomy 21, also called Down syndrome, is the example of a chromosomal disorder in lecture. The chromosome-number change is three copies of chromosome 21 rather than two.

qs.q: Which questions should be addressed before diagramming parents in a Punnett square? Select all that apply.
c: Should X/Y or A/a notation be used?
Is the defective allele dominant or recessive?
How many defective genes are needed for disease, and are there carriers?
What genotypes represent disease, carrier status, and normal genes?
Can the inheritance type be ignored until after the risk is calculated?
qs.e: Slide 13 directs the student to establish notation, inheritance pattern, required defective copies, and genotype meanings before diagramming the parents. It also asks the student to decide whether the specified risk uses two or four outcomes.

qs.q: After deciding how to diagram the parents, what sequence does the Punnett square guide recommend?
c: Fill in possible children → label each child’s status → reread the question and calculate the specified risk
Calculate a risk → ignore the question → label only the parents
Label all children affected → decide the inheritance type
Skip possible children → report carrier status as disease risk
qs.e: The guide emphasizes completing and classifying the possible children before calculating risk. Rereading the question helps ensure the calculation answers the risk actually requested.

qs.q: Which notation and risk denominator are listed in Slide 14’s sex-linked Punnett square setup?
c: X and Y; out of 2
A and a; out of 2
X and Y; out of 4
A and a; out of 4
qs.e: Slide 14 specifies X/Y notation and “out of 2” for its setup. Slide 13 also instructs students to reread the question and calculate the risk specified, so the requested group should not be ignored.

qs.q: In the X-linked recessive model on Slide 14, how many defective copies are needed for disease?
c: Females need two; males need one.
Females need one; males need two.
Both females and males need two.
Both females and males need none.
qs.e: Slide 14 states that females need two defective genes and males only one in this model. Females with one defective copy can be carriers.

qs.q: Which notation and denominator are used in the autosomal Punnett square setups on Slides 15 and 16?
c: A and a; out of 4
X and Y; out of 2
A and a; out of 2
X and Y; out of 4
qs.e: Both autosomal setups use A/a notation and calculate out of four. The defective allele is A for dominant disease and a for recessive disease.

qs.q: Using the autosomal dominant model, an affected Aa parent and a normal aa parent have what predicted risk of an affected child?
qs.e: The four Punnett square outcomes are Aa, Aa, aa, and aa. Because A is dominant and defective, two of four outcomes represent disease.

qs.q: Using the autosomal recessive model, what is the predicted disease risk for a child of two Aa carriers?
qs.e: The outcomes are AA, Aa, Aa, and aa. Only aa has the two defective recessive alleles required for disease, giving one affected outcome out of four.

qs.q: Which major difference between malignant and benign tumors is tested on Slide 18?
c: Malignant tumors are more likely to metastasize.
Malignant tumors are more likely to be encapsulated.
Malignant tumors rarely cause generalized effects such as weight loss.
Malignant tumors tend to grow more slowly.
qs.e: Greater likelihood of metastasis is the distinguishing feature targeted by this practice question. The other choices are not the malignant-versus-benign distinction being tested.

qs.q: The practice question on single-gene disorders asks which cell type usually contains the causative mutation. Which choice fits the notes’ transmission of inherited traits through gametes?
c: A cancer cell
A germ cell
A microorganism
A somatic cell
qs.e: A germ cell is the choice consistent with the notes’ description of inheritance through gametes. Slide 19 tests this distinction from cancer cells, microorganisms, and somatic cells.

qs.q: Which rationale for radiation treatment of cancer is presented as the mechanism in Slide 20’s practice question?
c: It generates free radicals that can damage cancer cells and interfere with replication.
It prevents VEGF production to deprive cancer of its blood supply.
It specifically blocks the replication of necessary cellular enzymes.
It prevents cell division without involving free-radical damage.
qs.e: The radiation mechanism described is generation of free radicals that damage cancer cells and interfere with replication. The VEGF and enzyme-replication statements are alternative choices, not that mechanism.

qs.q: Which statements are explicitly present in the radiation-treatment material? Select all that apply.
c: Free radicals can damage cancer cells and interfere with replication.
Radiation can damage normal cells as well as cancer cells.
Radiation remains an accepted treatment strategy for cancer.
Radiation damages only cancer cells.
Slide 21 supplies a detailed answer explaining why treatment remains accepted.
qs.e: Slide 20 supplies the free-radical mechanism, and Slide 21’s question states that radiation remains accepted despite damage to both normal and cancer cells. Slide 21 asks for the rationale but does not provide its answer.

qs.q: Slide 32 labels the CAUSE of a disease as a ______.
qs.e: Slide 32 equates a predisposing factor with the cause and places it before disease in the sequence PF → disease → signs/symptoms.

qs.q: Which sequence correctly distinguishes predisposing factors from signs and symptoms?
c: Predisposing factor → disease → signs and symptoms
Signs and symptoms → predisposing factor → disease
Disease → predisposing factor → normal genes
Signs and symptoms → normal genes → predisposing factor
qs.e: Slide 32 identifies signs and symptoms as results of disease, not its predisposing causes. Its sequence is PF → disease → signs/symptoms.

qs.q: What term names the process of producing blood cells from hematopoietic stem cells?
qs.e: Hematopoietic function concerns how the body makes blood cells. Hematopoiesis begins with stem cells in red bone marrow, whose descendants differentiate into mature circulating cells.

qs.q: Which pairings correctly identify the three marrow cell lines and their main jobs? Select all that apply.
c: Erythrocytes = RBCs; carry oxygen
Leukocytes = WBCs; defend against infection and foreign material
Thrombocytes = PLTs; form the primary hemostatic plug
Erythrocytes = WBCs; defend against infection
Thrombocytes = RBCs; carry oxygen
qs.e: The instructor emphasized knowing both names for each line. RBCs transport oxygen, WBCs provide defense, and platelets participate in primary hemostasis.

qs.q: Which statement correctly matches the named hematopoietic growth factors with their clinical uses?
c: Synthetic EPO-type drugs treat anemias; G-CSF is used when neutrophils are too low
Synthetic EPO-type drugs treat low platelets; G-CSF treats excess RBCs
EPO and G-CSF both break down fibrin
EPO and G-CSF are ABO antibodies
qs.e: Growth factors regulate hematopoiesis. The notes name EPO and G-CSF and emphasize that synthetic versions can be administered clinically.

qs.q: Which sequence correctly describes the primary erythropoiesis feedback loop?
c: Hypoxia → marrow releases EPO → kidney produces RBCs
High tissue oxygen → kidney releases EPO → RBC destruction
Hypoxia → kidney releases EPO → marrow makes RBCs → increased oxygen-carrying capacity
Blood loss → liver makes platelets → increased oxygen-carrying capacity
qs.e: Hypoxia means insufficient oxygen at the tissues and is the primary stimulus. The kidney supplies EPO, while bone marrow produces the RBCs.

qs.q: Which statement correctly combines the lecture's RBC production estimate and oxygen-transport mechanism?
c: About 200 × 10⁹ RBCs daily; iron in hemoglobin binds oxygen picked up at the lungs and delivered to tissues
About 200 × 10⁹ RBCs yearly; platelets carry oxygen to tissues
About 1% of RBCs daily; bilirubin binds oxygen in the lungs
About 200 RBCs daily; intrinsic factor carries oxygen
qs.e: The diagram showed production on the order of 200 × 10⁹ RBCs per day. RBC oxygen transport depends on iron within hemoglobin.

qs.q: What are the slightly immature RBCs released from marrow called?
qs.e: The developmental sequence shown was hemocytoblast → proerythroblast → intervening stages → reticulocyte → erythrocyte. Reticulocytes are almost-mature RBCs.

qs.q: Approximately what percentage of circulating RBCs are normally reticulocytes?
qs.e: About 1% of circulating RBCs are reticulocytes at a given time. Their proportion provides an index of marrow activity.

qs.q: Which interpretations of a reticulocyte count agree with the notes? Select all that apply.
c: A low count indicates slower-than-usual new RBC production
A low count can reflect missing nutritional building blocks or marrow suppression
A low count identifies the exact cause of reduced production
A high count indicates accelerated RBC production
After hemorrhage, a functioning marrow is expected to produce a high count
qs.e: Reticulocytes indicate how actively marrow is producing RBCs, not the specific cause of impaired production. Blood loss was the common trigger named for an elevated count.

qs.q: Which ABO antigen/plasma-antibody pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
c: Type A: A antigen and anti-B
Type B: B antigen and anti-A
Type AB: A and B antigens and neither antibody
Type O: neither antigen and both anti-A and anti-B
Type O: A and B antigens and neither antibody
qs.e: ABO grouping uses RBC surface antigens. The notes pair A with anti-B, B with anti-A, AB with neither antibody, and O with both antibodies.

qs.q: When and how do ABO antibodies normally develop according to the recording?
c: They are present at birth only after an incompatible transfusion
They develop spontaneously by about 3–6 months, probably in response to similar environmental antigens
They develop only after exposure to Rh-positive blood
They develop only after marrow failure
qs.e: The notes state that babies are not born with these ABO antibodies. Their development does not require a wrong-type transfusion; the environmental explanation is presented as probable.

qs.q: What happens when an incompatible transfusion brings an RBC antigen together with its corresponding antibody?
c: Intrinsic factor production increases
RBCs become macrocytic without destruction
Hemolysis, meaning RBC bursting, can occur
Plasmin forms a platelet plug
qs.e: The notes link wrong-type transfusion to antigen–antibody interaction and RBC destruction. Hemolysis is described as RBC bursting.

qs.q: Which statement about the Rh system matches the notes?
c: Rh typing uses the C antigen because D is absent in everyone
