Rh was named for the rhesus monkey; antigens were discovered in 1940, and D is the most reactive antigen used for typing
Rh-positive means the RBC lacks D
Rh contains only one antigen, E
qs.e: The notes name C, D, and E among Rh antigens. Rh-positive cells have the D/Rh antigen, whereas Rh-negative cells do not.

qs.q: Which statements correctly distinguish anti-D from ABO antibodies? Select all that apply.
c: An Rh-negative person makes anti-D only after exposure to Rh-positive blood
A wrong transfusion can provide the exposure needed for anti-D formation
An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus can become exposed
After sensitization, later exposures can lead to destruction of Rh-positive cells
Anti-D appears spontaneously in all Rh-negative babies by 3–6 months
qs.e: Unlike ABO antibodies, anti-D requires actual exposure to Rh-positive blood. The notes emphasize that an unexposed Rh-negative person does not make this antibody.

qs.q: What term means too many red blood cells?
qs.e: Polycythemia is excess RBCs. The notes identify a marrow disorder and chronic hypoxia as its two predisposing categories.

qs.q: Which comparison of polycythemia causes is correct?
c: Polycythemia vera is a nutritional deficiency; chronic hypoxia suppresses EPO
Polycythemia vera is a blood cancer with marrow overproduction; chronic hypoxia is the much more common reason for excess RBCs
Both causes require loss of intrinsic factor
Chronic hypoxia causes polycythemia by prematurely destroying RBCs
qs.e: In polycythemia vera, marrow itself overproduces RBCs and often other cell lines. Chronic hypoxia repeatedly stimulates kidney EPO production and therefore increased marrow RBC output.

qs.q: Which examples or applications of chronic hypoxia were included in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Smoking
Chronic lung disease such as COPD
Living at high altitude, where there is less oxygen in the air
Athletes training at altitude to increase RBCs and hopefully improve muscle oxygen delivery and endurance
Loss of intrinsic factor as a direct altitude-training mechanism
qs.e: Smoking, COPD, and high-altitude living were listed as chronic-hypoxia settings. Athletes may exploit the resulting rise in RBC production to seek better endurance.

qs.q: Which pair of effects explains why polycythemia can stress circulation?
c: Lower viscosity and lower volume
Higher viscosity, making blood harder to push, and higher volume, stressing the heart and vessels
Lower viscosity with fewer clots and reduced cardiac stress
Higher volume with no effect on flow or cardiovascular workload
qs.e: More viscous blood has greater sluggish-flow and clot risk. Increased blood volume also stresses the heart and vessels.

qs.q: Which description best defines anemia in these notes?
c: Above-normal RBCs with increased viscosity
Below-normal RBCs or hemoglobin, reducing tissue oxygen delivery
An isolated excess of plasma antibodies
An unstable platelet plug
qs.e: Anemia means insufficient RBCs or hemoglobin for normal oxygen delivery. The illustrated anemic smear had fewer cells than the normal smear.

qs.q: Which groups contain only symptoms listed for anemia? Select all that apply.
c: Fatigue, weakness, and dizziness
Pale skin and rapid heartbeat
Shortness of breath and chest pain
Headache, leg pain, and insomnia
Increased RBC count and increased blood viscosity
qs.e: All four symptom groups were included in the anemia presentation. The notes frame these symptoms as manifestations of oxygen-delivery failure, whereas excess RBCs and viscosity belong to polycythemia.

qs.q: Which anemia category–example pairings match the four-category framework? Select all that apply.
c: Nutritional deficiency: iron, B12, or B9 deficiency
Bone marrow failure: aplastic anemia with empty or fatty marrow
Blood loss: GI bleeding, trauma, or postoperative hemorrhage
Excessive destruction: sickle cell, toxins, burns, mechanical valves, or autoimmune RBC attack
Nutritional deficiency: acute loss of whole blood from trauma
qs.e: The four predisposing categories are nutritional deficiencies, marrow failure, blood loss, and excessive or premature destruction. Classifying the mechanism is the key to scenario questions.

qs.q: An iron-deficient patient has microcytic, hypochromic RBCs. What does that mean, and which CBC pattern is expected?
c: Large, dark cells; increased MCV and MCHC
Small, pale cells; decreased MCV and MCHC
Normal-sized, normal-colored cells; normal MCV and MCHC
Large, immature-looking cells; decreased MCV
qs.e: Microcytic means small, and hypochromic means pale because the cells lack hemoglobin/iron. Smaller volume lowers MCV, and reduced hemoglobin concentration lowers MCHC.

qs.q: Which statement correctly identifies the CBC indices emphasized for classifying anemia?
c: MCV means mean corpuscular volume and reflects RBC size; MCHC means mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration and reflects hemoglobin concentration within cells
MCV measures platelets; MCHC measures WBCs
MCV means mean clotting volume; MCHC measures bilirubin
MCV and MCHC are both names for the total RBC count
qs.e: MCV and MCHC classify the size and color-related features of anemia. The CBC also reports hemoglobin, RBC count, platelets, and WBCs, so interpretation should not stop at hemoglobin alone.

qs.q: Why do deficiencies of B12 and B9 cause macrocytic/megaloblastic anemia?
c: These vitamins are needed for DNA construction in rapidly dividing marrow cells; deficiency disrupts maturation and produces large, often immature-looking RBCs
These vitamins normally destroy RBC hemoglobin
These vitamins directly form platelet plugs
These vitamins prevent all RBC differentiation by binding anti-D
qs.e: B12 is cobalamin, and B9 is folic acid or folate. Both support DNA production; macrocytic means large, and megaloblastic describes the big, immature-looking appearance noted in the lecture.

qs.q: What substance made by gastric parietal cells is needed for B12 absorption?
qs.e: Intrinsic factor is made by parietal cells in the gastric mucosa. According to the notes, it protects delicate B12 from digestive enzymes until absorption from gut into blood.

qs.q: Which situations were listed as ways to lose intrinsic factor production or activity? Select all that apply.
c: Chronic gastric inflammation or gastritis
Removal of part of the stomach during cancer or weight-loss surgery
Certain drugs that interfere with IF production or activity
A vegan diet by itself
Ileal disease by itself
qs.e: Gastritis, loss of gastric parietal cells, and certain drugs can impair IF availability or function. Vegan diet and ileal disease were contrasted as other reasons for B12 deficiency, not automatically IF problems.

qs.q: Which patient specifically meets the notes' definition of pernicious anemia?
c: A patient with B12-deficiency anemia because insufficient intrinsic factor prevents absorption
A patient with B12 deficiency attributed only to a vegan diet
A patient with B12 deficiency attributed only to ileal disease
A patient with iron deficiency after chronic bleeding
qs.e: Use the name pernicious anemia only when insufficient intrinsic factor causes the B12 deficiency. Other causes remain B12-deficiency anemia without this specific label.

qs.q: Which comparison correctly explains the neurological findings of vitamin deficiency?
c: B12 supports normal myelin around axons, which speeds conduction; B12 deficiency can cause neurological changes, unlike the folate-deficiency package described
Folate deficiency always causes the same neurological package as B12 deficiency
B12 affects only platelet plugs, not myelin
Normal myelin slows conduction and causes ataxia
qs.e: The notes link B12 deficiency to abnormal myelin and neurological findings. They specifically emphasize that folate deficiency does not cause this neurological package.

qs.q: What term describes numbness, tingling, or odd sensations associated with B12 deficiency?
qs.e: Paresthesias are abnormal sensations such as numbness or tingling. They are part of the neurological findings associated with B12 deficiency.

qs.q: What term in lecture means coordination problems?
qs.e: Ataxia means impaired coordination. B12 deficiency can also alter position or vibratory sense, including the ability to tell where a limb is in space.

qs.q: Why did the instructor emphasize B9 supplementation for pregnant patients?
c: B9 deficiency is linked to fetal neural-tube defects such as spina bifida, in which vertebrae fail to close in the back
B9 supplementation prevents Rh antigen formation
B9 deficiency exclusively causes maternal anti-D production
B9 closes an unstable platelet plug by producing fibrin
qs.e: Spina bifida leaves an opening in the vertebral region. The practical point was to ensure pregnant patients receive their supplements.

qs.q: Which progression matches the pictured degrees of spina bifida severity?
c: Bony defect only → protruding meninges with or without spinal nerves → protruding cord
Protruding cord → iron deficiency → absent Rh antigen
Platelet plug → fibrin clot → plasmin
Normal vertebrae → increased RBC count → jaundice
qs.e: The notes describe a bony defect without protrusion, then protruding meninges with or without nerves, and then actual cord protrusion. Exposed nerves or cord may be damaged, potentially causing paralysis.

qs.q: What term describes cracked, inflamed corners of the mouth that can accompany B-vitamin deficiency anemias?
qs.e: Cheilosis or cheilitis was shown as a clinical clue to B-vitamin deficiency anemias. The described finding is inflammation and cracking at the mouth corners.

qs.q: Which description of aplastic anemia matches the notes?
c: Marrow overproduces only RBCs in response to altitude
Marrow fails to produce cell lines, lowering RBCs and often WBCs and platelets; causes include radiation, toxic drugs or chemicals, and marrow cancer
RBCs are destroyed only by anti-D
Iron deficiency makes marrow produce excessive platelets in every case
qs.e: Aplastic anemia is marrow failure, illustrated by empty or fatty marrow. Because production is impaired, more than the RBC line may fall.

qs.q: How does acute blood-loss anemia initially differ from chronic slow GI blood loss?
c: Acute loss initially has normal MCV and MCHC; chronic loss can become microcytic and hypochromic after iron stores are depleted
Acute loss immediately makes all cells macrocytic; chronic loss always preserves iron
Both always cause low MCV and MCHC immediately
Acute loss prevents hemoglobin synthesis in every remaining cell
qs.e: Acute hemorrhage removes whole blood rather than initially impairing hemoglobin construction, leaving cells normocytic and normochromic. The GI-bleed slide showed pumping or oozing bleeding, an exposed vessel, and red or black clot.

qs.q: What term means low blood volume?
qs.e: The notes break it down as hypo = low, vol = volume, and -emia = blood. Large blood loss over a short time causes a volume problem in addition to anemia.

qs.q: Which example monitoring schedule did the instructor give for catching postoperative or post-procedure bleeding?
c: Every 15 minutes in the first hour, then every 30 minutes in the next hour
Once after the first day
Every 3–6 months
Only after blood pressure becomes low
qs.e: This was an example schedule, not a universal protocol. Frequent vital signs help detect bleeding before compensation fails.

qs.q: A postoperative patient's heart rate is climbing while blood pressure remains normal. What is the best interpretation from the notes?
c: Normal BP rules out a significant volume problem
Tachycardia may be compensating for blood loss; concern should begin before hypotension appears
The kidney has stopped making EPO because oxygen is high
Shock must be absent until reticulocytes decrease
qs.e: Heart rate rises first to move remaining blood into arteries faster and can temporarily preserve BP. Hypotension appears when compensation can no longer maintain pressure, so waiting for it delays recognition.

qs.q: What simplified definition of shock did the instructor give for this course?
c: Any high reticulocyte count
BP has fallen enough that major organs are inadequately perfused and begin to fail
Any transient rise in heart rate with adequate perfusion
An increase in circulating RBC mass
qs.e: In severe volume loss, failing compensation can lead to a BP drop and inadequate organ perfusion. The notes trace this to shock, multi-organ failure, and possible death.

qs.q: Which mechanisms of hemolytic anemia were described? Select all that apply.
c: Sickled cells appear defective and are destroyed by the body
Toxic chemicals or bacterial toxins destroy RBCs
Severe burns damage RBCs, and artificial valves can mechanically smash them when closing
Autoimmune disease directs an attack against the person's own RBCs
Missing intrinsic factor directly bursts circulating RBCs
qs.e: Hemolytic anemia involves excessive or premature RBC destruction. The notes include chemical, physical, mechanical, and immune mechanisms, noting that even flexible artificial valves can damage RBCs.

qs.q: Why can excessive RBC destruction produce jaundice?
c: Hemoglobin breakdown produces bilirubin, adding bilirubin to the bile/liver pathway and causing yellow discoloration
Intrinsic factor is converted into fibrin
Platelets turn into oxygen-binding iron
EPO directly stains the skin yellow
qs.e: The sequence emphasized is hemoglobin breakdown → bilirubin → jaundice. Increased hemolysis increases the bilirubin entering the bile/liver pathway.

qs.q: Which sequence gives all five stages of hemostasis in the order taught?
c: Vessel spasm → platelet plug → fibrin clot → clot remains during healing → clot degradation
Platelet plug → clot degradation → vessel spasm → healing → fibrin clot
Fibrin clot → vessel spasm → clot degradation → platelet plug → healing
Clot degradation → platelet plug → healing → vessel spasm → fibrin clot
qs.e: Hemostasis is how bleeding stops. The sequence first limits blood loss, then plugs and stabilizes the injury, retains the clot during repair, and finally removes it.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes the first two stages of hemostasis?
c: Injury and prostaglandins such as thromboxane A2 promote vessel constriction; platelets adhere to the injured wall and one another to form an unstable plug
Plasmin first forms a stable platelet plug, then increases bleeding
The liver releases platelets directly onto intact tissue
Platelet adhesion eliminates any need for fibrin stabilization
qs.e: Vasoconstriction limits blood leaving the injured vessel. Contact with the injured wall and prostaglandins promote the platelet plug, but blood flow can knock this unstable plug loose.

qs.q: Which statements correctly distinguish platelets from clotting factors? Select all that apply.
c: Platelets come from marrow and make the primary hemostatic plug
Clotting factors come from the liver
The coagulation cascade produces fibrin for secondary hemostasis
Fibrin stabilizes the plug and holds it while the vessel heals
The cascade's end product is a platelet rather than fibrin
qs.e: Platelets and clotting factors are not interchangeable. Platelets form the initial plug, while the coagulation cascade lays down fibrin to stabilize it.

qs.q: What removes the fibrin clot after its role in healing?
c: Plasmin breaks down fibrin
Intrinsic factor breaks down RBC antigens
EPO breaks down the platelet marrow
Thromboxane A2 converts fibrin into hemoglobin
qs.e: Clot degradation is the fifth stage of hemostasis. Plasmin breaks fibrin down as part of the checks and balances that prevent clots from remaining forever.

qs.q: Which comparison of intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation activation matches the notes?
c: Intrinsic: vessel injury, such as atherosclerosis; extrinsic: tissue injury, such as a cut or trauma involving tissue factor
Intrinsic: only surrounding tissue injury; extrinsic: only atherosclerosis
Both require an incompatible transfusion
Intrinsic makes RBCs; extrinsic makes intrinsic factor
qs.e: The notes distinguish injury to the blood vessel from injury to tissues. Atherosclerosis illustrates why the pathways are not totally redundant: a vessel may be injured without injury to surrounding tissue.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe hemostasis and its checks and balances? Select all that apply.
c: Vessel spasm precedes formation of the platelet plug.
The initial platelet plug is unstable; the coagulation cascade produces a fibrin clot.
Clotting factors circulate inactive and sequentially activate other factors.
Plasmin acts later, and circulating anticoagulant factors help limit clotting to where it is needed.
Platelets and clotting factors are interchangeable names for the same blood component.
qs.e: The notes summarize hemostasis as spasm → platelet plug → fibrin clot → plasmin later. Sequential factor activation builds the clot, while anti-clotting factors help prevent clotting everywhere.

qs.q: Which comparison correctly explains intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation pathways?
c: Intrinsic begins with tissue injury; extrinsic begins with vessel injury; they never join.
Intrinsic begins with vessel injury, such as atherosclerosis; extrinsic begins with tissue injury, such as a cut releasing tissue factor; they join and produce fibrin.
Intrinsic begins only after trauma to surrounding tissue; extrinsic begins only with atherosclerosis.
Both start on the same factor, and only the extrinsic pathway produces fibrin.
qs.e: Vessel injury activates the intrinsic pathway, whereas tissue injury activates the extrinsic pathway. Atherosclerosis illustrates why they are not entirely redundant, although the instructor noted that newer research suggests more overlap than textbooks initially taught.

qs.q: What term means too few platelets, leading to bleeding because a stable plug cannot be built?
qs.e: Thrombocytopenia is a platelet-number problem. With too few platelets, effective plug formation is impaired.

qs.q: Which mechanisms predispose a patient to thrombocytopenia? Select all that apply.
c: Radiation, toxic drugs or chemicals, or marrow cancer depress platelet production.
An enlarged spleen sequesters additional platelets.
An enlarged spleen excessively clears old or defective cells, including platelets.
Autoimmune antibodies attack platelets.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics directly stop marrow platelet production by removing bacterial vitamin K.
qs.e: Platelet counts can fall because of reduced marrow production, splenic sequestration or over-clearing, and autoimmune destruction. The notes distinguish antibiotic-related loss of bacterial vitamin K from a marrow problem.

qs.q: What medical term in lecture means nosebleed?
qs.e: Epistaxis means nosebleed. It is one of the bleeding manifestations discussed with platelet problems.

qs.q: What term describes pinpoint bleeds in the skin?
qs.e: Petechiae are pinpoint skin bleeds. Platelet problems can also cause easy bruising because plugs do not form effectively.

qs.q: Which treatment explanation matches the instructor's discussion of autoimmune platelet destruction?
c: Splenectomy increases sequestration, immunosuppressants strengthen antibody attack, and plasma exchange returns the patient's antibodies.
Splenectomy removes the platelet-sequestering and clearing organ; immunosuppressants quiet immune attack; plasma exchange discards antibody-containing plasma and returns cells with synthetic plasma.
Plasma exchange removes all blood cells permanently while retaining the patient's plasma.
Two or three plasma exchanges always cure every autoimmune disease.
qs.e: These treatments address splenic removal of platelets or the immune attack itself. The dialysis-like plasma exchange process can put some patients into remission after two or three rounds, but not every autoimmune disease responds.

qs.q: A patient has a normal platelet count but bruises easily while taking daily baby aspirin. Which interpretation matches the notes?
c: Normal platelet counts rule out a platelet-related bleeding problem.
The aspirin is intended mainly to treat headaches and cramps.
Aspirin impairs platelet clumping, so bleeding can increase despite a normal count; this dose is intended for an antiplatelet effect.
Aspirin prevents bleeding by increasing platelet plug formation.
qs.e: Aspirin is the prototype antiplatelet drug: platelets may be present but unable to clump effectively. Daily baby aspirin or one adult aspirin every other day was described as antiplatelet dosing, not pain treatment; one baby aspirin will not treat pain.

qs.q: Which statements correctly match antiplatelet drugs, uses, and adverse effects? Select all that apply.
c: Bleeding is a shared adverse effect, and aspirin carries GI bleeding and hemorrhagic stroke risks.
Clopidogrel (Plavix), prasugrel (Effient), and ticlopidine (Ticlid) are P2Y12 blockers used in ACS, stent, stroke, or PAD settings.
Ticlopidine can also cause thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and TTP.
PDE inhibitors include dipyridamole (Persantine), used with warfarin after valve replacement, and cilostazol (Pletal), used for claudication.
GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors primarily prevent bleeding by strengthening platelet plugs.
qs.e: The notes group these drugs by antiplatelet class and emphasize bleeding as their shared adverse effect. Ticlopidine has additional listed blood-cell complications, while the two PDE inhibitors have different named applications.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a thrombus from an embolus and identifies the excessive-clotting problem?
c: A thrombus is a clot where it formed; an embolus is a clot that traveled; excessive clotting can produce thromboembolic events such as MI, ischemic stroke, PE, and DVT.
A thrombus travels, while an embolus always remains where it formed.
Both terms mean a shortage of clotting factors that causes only hemorrhage.
Thromboembolic events are limited to platelet shortages and cannot involve excessive clotting.
qs.e: The notes distinguish a stationary clot from a traveled clot. Too many factors or too much clotting is associated with thromboembolic events, whereas too few working factors creates a bleeding problem.

qs.q: Which conditions or mechanisms belong on the notes' list of causes of insufficient working clotting factors? Select all that apply.
c: Liver disease reduces synthesis of clotting factors.
Vitamin K deficiency leaves many factors unable to function properly.
Hereditary disorders such as hemophilia, with Factor VIII as the example, affect clotting.
Increased consumption uses factors faster than they can be replaced.
Bone marrow platelet production is the liver's primary clotting-factor function.
qs.e: The four listed causes are liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, hereditary disorders, and increased consumption. The notes emphasize the distinction: platelets come from marrow, whereas working factors depend on the liver and vitamin K.

qs.q: Which explanation correctly links diet, bile, liver disease, and broad-spectrum antibiotics to vitamin K-related clotting problems?
c: Vitamin K is water-soluble, so bile loss does not affect its absorption.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics improve vitamin K supply by eliminating vitamin K-producing bacteria.

Low dietary intake can reduce vitamin K; bile is needed to absorb this fat-soluble vitamin; liver disease can impair both factor synthesis and vitamin K absorption; broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce the bacterial vitamin K source.
All four mechanisms cause bleeding exclusively by suppressing platelet production in marrow.
qs.e: Vitamin K deficiency can reflect poor intake, impaired absorption without bile, or loss of helpful gut bacteria after broad-spectrum antibiotics. Liver disease can impair clotting in two ways: reduced factor synthesis and reduced vitamin K absorption through inadequate bile.

qs.q: Expand DIC, the term for widespread clotting inside blood vessels.
qs.e: Disseminated means widespread, intravascular means inside vessels, and coagulation means clotting. DIC is the notes' example of factor deficiency caused by increased consumption.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe DIC? Select all that apply.
c: It is a complication of another critical illness rather than a primary disease.
Severe infection, multiple trauma, and advanced cancer are named settings.
Inflammation and its chemical mediators are thought to activate coagulation cascades.
Microthrombi can cause ischemia and organ failure, while factor consumption can cause hemorrhage.
Clotting factors accumulate unused, preventing any possibility of bleeding.
qs.e: DIC combines widespread microclot formation with depletion of factors needed to stop bleeding. The notes describe critically ill, often ICU, patients and link cascade activation to inflammatory mediators.

qs.q: Which statements about white blood cell groups and granulocytes match the notes? Select all that apply.
c: The three main WBC groups are granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes.
Neutrophils, basophils, and eosinophils are granulocytes, with granules visible under the microscope.
Neutrophils are first-line phagocytes for bacteria and foreign material; lysosomal enzymes digest engulfed material.
Eosinophils damage parasites with granule enzymes and accumulate in allergy or asthma; their enzymes can have pro-inflammatory or anti-inflammatory effects.
Basophils are lymphocytes, and eosinophils primarily engulf large parasites whole.
qs.e: The lecture emphasized the granulocyte trio; the notes also mention the usual basophil allergy/histamine pairing. Parasites can be too large to phagocytose, so eosinophil granule enzymes damage them; differing inflammatory effects were presented as possible subtype-related checks and balances.

qs.q: Which set correctly matches neutrophil aliases, maturity, and nuclear appearance?
c: PMN means monocyte; segs are immature with horseshoe nuclei; bands are mature with segmented nuclei.
Neutrophil is also called a polymorphonuclear leukocyte or PMN; segs are mature with segmented nuclei; bands are immature with horseshoe or band-shaped nuclei.
Segs and bands are separate lymphocyte groups unrelated to neutrophils.
Both segs and bands are mature eosinophils.
qs.e: Several names refer to neutrophils rather than separate cell types. CBCs often distinguish mature segs from immature bands.

qs.q: A CBC shows a 'shift to the left.' Which interpretation and naming history match the lecture?
c: More mature segs are present because the marrow stopped producing neutrophils; segs were on the left of old slips.
More bands than usual are present, commonly with infection or inflammation; accelerated marrow production releases immature cells, and old lab slips listed bands on the left.
The phrase means fewer lymphocytes and comes from the location of the spleen.
It is a random formatting quirk without clinical meaning.
qs.e: A left shift is a clue that marrow is responding to infection or inflammation by releasing more bands. The lecture also used 'neutrophilia' for too many neutrophils; the historical term persisted even after lab layouts changed.

qs.q: Which combined mapping of monocytes and lymphocytes is correct?
c: Monocytes are blood phagocytes that become macrophages or dendritic cells in tissue; B cells mature in bone marrow and support antibody/humoral immunity; T cells mature in thymus and support cell-mediated immunity; NK cells are innate.
Monocytes become platelets in tissue; B cells mature in thymus; T cells mature in marrow; NK cells produce all antibodies.
Monocytes are tissue-only cells; B and T cells are granulocytes; NK cells are clotting factors.
B, T, and NK cells all provide only adaptive antibody-mediated immunity.
qs.e: The notes connect cell names to location and immune function. B and T cells are presented with adaptive immunity, while NK cells are explicitly identified as innate.

qs.q: What general term means too few leukocytes or white blood cells?
qs.e: Leukopenia is the general term for a WBC deficiency. The suffix -penia means deficiency.

qs.q: Which comparison of WBC deficiency terms and clinical concern matches the notes?
c: Neutropenia means too many neutrophils, and granulocytopenia means absent lymphocytes.
Neutropenia means too few neutrophils; granulocytopenia means too few granulocytes and is often used similarly; agranulocytosis indicates neutrophils are nearly absent.
Agranulocytosis means a mild increase in neutrophils; the prefix a- means increased.
Neutropenia is low concern because neutrophils are uncommon and arrive last.
qs.e: The prefix a- means absence or nearly without. Neutropenia is especially concerning because neutrophils are the most plentiful WBCs and the first phagocytes on scene.

qs.q: According to the instructor's number, agranulocytosis means a neutrophil count below what value?
qs.e: The instructor used a neutrophil count below 200 to illustrate a count so low it is almost like having none. This is much lower than the normal frame given in the lecture.

qs.q: What approximate normal neutrophil count range did the instructor give?
qs.e: The lecture gave approximately 3,000–7,000 as the normal frame for neutrophils. It contrasted this with the below-200 count used for agranulocytosis.

qs.q: Which mechanisms can cause neutropenia? Select all that apply.
c: Marrow damage from radiation, drugs, chemicals, or marrow cancer reduces production.
Autoimmune destruction targets neutrophils.
Splenomegaly causes excessive clearing of neutrophils.
A severe wound or infection draws neutrophils into tissue faster than marrow can replace circulating cells.
Increased consumption means neutrophils remain unused in the bloodstream.
qs.e: Neutropenia can result from production failure, destruction, splenic over-clearing, or increased consumption. In a raging infection, migration into tissue can drain circulating neutrophils faster than they are replaced.

qs.q: Which synthetic growth factor is given to push marrow to make neutrophils? Give its abbreviation.
qs.e: G-CSF stands for granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. It stimulates marrow neutrophil production.

qs.q: Which applications of general cancer rules to leukemia are supported by the notes? Select all that apply.
c: Poorly differentiated blasts cannot perform mature immune functions.
Blasts crowding the marrow can produce anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia together.
Leukemic cells can infiltrate organs, and nutrient stealing plus cytokine-related anorexia contribute to anorexia/cachexia.
Pain can result from marrow expansion, infiltration, ischemia, and tissue damage.
A marrow full of blasts guarantees effective immunity because every additional white cell functions normally.
qs.e: Leukemia applies the cancer rules of abnormal function, crowding, spread, anorexia/cachexia, and pain to blood-line cells. A healthy marrow differentiates stem cells into functional cells, whereas leukemia marrow is crowded with poorly differentiated cells.

qs.q: Which comparison correctly describes blasts and acute versus chronic leukemia?
c: Blasts are fully mature WBCs; acute leukemia progresses slowly; chronic leukemia is not cancer.

Blasts are very immature WBC precursors; acute leukemia is sudden, blast-heavy, poorly differentiated, and makes patients sick quickly; chronic leukemia has more mature-appearing cells and a slower course.
Blasts are platelet fragments; chronic leukemia contains no abnormal cells.
Acute and chronic leukemia differ only in the site of marrow sampling.
qs.e: Blasts are very immature, poorly differentiated white-cell precursors. Chronic leukemia may look more mature and progress more slowly, but it remains cancer.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes marrow sampling and its goals?
c: Aspiration removes solid chunks; biopsy removes only fluid; neither helps identify leukemia type.

Aspiration withdraws fluid; biopsy uses a bigger needle for marrow chunks; the usual site is the iliac crest, with tibia or sternum as alternatives; specimens assess differentiation, stage, and specific leukemia type.
The sternum is always the first-choice site because its periosteum offers no resistance.
Marrow specimens are collected only to measure circulating plasma antibodies.
qs.e: The notes distinguish fluid aspiration from a tissue biopsy and identify the iliac crest as the usual site. The instructor described the sternum as an alternative when other sites cannot be used and noted its tough periosteum.

qs.q: Which sequence matches the stem-cell/bone-marrow transplant process in lecture?
c: Reinfuse cells → collect cells → freeze cells → give marrow-wiping treatment.
Collect patient or donor blood/marrow cells → purify and concentrate in the lab → cryopreserve → give high-dose chemotherapy and/or radiation to wipe marrow → thaw and reinfuse cells.
Give low-dose aspirin → discard all collected cells → replace only plasma.
Collect cells → reinfuse them while frozen → omit marrow-directed treatment.
qs.e: The collected cells are processed and frozen before the patient's marrow-wiping treatment. They are then thawed and reinfused.

qs.q: In the transplant notes, what does 'allogeneic' mean?
c: Cells obtained from a donor
Only the patient's own cells
Synthetic replacement plasma
Unprocessed clotting factors
qs.e: Allogeneic means donor cells. The collection step can use patient or donor blood/marrow, but the term specifically identifies the donor source.

qs.q: Which statement correctly summarizes marrow production and hematopoietic regulation?
c: Marrow makes erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes; hematopoiesis is growth-factor driven, and synthetic EPO and G-CSF can be given.
Marrow makes only platelets; the liver makes all erythrocytes and leukocytes.
Hematopoiesis occurs independently of growth factors.
EPO and G-CSF are antibodies that destroy blood-cell precursors.
qs.e: Marrow produces all three listed blood-cell categories. The notes emphasize growth-factor-driven hematopoiesis and the clinical use of synthetic versions.

qs.q: Which chain correctly connects the RBC's job to erythropoiesis?
c: RBCs carry oxygen through iron in hemoglobin; hypoxia stimulates kidney EPO, which stimulates marrow RBC production.
RBCs carry oxygen through platelet granules; hypoxia suppresses kidney EPO.
The spleen produces EPO, which makes the liver produce neutrophils.
Hemoglobin carries antibodies, while kidney EPO creates fibrin.
qs.e: The RBC's oxygen-carrying role depends on iron in hemoglobin. The production chain is hypoxia → kidney EPO → marrow RBCs.

qs.q: Which interpretation of reticulocytes matches the notes?
c: Reticulocytes normally represent about 10% of RBCs; a high count always means marrow failure.
Reticulocytes normally represent about 1% of RBCs; a low count suggests sluggish marrow or missing ingredients, while a high count indicates a marrow response, most commonly to blood loss.
Reticulocytes are clotting factors; their count measures liver synthesis.
A low reticulocyte count proves the marrow is responding strongly to hemorrhage.
qs.e: The notes give approximately 1% as the reticulocyte proportion. The count helps distinguish inadequate production from an active marrow response.

qs.q: Which comparison of ABO and Rh antibody development matches the notes?
c: Both require a transfusion before any antibodies develop.
ABO antibodies develop by 3–6 months without transfusion; Rh antibodies develop only after exposure.
Rh antibodies develop by 3–6 months without exposure; ABO antibodies require exposure.
Neither ABO nor Rh antibodies can develop after infancy.
qs.e: The notes contrast ABO antibody development without transfusion with Rh antibody development only after exposure. The age given for ABO antibodies is 3–6 months.

qs.q: Which summary correctly distinguishes polycythemia vera from secondary polycythemia?
c: PV is marrow cancer; secondary polycythemia is linked to chronic hypoxia, with smoking, COPD, altitude, and athletes listed as examples; increased viscosity and volume are key effects.
PV is always caused by low vitamin K, whereas secondary polycythemia is always marrow cancer.
Both cause reduced blood viscosity and reduced blood volume.
Secondary polycythemia means an autoimmune loss of platelets.
qs.e: The notes identify PV as marrow cancer and secondary polycythemia as a response associated with chronic hypoxia. Increased viscosity and volume explain the emphasized effects.

qs.q: Which are the four broad causes of anemia listed in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Nutritional problems
Marrow failure
Blood loss
Hemolysis
Excessive RBC production from chronic hypoxia
qs.e: The four categories are nutrition, marrow failure, blood loss, and hemolysis. Excess RBC production from chronic hypoxia belongs with secondary polycythemia.

qs.q: Which RBC appearance and index pattern matches iron-deficiency anemia in lecture?
c: Macrocytic and hyperchromic, with increased MCV and MCHC
Microcytic and hypochromic, with decreased MCV and MCHC
Normocytic and normochromic, with no relationship to iron
Megaloblastic, with MCV decreased and MCHC increased
qs.e: The notes associate iron deficiency with small, hypochromic RBCs. Both MCV and MCHC are listed as decreased.

qs.q: Which anemia pattern is associated with vitamin B12 or B9 deficiency?
c: Microcytic/hypochromic
Macrocytic/megaloblastic
Polycythemic with increased volume
An isolated platelet-function defect
qs.e: The notes group B12 and B9 deficiencies with macrocytic/megaloblastic anemia. This contrasts with the microcytic/hypochromic iron-deficiency pattern.

qs.q: Which statements match the notes' discussion of pernicious anemia and vitamin-related consequences? Select all that apply.
c: Pernicious anemia is associated with absence of intrinsic factor.
The intrinsic-factor discussion names parietal cells, gastritis, gastrectomy, and some drugs.
B12-related neurological problems are linked to myelin.
B9 deficiency is associated with spina bifida.
Pernicious anemia is defined as hemorrhage caused by aspirin.
qs.e: The notes link pernicious anemia to absent intrinsic factor and name the associated gastric and drug contexts. They distinguish B12's myelin-related neurological effects from the B9–spina bifida association.

qs.q: Which symptom group matches the B12-related neurological findings in lecture?
c: Paresthesia, ataxia, and impaired position/vibration sensation
Epistaxis, petechiae, and isolated platelet clumping failure
Claudication, GI bleeding, and retroperitoneal bleeding
Only jaundice, with no neurological effects
qs.e: B12 neurological effects are linked to myelin and include paresthesia, ataxia, and position/vibration problems. These are separate from platelet-related bleeding signs.

qs.q: Which assessment summary matches acute blood loss in lecture?
c: Expect microcytic/hypochromic cells immediately and assess blood pressure before heart rate.
Expect a normocytic/normochromic pattern; watch heart rate first, then blood pressure; shock means organs are not adequately perfused.
Expect macrocytic/megaloblastic cells, and define shock as a high reticulocyte count.
Ignore heart rate because acute bleeding affects only platelet function.
qs.e: The notes associate acute bleeding with normocytic/normochromic anemia. They prioritize watching heart rate before blood pressure and define shock in terms of inadequate organ perfusion.

qs.q: Which statements about hemolysis match the notes? Select all that apply.
c: Sickle-related disease is a listed cause.
Toxins and burns are listed causes.
Mechanical valves and autoimmune processes are listed causes.
Hemolysis can lead to jaundice.
Hemolysis means excess production of functional RBCs without cell destruction.
qs.e: The named hemolysis causes include sickle, toxins, burns, mechanical valves, and autoimmune processes. Jaundice is the highlighted consequence.

qs.q: Which statement correctly combines the intended benefit of antiplatelets with the GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor details?
c: Antiplatelets intentionally help prevent arterial clots associated with ischemic stroke, TIA, stable angina, ACS, PAD, and MI; ReoPro, Integrilin, and Aggrastat are potent GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors with GI, urinary, and retroperitoneal bleeding risks.
Antiplatelets are intended to cause arterial clots; GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors prevent every form of bleeding.
ReoPro, Integrilin, and Aggrastat are PDE inhibitors used only for vitamin K replacement.
Antiplatelets treat headaches at baby-aspirin doses, and their only adverse effect is jaundice.
qs.e: The same reduction in platelet clumping that prolongs bleeding is used deliberately to prevent arterial clots. The notes identify the GP IIb/IIIa drugs as potent and list several serious bleeding locations.

qs.q: Approximately how long can released platelets hang out in the spleen, and why can splenomegaly lower the circulating count?
c: Up to about 8 hours; an enlarged spleen sequesters more platelets and excessively clears them.
About 3–6 months; the spleen stops liver factor synthesis.
About 1 minute; an enlarged spleen prevents all marrow growth-factor signaling.
About 7 days; platelets turn into neutrophils in the spleen.
qs.e: The notes give an approximately 8-hour splenic hangout after platelet release. A large spleen can both hold more platelets and over-clear cells.

qs.q: A critically ill patient has DIC but currently shows obvious bleeding without obvious signs of microclots. Which interpretation matches the lecture?
c: DIC is excluded because every patient must visibly show both problems.
DIC can still be present: its paradox is abnormal clotting and bleeding together, but some patients show only one side.
Bleeding proves that no clotting factors have been consumed.
The patient must have a primary disease called DIC unrelated to the critical illness.
qs.e: DIC's underlying pattern combines microclotting with factor consumption and hemorrhage. The instructor cautioned that an individual patient may visibly show only one side.

qs.q: Which assessment and intervention focus matches the neutropenia slide prompt?
c: Assess infection risk, fever, and mucous membranes; consider protective precautions and drugs that stimulate production.
Assume infection is impossible because there are fewer inflammatory cells.
Focus only on aspirin dosing and ignore fever.
Treat every low neutrophil count as a vitamin K absorption problem.
qs.e: The slide prompted attention to infection risk, fever, mucous membranes, protective precautions, and production-stimulating drugs. This follows from losing important early phagocytes.

qs.q: Which statements describe the four immune-system functions and their overlap? Select all that apply.
c: Immunity provides resistance to disease by defending against pathogens.
Self-versus-non-self recognition identifies foreign molecules for removal.
Inflammation defends against harmful agents and begins healing.
Cancer surveillance recognizes abnormal cells, using recognition mechanisms that also help identify pathogens.
Each function operates as a completely separate system.
qs.e: The four functions are immunity, self-versus-non-self recognition, inflammation, and cancer surveillance. They overlap rather than operating as four separate machines.

qs.q: What is another name for antigenic determinant sites, the uniquely shaped surface markers recognized by immune cells?
qs.e: Almost every cell has surface antigens with distinctive molecular shapes called antigenic determinant sites or epitopes. White cells recognize which shapes belong to the body.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes antigens, autoantigens, and antibodies?
c: Every antigen is harmful, whereas every antibody is a normal cell marker.
Autoantigens are normal body markers; antibodies are made against antigens identified as foreign.
Antibodies are membrane markers, whereas antigens are made to remove antibodies.
Foreign antigens are left alone, whereas autoantigens are normally targeted.
qs.e: An antigen is a marker used to distinguish self from non-self and is not inherently good or bad. Autoantigens are normal body markers; antibodies are made to help eliminate antigens recognized as foreign.

qs.q: Which description correctly identifies the two major immune-system components and the primary lymph structures?
c: Immune cells and their products, plus lymph structures; bone marrow and thymus are sites of immune-cell production or maturation.
Antibodies and cytokines only; tonsils and appendix produce all immune cells.
Lymph structures only; bone marrow and thymus merely filter lymph.
Immune cells and skin only; spleen and lymph nodes are the primary maturation structures.
qs.e: The two components are immune cells—including white cells and their products such as antibodies and cytokines—and lymph structures. Bone marrow and thymus are primary structures, and failure especially of bone marrow greatly impairs immunity.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe secondary lymph structures? Select all that apply.
c: Examples include the spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, and appendix.
Peyer's patches are GI lymphoid patches; MALT is mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue in respiratory, GI, and reproductive systems.
They trap antigens and promote interaction with mature immune cells.
The notes describe filtering foreign material from lymph; losing a secondary organ reduces efficiency but is not equivalent to losing bone marrow.
They are the primary sites where immune cells are born or mature.
qs.e: Secondary structures trap foreign material and bring antigens together with mature immune cells. People can lose structures such as tonsils or the appendix without becoming constantly ill, unlike the major impairment associated with primary-structure failure.

qs.q: Which comparison of innate and adaptive immunity matches the notes?
c: Innate is acquired and specific; adaptive is present at birth and nonspecific.
Both are ready at birth and target one antigen per cell.
Innate is natural/native/nonspecific and immediately available; adaptive is specific/acquired and develops later.
Adaptive acts first and activates an otherwise inactive innate system.
qs.e: Innate immunity is present at birth, responds immediately to foreign material, and holds pathogens while helping activate adaptive immunity. Adaptive immunity starts more slowly but is more effective because it targets particular antigens.

qs.q: Which list contains all five innate-immunity components, and why does a skin break matter?
c: T cells, B cells, memory cells, plasma cells, antibodies; a skin break stops antibody production.
Skin/mucous membranes, phagocytic white cells, NK cells, cytokines, complement; a skin break removes a first-line barrier.
Bone marrow, thymus, spleen, tonsils, appendix; a skin break removes primary maturation sites.
IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE; a skin break prevents placental transfer.
qs.e: The five innate components are barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, cytokines, and complement. Intact skin and mucous membranes prevent entry, and preventing infection is more efficient than clearing an established infection.

qs.q: Which statements describe phagocytic white cells and antigen presentation as taught in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: The main phagocytes named are neutrophils and monocyte-macrophages.
They engulf and digest foreign particles, tumor cells, and virus-infected cells.
They help hold the line until adaptive immunity starts.
As APCs, they process antigens and display them on their membranes for T-cell recognition.
Their antigen display prevents activation of adaptive immunity.
qs.e: Phagocytes both remove targets and act as antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Displaying processed antigen to T cells connects the innate response to activation of adaptive immunity.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes natural killer cells?
c: They are adaptive lymphocytes that require helper T activation before engulfing bacteria.
They are the only innate lymphocytes and kill tumor or virus-infected cells with toxins or enzymes rather than phagocytosis.
They produce antibodies against one specific antigen.
They are another name for B lymphocytes.
qs.e: NK cells are the only lymphocytes classified as innate in these notes; T and B cells are adaptive. NK cells damage target cells by releasing toxins or enzymes, not by engulfing them.

qs.q: What term names hormone-like proteins released by certain white cells to regulate other white cells?
qs.e: Cytokines are signals through which white cells direct the immune response of other white cells. Their functions can overlap, so one cytokine may have more than one effect.

qs.q: Which statements about cytokine examples, effects, and clinical use match the notes? Select all that apply.
c: Examples include interferons, interleukins, tumor necrosis factor, and colony-stimulating factor.
CSF/growth factors help regulate white-cell production, maturation, and activity; cytokine effects can increase or decrease these processes.
Cytokines can mediate inflammation and produce fever.
Synthetic cytokines and cytokine-blocking drugs are used clinically, so knowing a cytokine's function helps explain a drug order.
Each cytokine performs exactly one function and cannot overlap with another cytokine.
qs.e: Cytokines regulate cell development and activity as well as inflammation and fever. Their overlapping functions help explain why either giving a synthetic cytokine or blocking a cytokine may be clinically useful.

qs.q: How do cytokines produce fever, and why can fever help according to lecture?
c: They lower the hypothalamic set point and make all white cells inactive.
They raise the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point; higher temperatures hinder many pathogens and increase some white-cell activity.
They activate B-cell membrane IgD, which directly cools the body.
They prevent inflammation and stop all pathogen recognition.
qs.e: Cytokines act on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center to raise its set point. The notes describe fever as useful because many pathogens cannot survive the higher temperature and some white cells become more active.

qs.q: Approximately how many plasma proteins make up the complement cascade in lecture?
qs.e: Complement is a cascade of about 20 plasma proteins that circulate in inactive form, with one factor activating the next. Like clotting it is a cascade, but its outcome is enhanced immune clearance and inflammation rather than a clot. ⚠ Conflict: her lecture/handout says about 20 plasma proteins; the full Patho study sheet says 10. Go with her lecture (~20) unless she says otherwise.

qs.q: Complement activation causes mast cells and basophils to degranulate. Which interpretation is correct?
c: Similar cells release granule mediators such as histamine, leukotrienes, and bradykinin, promoting inflammation.
They release antibodies that enter infected cells.
They become primary lymph structures and mature T cells.
They stop all inflammation by removing cytokine receptors.
qs.e: Mast cells are described as very similar to basophils, and their granules contain inflammatory mediators. Inflammation is the key word emphasized for complement, which supports phagocytes and antibodies in pathogen clearance.

qs.q: What term means chemical signaling that calls white blood cells to the area where they are needed?
qs.e: Chemotaxis directs white cells toward an area needing defense. Complement activation enhances this recruitment.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly describes two effects of complement activation?
c: Lysis coats complexes; opsonization raises the hypothalamic set point.
Lysis bursts pathogens or abnormal cells; opsonization coats antigen-antibody complexes to improve phagocyte attachment.
Lysis produces memory B cells; opsonization matures cells in the thymus.
Lysis suppresses self-reactive cells; opsonization prevents phagocytosis.
qs.e: Lysis bursts targets, including cells that have become cancerous. Opsonization adds complement pieces to antigen-antibody complexes, improving the antibody 'handle' that helps phagocytes ingest difficult-to-grab encapsulated bacteria.

qs.q: Which statement correctly compares the adaptive branches and their target specificity?
c: Each T or B cell recognizes any foreign antigen; both branches act only outside cells.
Each T or B cell is programmed for one specific foreign antigen; T cells address intracellular microbes, while B-cell antibodies address extracellular microbes.
T cells make antibodies that enter cells, while B cells kill infected cells directly.
Only NK cells provide adaptive immunity.
qs.e: Cell-mediated immunity uses T cells for microbes inside cells, usually viruses, by killing the infected cell because T cells cannot enter it. Humoral immunity uses B-cell antibodies for extracellular microbes, usually bacteria, because antibodies cannot enter cells.

qs.q: A bacterium is located inside a host cell. Which branch takes this job according to lecture?
c: Humoral immunity, because antibodies can enter any infected cell.
Cell-mediated immunity, because T cells handle intracellular targets even when the microbe is a bacterium.
Only complement, because T cells recognize viruses but never bacteria.
Only secretory IgA, because all bacteria are mucosal targets.
qs.e: The usual pairing is T cells with viruses and B cells with bacteria, but location is the key distinction. When bacteria enter cells, T cells take that job too.

qs.q: Which membrane marker identifies helper T cells?
qs.e: CD4 is the helper T-cell membrane marker. The notes emphasize that almost all white cells have identifying markers.

qs.q: Which statements explain why helper T cells are called the adaptive immune system's master switch? Select all that apply.
c: An APC must show the helper T cell the antigen it is programmed to recognize.
The helper T cell releases cytokines that activate other T cells and B cells.
Helper T signals also improve the efficiency of macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells.
Loss of helper T cells prevents adaptive activation and makes innate immunity work less efficiently.
Innate immunity cannot begin any response until helper T cells activate it.
qs.e: Helper T cells are required to activate the rest of adaptive immunity in these notes. Innate immunity does not require helper T activation to begin, although helper T signals make innate cells more efficient.

qs.q: Which comparison of cytotoxic T cells and NK cells is correct?
c: CD8 cytotoxic T cells and NK cells both release toxins or enzymes, but cytotoxic T cells require helper activation and target one specific foreign antigen.
Both are innate, nonspecific cells requiring no helper activation.
CD8 cytotoxic T cells engulf targets, whereas NK cells make antibodies.
NK cells are antigen-specific adaptive cells; cytotoxic T cells attack anything foreign without activation.
qs.e: Cytotoxic/killer T cells carry CD8 and, like NK cells, kill tumor and virus-infected cells using toxins or enzymes. Unlike NK cells, they are adaptive, require helper T activation, and target a specific foreign antigen.

qs.q: Which statements about suppressor/regulatory T cells match the notes? Select all that apply.
c: They slow or stop the immune response after the pathogen is gone.
They suppress self-reactive white cells.
They help prevent autoimmune disease.
They are believed to be a subset of CD4+ or CD8+ cells.
Their main purpose is to sustain the immune response indefinitely.
qs.e: Regulatory T cells provide checks and balances by ending unnecessary responses and restraining attacks on normal self. The handout content in lecture describes them as believed to be a subset of CD4+ or CD8+ cells.

qs.q: Which description of memory T cells preserves both their established role in lecture and the lecturer's tentative longevity explanation?
c: They disappear immediately after infection; reduced ATP production explains their role.
They persist and enable rapid recognition on re-exposure; the lecturer suggested more mitochondria and ATP may help explain their longevity.
They require a permanently large army of active killer cells to recognize the pathogen.
They are short-lived cells that secrete all five antibody classes.
qs.e: Memory T cells persist so a later exposure can rapidly mobilize defenses without maintaining a large standing army of helper and cytotoxic cells. The mitochondria/ATP explanation was presented as something the lecturer had read and as a possibility, not a certainty.

qs.q: What happens to B cells after helper T activation?
c: They become NK cells and abandon antigen specificity.
They specialize into antibody-producing plasma cells and persistent memory B cells.
They become primary lymph organs.
They only suppress self-reactive T cells.
qs.e: Activated B cells specialize into plasma cells and memory B cells. Antibodies bind surface antigens to form antigen-antibody complexes, providing handles for phagocytes, while memory B cells rapidly drive plasma-cell proliferation and a large antibody burst on re-exposure.

qs.q: Which antibody class is most plentiful and is the only class that crosses the placenta?
qs.e: IgG is the most plentiful antibody class and the only placental-crossing class named in lecture. Maternal IgG supplies most newborn protection for the first few months.

qs.q: A student reviews a genetic inability to make IgA. Which finding and explanation best match the notes?
c: Eye, respiratory, and GI infections, because IgA in tears, saliva, and GI/respiratory secretions protects mucosal portals of entry.
Failure of placental antibody transfer, because only IgA crosses the placenta.
Loss of the earliest antibody response, because IgA is the first class to appear.
Loss of parasite defense only, because IgA exclusively mediates parasite responses.
qs.e: Secretory IgA protects mucous membranes and is found in tears, saliva, and GI and respiratory secretions. Inability to make IgA is linked in lecture to eye, respiratory, and GI infections.

qs.q: Which interpretation of hepatitis antibody results matches the notes?
c: IgM means an infection occurred at some unknown remote time, while IgG precisely dates it.
IgM suggests recent or current infection; IgG indicates infection sometime previously but cannot distinguish 2 months from 2 or 10 years.
IgG always proves current infection, and IgM lasts indefinitely.
Neither IgM nor IgG provides any information about exposure timing.
qs.e: IgM appears first and does not persist, making it the 'now' antibody in lecture. IgG lasts and indicates infection sometime, but its presence alone does not date that infection.

qs.q: Which description identifies IgD?
c: An antibody usually free in blood that crosses the placenta.
An antibody on the B-cell membrane that promotes proliferation and more antibody production when its antigen binds.
The main secretory antibody of tears and saliva.
The first antibody to appear during a current infection.
qs.e: IgD is not usually free in blood; it sits on the B-cell membrane like a monitor. Continued antigen binding stimulates B-cell proliferation and more antibody production.

qs.q: Which antibody class is associated with allergic reactions and defense against parasites?
qs.e: IgE is associated with both allergy and parasite defense. The lecturer emphasized that the allergy role is more often remembered locally because parasite disease is uncommon in the setting described.

qs.q: Which statement correctly defines active and passive immunity?
c: Active is innate immunity; passive is adaptive immunity.
Both are adaptive: active requires your immune system to generate the response, while passive involves receiving antibodies or immune cells from another source.
Both require your immune system to manufacture the received antibody.
Active means an injection, while passive means an infection.
qs.e: Active and passive immunity are both types of adaptive immunity. The distinction is who generates the protection, not whether it is delivered by a shot.

qs.q: Which examples represent active immunity? Select all that apply.
c: Making antibodies after getting strep throat.
Receiving a vaccine containing antigen and then making your own antibodies.
Receiving maternal antibodies across the placenta.
Receiving gamma globulin after a hepatitis B needle stick.
Receiving antibodies made by someone else.
qs.e: Infection and vaccination are active when the recipient's immune system generates the response. Placental antibodies and gamma globulin are passive because another source made the antibodies.

qs.q: Why is a gamma globulin injection after a hepatitis B needle stick classified differently from a vaccine?
c: Gamma globulin is IgG antibody and provides passive immunity; a vaccine supplies antigen and produces active immunity.
Both supply antigen and therefore provide active immunity.
Both supply IgG and therefore provide passive immunity.
Gamma globulin is innate immunity, while a vaccine is passive immunity.
qs.e: The contents of the syringe determine the classification. Gamma globulin supplies ready-made antibody, whereas vaccine antigen requires the recipient to make an immune response.

qs.q: Which comparison of onset and duration matches active and passive immunity?
c: Passive begins immediately but is short-term; active takes days to weeks initially but is long-lasting.
Passive takes weeks and lasts indefinitely; active begins instantly and disappears quickly.
Both begin immediately because both already contain antibody.
Both are short-term because neither recipient can replace antibodies.
qs.e: Passive protection begins when antibodies arrive but fades as they break down, because the recipient did not learn to replace them. Active immunity takes time to develop, but the recipient's system knows how to make more antibodies.

qs.q: In the lecturer's COVID vaccine example, protection was described as developing after approximately how long?
qs.e: The example illustrates the delay in active immunity while antibodies build up. The general initial active-immunity timeframe given is a few days to weeks.

qs.q: Which pattern best illustrates immunodeficiency as defined in lecture?
c: One or more immune branches fail, causing persistent or hard-to-treat infections, infections from ordinarily harmless organisms, and increased cancer incidence.
Only excessive fever occurs, without changes in infection risk.
All immune branches must fail before the term applies.
Cancer risk falls because abnormal-cell surveillance is unnecessary.
qs.e: Immunodeficiency means one or more immune branches are not working. Infection problems reflect impaired defense, and increased cancer incidence reflects failed cancer surveillance.

qs.q: Which statements about the scope and severity of immunodeficiency match the notes? Select all that apply.
c: Severity depends on how many immune branches are affected.
A deficiency may involve only one antibody class or all antibodies.
B cells and T cells may both be affected.
A deficiency may involve only phagocytes or only complement.
Immunodeficiency always affects every branch equally.
qs.e: Immunodeficiency ranges from a narrow defect to combined branch failure. The lecturer specifically contrasts single antibody-class problems with all-antibody, combined B/T, phagocyte, and complement deficiencies.

qs.q: Which list contains the five immunodeficiency types named in the handout content?
c: B-cell, T-cell, combined T/B-cell, complement-system, and phagocytosis disorders.
IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, and IgE only.
Primary, secondary, active, passive, and acquired immunity.
Skin, fever, allergy, vaccination, and cancer surveillance.
qs.e: The five categories are B-cell deficiency, T-cell deficiency, combined T/B-cell deficiency, complement disorders, and phagocytosis disorders. Complement disorders can involve missing components, while phagocytosis disorders involve neutrophils or monocytes/macrophages.

qs.q: A phagocyte engulfs an organism but cannot kill it after ingestion. Which defect matches the notes?
c: Missing enzymes needed to kill the ingested organism.
Loss of mobility despite intact killing enzymes.
Loss of chemotaxis despite intact killing enzymes.
Excess placental IgG transfer.
qs.e: One listed phagocyte failure pattern preserves engulfment but lacks the enzymes needed to kill what was ingested. Getting a target inside the phagocyte is therefore not sufficient for successful clearance.

qs.q: A phagocyte can kill organisms but no longer knows where to go. Which function has failed?
c: Antibody secretion.
Chemotaxis.
Placental transfer.
B-cell proliferation.
qs.e: Loss of chemotaxis removes the directional chemical guidance needed to reach a threatened area. Killing ability can remain intact even though the cell cannot locate its target.

qs.q: A phagocyte senses where it should go but cannot physically get there. What ability has it lost?
qs.e: The notes distinguish loss of mobility from loss of chemotaxis. This cell knows the destination but cannot travel to it.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly describes complement failure patterns in lecture?
c: Missing activating factor: inflammation cannot be generated through that tool; missing inhibiting factor: inflammation cannot be slowed once started.
Missing activating factor: uncontrolled inflammation; missing inhibiting factor: no inflammatory response.
Both defects only prevent antibody production.
Both defects only affect T-cell memory.
qs.e: An absent activating factor interrupts complement's inflammatory defense. An absent inhibiting factor removes a brake, so inflammation cannot be slowed once it begins.

qs.q: Which comparison correctly distinguishes primary from secondary immunodeficiency?
c: Primary is present from birth and linked to inherited gene defects/mutations causing defective white cells; secondary is acquired later.
Primary is always due to medications; secondary is always inherited.
Primary affects only complement; secondary affects only antibodies.
Primary means active immunity; secondary means passive immunity.
qs.e: Primary immunodeficiency is described as being born with a gene defect or mutation that produces white cells unable to do their job. Secondary immunodeficiency develops later from acquired causes.

qs.q: Which causes of secondary immunodeficiency are explicitly named in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Infection, such as AIDS.
Cancer, such as leukemia.
Immunosuppressive drugs.
Failure of another organ affecting immunity.
An inherited defect present from birth.
qs.e: The notes name infection, cancer, immunosuppressive drugs, and another organ's failure as acquired causes. An inherited defect present from birth belongs to the primary category.

qs.q: Which pairings correctly connect a failed immune function with an expected consequence? Select all that apply.
c: Failed cancer surveillance → increased cancer incidence.
Genetic inability to make IgA → eye, respiratory, and GI infections.
Loss of helper T cells → failure to activate the rest of adaptive immunity and less-efficient innate responses.
Loss of a complement inhibiting factor → difficulty slowing inflammation once it starts.
Removal of the appendix → the same degree of impairment as loss of bone marrow.
qs.e: The notes connect specific defects to predictable failures in defense or regulation. Loss of a secondary lymph structure such as the appendix is not equivalent to losing a primary structure such as bone marrow.

qs.q: On a second exposure to a previously encountered pathogen, which coordinated response best matches the notes?
c: Memory T cells rapidly mobilize cellular defenses, while memory B cells drive plasma-cell proliferation and a large antibody burst.
All immunity must start from scratch because memory cells disappear after recovery.
Passive antibodies teach the recipient to replace themselves indefinitely.
NK cells become plasma cells and secrete IgD into the blood.
qs.e: Memory T and B cells persist after the initial infection and accelerate responses on re-exposure. This can mobilize cellular defenses and increase antibody production before the person becomes sick again.

qs.q: A patient was born with an inherited gene mutation that produces defective white blood cells that cannot do their job. This is an example of which type of immunodeficiency?
c: Primary immunodeficiency
Secondary immunodeficiency
Autoimmune disorder
Hypersensitivity reaction
qs.e: Primary immunodeficiency is present from birth and is caused by an inherited gene defect or mutation that makes defective white cells. Secondary immunodeficiency is acquired later in life from something such as infection, cancer, or drugs.

qs.q: Liver failure can compromise a person's immunity because the liver makes:
c: Complement factors
Helper T cells
Natural killer cells
IgD antibodies
qs.e: The instructor stated that the liver makes complement factors, so liver failure removes part of the complement arm of defense. Without adequate complement you lose inflammation, chemotaxis, lysis, and opsonization.

qs.q: Some kidney diseases damage the glomerular membrane so that antibodies, which are normally too big to leak, spill into the urine. The result is:
c: Too few antibodies in the blood where they protect you
Too many antibodies in the blood
Excessive inflammation that cannot be stopped
Defective white cells that cannot do the job
qs.e: Normally antibodies are too large to cross the glomerular membrane. When that membrane is damaged, antibody is lost in the urine instead of circulating in the blood to protect the patient.

qs.q: AIDS is correctly classified as which type of disorder?
c: An immunodeficiency disorder
An autoimmune disorder
A hypersensitivity disorder
A chronic inflammatory disorder
qs.e: AIDS stands for Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome, so it is an immunodeficiency, not an autoimmune disorder. Students often say the acronym and forget what it actually means.

qs.q: Most viruses contain either RNA or DNA. A retrovirus such as HIV contains:
c: RNA only
DNA only
Both RNA and DNA
Neither RNA nor DNA
qs.e: The instructor emphasized that a retrovirus has RNA only. Because it has no DNA of its own, it must first copy its RNA into DNA using reverse transcriptase.

qs.q: Which substance changes the viral RNA of HIV into viral DNA inside the host cell?
c: Reverse transcriptase
Complement activating factor
Opsonizing antibody
A cytokine
qs.e: Reverse transcriptase is the enzyme named on the handout that converts viral RNA into viral DNA. That viral DNA is then inserted into the host cell's DNA.

qs.q: What is the main real-world blood route of HIV transmission described by the instructor?
c: Shared needles among IV drug users
Screened U.S. blood transfusion
Handshake with an infected person
Sharing a toilet seat
qs.e: U.S. blood has been screened since the mid-1980s, so transfusion is not the main blood route. Shared needles among IV drug users are the major route; healthcare needle sticks are rare but have transmitted it.

qs.q: About what risk of HIV transmission did the instructor give for a screened U.S. blood transfusion?
c: About 1 in 2 million
About 1 in 20
About 1 in 2,000
About 1 in 200,000
qs.e: The middle-of-the-road figure she used was about 1 in 2 million transfusions. She also noted that about 4.5 million Americans a year would die without a needed transfusion, so patients who need blood should receive it.

qs.q: Perinatal transmission of HIV usually occurs:
c: Through exposure to mom's blood in labor and delivery, or through breastfeeding
Across the placenta during the pregnancy
Through casual contact with the newborn after birth
Through a handshake or shared glass
qs.e: The placenta is a good barrier, so in utero transmission is not the usual route. Transmission usually happens at delivery through exposure to mom's blood or later through breastfeeding, and it depends on mom's viral load.

qs.q: How long can the latent phase of HIV infection last even without antivirals?
c: Up to 10 years or more
About 2 to 3 days
Only about one week
Exactly 6 months
qs.e: The latent phase can last up to 10 years or more without treatment, and drugs may stretch it longer. During this time the virus is present and the person can still transmit it.

qs.q: The diagnosis changes from HIV infection to AIDS when the helper T (CD4) count falls below:
qs.e: The AIDS threshold is a CD4 count below 200 OR development of an AIDS-defining illness. This is a favorite test number, so memorize 200.

qs.q: The normal helper T (CD4) count range given by the instructor is about:
c: Below 200
qs.e: Normal helper T counts run about 600 to 1,200. Knowing the normal frame makes the below-200 AIDS threshold meaningful.

qs.q: With the cheaper screening tests used on large numbers of people, the HIV window period is about:
c: 1 to 3 months
2 to 3 weeks
2 to 3 years
1 to 2 days
qs.e: The window period length depends on the test. The cheaper mass screening tests have a window of about 1 to 3 months.

qs.q: Blood banks use a more expensive test that shortens the window period to about:
c: 2 to 3 weeks
1 to 3 months
6 to 12 months
24 hours
qs.e: The more expensive blood bank test shortens the window to about 2 or 3 weeks. Even so, no test can detect infection during the window, which is why standard precautions are used on everybody.

qs.q: A patient's EIA screening test is positive but the follow-up Western blot is negative. This means:
c: The EIA was a false positive
The patient definitely has HIV infection
The patient has AIDS
A third test will confirm AIDS
qs.e: The Western blot is the confirmatory test: a positive result confirms HIV infection, and a negative result means the EIA was a false positive. Screens are designed to favor false positives so infected people do not fall through.

qs.q: Which statement is true of the home oral swab HIV test?
c: You read it in about 20 minutes; it is EIA only, and a positive still needs a Western blot
The lab runs both tests and phones the result in 3 to 7 days
It is a Western blot that takes 1 to 3 months
A positive result by itself confirms AIDS
qs.e: The home oral swab is EIA only and read by the user in about 20 minutes. The home finger-stick mail-in kit is the one where the lab runs both tests and phones results in about 3 to 7 days.

qs.q: Without antivirals, death after an AIDS diagnosis occurs in about:
c: 2 to 3 years
2 to 3 weeks
24 hours
10 to 15 years
qs.e: Without antivirals the instructor gave a survival figure of about 2 to 3 years. Antivirals have slowed progression enough that AIDS is now treated as a chronic illness.

qs.q: The most common AIDS pneumonia is caused by:
c: Pneumocystis jirovecii
Mycobacterium avium complex
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Haemophilus influenzae
qs.e: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) from Pneumocystis jirovecii is the most common AIDS pneumonia. The old name Pneumocystis carinii refers to the animal form.

qs.q: Oral hairy leukoplakia in an AIDS patient is caused by:
c: Epstein-Barr virus
Candida
Herpes simplex
Pneumocystis jirovecii
qs.e: Epstein-Barr virus can cause oral hairy leukoplakia. Candida, CMV, and herpes simplex cause other mouth and esophagus lesions with painful eating and swallowing.

qs.q: Kaposi sarcoma is best described as:
c: A vascular malignancy, a cancer of the cells lining some smaller blood vessels
A fungus that causes the most common AIDS pneumonia
An opportunistic bacterium with TB-like symptoms
Inflammation of the stomach and intestines
qs.e: Kaposi sarcoma is a cancer of the cells lining some smaller blood vessels, so it presents as raised reddish-purple skin lesions on the trunk, head, or neck. It can also involve internal organs and cause organ dysfunction.

qs.q: For weight loss to count as AIDS wasting syndrome, it must occur:
c: Without an opportunistic infection or cancer that could explain it
Only when the patient also has Pneumocystis pneumonia
Only after a blood transfusion
Only in patients with a normal helper T count
qs.e: Wasting syndrome requires weight loss that is NOT explained by an opportunistic infection or cancer. In parts of Africa with a lot of AIDS it is called slim disease.

qs.q: An undetectable viral level is not the same as cured because:
c: Viral DNA is still sitting in host-cell DNA and can still make new virus
The patient is still contagious through a handshake
The virus hides in the meninges and cannot be tested
Complement is still generating inflammation
qs.e: Antivirals slow replication but cannot remove the viral DNA inserted into host-cell DNA. That is why the instructor refuses to say AIDS has been cured.

qs.q: Which antibody is the most plentiful and is the one that crosses the placenta?
c: IgG
IgA
IgM
IgE
qs.e: IgG is the greatest concentration and crosses the placenta ('goo-goo-gaga'), giving the newborn temporary protection. IgA defends secretions, IgM appears first with current infection, and IgE is allergy and parasites.

qs.q: In AIDS gastroenteritis, the primary symptom is diarrhea because:
c: The inflamed gut cannot absorb fluid
The esophagus is blocked by Candida lesions
The meninges are inflamed
Antibodies are lost in the urine
qs.e: Gastroenteritis is inflammation of the stomach and intestines, and an inflamed gut cannot absorb fluid. In AIDS it can last months, antibiotics often fail, and large fluid and nutrient losses cause weight loss.

qs.q: Which of the following are causes of SECONDARY (acquired) immunodeficiency? Select all that apply.
c: An infection such as AIDS
A cancer such as lymphoma
Immunosuppressive drugs
Another organ failure that hits immunity, such as liver or kidney failure
An inherited gene mutation present at birth
qs.e: Secondary immunodeficiency is acquired later in life from infection, cancer, immunosuppressive drugs, or organ failure. An inherited gene mutation is the cause of PRIMARY immunodeficiency, which is present from birth.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe how HIV replicates? Select all that apply.
c: HIV enters a host cell, usually a helper T cell
Reverse transcriptase changes the viral RNA into viral DNA
The viral DNA is inserted into the host cell's DNA
The host cell DNA becomes the protein recipe that makes more virus until the helper T breaks apart and releases new HIV
HIV is destroyed immediately when it enters the helper T cell
qs.e: HIV enters a helper T, converts RNA to DNA with reverse transcriptase, inserts that DNA into host DNA, and hijacks the cell's protein-making machinery. New virus is released when the helper T breaks apart, and the cycle repeats in other helper T cells.

qs.q: Which of the following can transmit HIV? Select all that apply.
c: Semen
Vaginal secretions
A handshake
A toilet seat
A shared drinking glass
qs.e: HIV spreads through semen and vaginal secretions, blood, and perinatally. It is NOT spread by casual contact such as handshakes, toilet seats, or shared glasses.

qs.q: Which statements are true of the latent phase of HIV infection? Select all that apply.
c: The person is infected but has no immunodeficiency symptoms yet
The immune system keeps viral levels low for a time
The person can still transmit the virus to others
The infected cell serves as a reservoir for the virus
The person already meets the diagnosis of AIDS
qs.e: The latent phase means the virus is present but the immune system is still keeping it in check, and the infected cell acts as a reservoir. It is dangerous because transmission can still occur, and it is NOT yet AIDS.

qs.q: Which of these are NOT opportunistic in an AIDS patient (that is, they can occur even with a normal immune system)? Select all that apply.
c: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
Mycobacterium avium complex
Cervical cancer
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
