qs.e: TB itself is not opportunistic, and cervical cancer and non-Hodgkin lymphoma can occur with a normal immune system. MAC is an opportunistic cousin of TB, and PCP is a classic opportunistic infection.

qs.q: Which organisms cause lesions of the mouth and esophagus in AIDS? Select all that apply.
c: Candida
Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
Herpes simplex
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Haemophilus influenzae
qs.e: Candida, CMV, and herpes simplex lesions make eating and swallowing painful and can cause retrosternal pain. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are the ordinary respiratory bugs that still cause infections in these patients.

qs.q: What are the four functions of the immune system? Select all that apply.
c: Immunity
Distinguishing self vs non-self
Inflammation
Cancer surveillance
Blood clotting
qs.e: The immune system provides immunity, distinguishes self from non-self, produces inflammation, and performs cancer surveillance. These functions overlap, and blood clotting is not one of them.

qs.q: Which are PRIMARY lymph organs? Select all that apply.
c: Bone marrow
Thymus
Spleen
Tonsils
Mucosal patches
qs.e: Primary lymph organs are bone marrow and thymus; the spleen, nodes, tonsils, appendix, and mucosal patches are secondary. Failure of a primary organ hurts more because the cells never get made or matured properly.

qs.q: Which are components (pieces) of INNATE immunity? Select all that apply.
c: Barriers
Phagocytes and antigen-presenting cells (APCs)
Natural killer (NK) cells
Cytokines
Antibodies made by plasma cells
qs.e: The five innate pieces are barriers, phagocytes/APCs, NK cells, cytokines, and complement. Antibodies made by plasma cells belong to adaptive immunity.

qs.q: Which statements correctly compare active and passive immunity? Select all that apply.
c: Active immunity takes longer to develop than passive immunity
Active immunity lasts longer than passive immunity
A vaccine gives active immunity because it delivers an antigen
Gamma globulin gives passive immunity because it delivers ready-made antibody
Passive immunity creates memory that lasts for years
qs.e: Active immunity (vaccine = antigen) is slow but long-lasting because the body makes its own response and memory. Passive immunity (gamma globulin = antibody) is fast but short because the person receives preformed antibody and makes no memory.

qs.q: A person is missing an ACTIVATING complement factor, so the complement system cannot generate ________.
qs.e: Without an activating factor, complement cannot be turned on at all, so one whole defense tool is missing. The key word for complement is inflammation.

qs.q: A person is missing an INHIBITING complement factor, so once inflammation starts it cannot be ________.
qs.e: Inhibiting factors act as the brakes on complement; without them inflammation runs unchecked once it begins. Note the contrast with a missing activating factor, where inflammation cannot be generated at all.

qs.q: An infection caused by an organism that does not bother a person with a normal immune system is called a(n) ________ infection.
qs.e: An opportunistic infection takes advantage of impaired immunity, which is why AIDS patients get organisms healthy people fight off easily. Recognizing this term is essential for interpreting AIDS complications.

qs.q: The time between HIV infection and seroconversion, when the blood test flips from negative to positive, is called the ________.
qs.e: During the window period no one knows the person is infected, so no one is preventing transmission. This is the dangerous part of the latent phase and the reason standard precautions are used on every patient.

qs.q: HAND, the neurocognitive disorder seen in some AIDS patients, stands for ________.
qs.e: HAND occurs in maybe half of AIDS patients, but most have no symptoms or only mild ones, and only a small percent progress to dementia. Most late-stage patients remain oriented and in touch with reality.

qs.q: In parts of Africa where wasting is extremely common, AIDS wasting syndrome is called ________.
qs.e: Wasting syndrome requires weight loss without an explaining opportunistic infection or cancer. In high-prevalence areas of Africa this wasting is so typical that the illness is called slim disease.

qs.q: Why does active immunity last longer than passive immunity? (Answer in a few words.)
qs.e: Active immunity produces memory cells, so the second response is fast and long-lasting. Passive immunity delivers ready-made antibody with no memory, so it fades quickly.

qs.q: Why is antibody protection a baby receives through the placenta considered PASSIVE rather than active immunity? (Answer in a few words.)
a: the baby did not make the antibodies
qs.e: The mother made the antibody and the baby simply received preformed IgG, so the baby's own immune system did not respond or build memory. That makes it passive immunity.

qs.q: What term means the absence of an immune response against a person's own antigens?
qs.e: Self-tolerance prevents an immune response directed against the person's own antigens. Its breakdown is the pathological change underlying autoimmunity.

qs.q: Which mechanisms maintain self-tolerance? Select all that apply.
c: Regulatory T cells suppress self-reactive immune cells and turn responses off.
Self-reactive B cells are eliminated during maturation in bone marrow.
Self-reactive T cells are eliminated during maturation in the thymus.
T-cell activation requires antigen display on the appropriate MHC class.
Helper T cells activate whenever they encounter an antigen without MHC display.
qs.e: The notes describe suppression, deletion during maturation, and appropriate MHC display as safeguards. The MHC requirement helps prevent activation against improperly displayed targets.

qs.q: Which description correctly combines the location and antigen-display role of Class I MHC?
c: Mainly macrophages/APCs; displays extracellular antigens obtained by phagocytosis.
Nearly all nucleated cells, mostly nonphagocytic cells; displays intracellular self antigens, viruses, and abnormal proteins from mutations.
Only regulatory T cells; displays antibodies.
Only bone marrow cells; displays exclusively extracellular antigens.
qs.e: MHC molecules are cell-surface displays for T-cell inspection. Class I presents intracellular antigens on nearly all nucleated cells, mostly cells not capable of phagocytosis.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly identifies the T cells that inspect each MHC class?
c: Class I–CD4 helper T; Class II–CD8 cytotoxic T.
Class I–B cells; Class II–regulatory T cells.
Class I–CD8 cytotoxic T; Class II–CD4 helper T.
Both classes–CD4 helper T only.
qs.e: Class I gates recognition by CD8 cytotoxic T cells, while Class II gates recognition by CD4 helper T cells. Without the appropriate antigen–MHC match, the T cell does not activate against that target.

qs.q: A macrophage phagocytizes a foreign antigen originating outside the cell. Which display is needed to activate a helper T cell?
c: Extracellular antigen displayed on Class II MHC.
Extracellular antigen displayed on Class I MHC.
Free antigen without any MHC display.
Antigen displayed on IgE attached to a mast cell.
qs.e: Class II MHC is found mainly on macrophages/APCs and displays antigens from extracellular sources. No Class II display means no helper-T activation.

qs.q: Which statement matches the recording's account of MHC typing for transplantation?
c: HLA is an inflammation marker measured by ESR.
MHC type is checked by urine culture, and matching is easy because there is one allele.
HLA testing measures only circulating antibodies and does not involve DNA.
HLA is the human name for MHC genes; DNA testing checks type, and the notes report about 128 genes coding one MHC molecule with 50–650 alleles.
qs.e: The recording notes identify HLA/DNA testing as the way MHC type is checked. They report about 128 genes and 50–650 alleles as the explanation for difficult transplant matching.

qs.q: Besides sequestered antigens, which theories of autoimmunity are listed in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Abnormal self-antigen structure.
Faulty T-cell receptor/MHC interaction.
Disorder of immune surveillance.
Antigenic mimicry.
Excessive maintenance of normal self-tolerance.
qs.e: The listed theories include all four selected mechanisms plus sequestered antigens. Autoimmunity reflects breakdown, rather than excessive maintenance, of self-tolerance.

qs.q: Antibodies against group A beta-hemolytic strep may also attack similar self antigens. What is this mechanism called?
qs.e: A foreign antigen resembles a self antigen closely enough that antibodies attack both. The notes link strep mimicry to heart damage in rheumatic heart disease and kidney damage in glomerulonephritis.

qs.q: Why can release of sequestered antigens after injury provoke an autoimmune response?
c: They are foreign antigens made by microorganisms.
They previously activated every lymphocyte during early development.
They are self antigens that did not encounter lymphocytes during early development and are later treated as foreign.
They prevent all antibody formation after injury.
qs.e: Sequestered antigens were not encountered by lymphocytes during early development. Injury can release them, allowing the immune system to treat them as foreign.

qs.q: Which patient has the highest autoimmune risk in the class practice item?
c: A male whose only listed factor is smoking.
A female whose mother has SLE.
An older male whose only listed factor is age.
A patient whose only listed finding is a high red-cell count.
qs.e: The notes emphasize genes and gender/hormones, with autoimmune disease more common in women. Triggers can include viruses, microorganisms, chemicals, or release of sequestered antigens; being female with a first-degree relative with SLE is the highest-risk practice combination.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes autoimmune disease distribution and course?
c: A quiet period proves the disease is cured.
Organ-specific disease necessarily affects many organs.
Systemic disease is restricted to one tissue.
Organ-specific disease targets one tissue, systemic disease affects many organs, and a remission is not a cure.
qs.e: Autoimmune disease can remit and exacerbate. Organ-specific disease stays on one tissue, whereas systemic disease affects many organs; SLE is the systemic example.

qs.q: In addition to ANA, which tests are listed as autoantibody tests? Select all that apply.
c: Anti-DNA.
Anti-CCP.
Antiphospholipid.
Rheumatoid factor.
ESR.
qs.e: ANA, anti-DNA, anti-CCP, antiphospholipid, and rheumatoid factor are listed as autoantibody tests. ESR is an inflammatory marker rather than an autoantibody test.

qs.q: In the listed autoantibody tests, what does ANA stand for?
qs.e: A positive ANA points toward autoimmunity, not infection. The notes distinguish it from inflammatory markers and cultures.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains CRP, fibrinogen, and ESR?
c: CRP and fibrinogen are liver-made acute-phase proteins induced by cytokines; ESR reflects how fast red cells settle and rises as these proteins increase.
All three specifically diagnose SLE.
ESR measures how fast white cells enter injured tissue.
CRP and fibrinogen are autoantibodies, and ESR proves infection.
qs.e: Cytokines signal the liver to make CRP and fibrinogen during inflammation. Red cells settle faster when these proteins are elevated; all three findings indicate inflammation rather than a specific disease.

qs.q: Which statements about autoimmune treatment, including SLE treatment, match the notes? Select all that apply.
c: Immunosuppressive drugs are immunomodulators.
Monoclonal antibodies are immunomodulators.
Corticosteroids are synthetic cortisol and have many side effects.
NSAIDs such as Motrin, ibuprofen, and aspirin are used for symptom control.
A positive ANA requires antimicrobial treatment rather than immune-directed treatment.
qs.e: The notes describe two treatment levels: immunomodulation and anti-inflammatory symptom control. Corticosteroids are included among immunomodulators and emphasized for their many side effects.

qs.q: What procedure filters antibodies out of plasma?
qs.e: Plasmapheresis is defined in lecture as filtering antibodies out of plasma. It is identified as a vocabulary item.

qs.q: What is the full name of SLE?
qs.e: SLE involves antibodies against many self antigens, including nuclear antigens such as DNA and RNA. It is the notes' worked example of systemic autoimmunity.

qs.q: Which sequence explains the repeating tissue-injury cycle in SLE?
c: IgE binds allergen → mast cells degranulate → isolated muscle damage.
T cells kill pancreatic cells → no antibody formation → complement is unnecessary.
Cell damage releases DNA → anti-DNA antibodies form and bind DNA → complexes deposit → complement and inflammation cause further damage.
Self-reactive cells are deleted → self-tolerance strengthens → complexes disappear permanently.
qs.e: SLE immune complexes can deposit in tissues anywhere in the body and activate complement. The resulting inflammation causes more damage and DNA release, creating a type III hypersensitivity cycle.

qs.q: Which SLE assessment and diagnostic statements are supported by the notes? Select all that apply.
c: Bruising, rash, and a malar or butterfly rash may occur.
Lupus arthritis and kidney involvement, including renal failure, may occur.
The heart, eyes, lungs, GI tract, and blood cells may be involved.
The disease remits and flares, and diagnosis follows ruling out other causes.
A quiet period excludes SLE and confirms permanent cure.
qs.e: SLE can affect skin, joints, kidneys, and multiple other organs and blood cells. Its fluctuating course does not establish cure, and the notes describe a rule-out diagnosis.

qs.q: Which statement best defines inflammation and the suffix -itis?
c: Inflammation means confirmed infection, and -itis identifies its organism.
Inflammation is tissue's reaction to injury regardless of cause; -itis means inflammation of the named organ.
Inflammation is exclusively an autoimmune response, and -itis means tissue repair is complete.
Inflammation occurs only when cultures are positive.
qs.e: Infection can cause inflammation, but inflammation is not proof of infection. The reaction is directed toward beginning healing after injury of any cause.

qs.q: Which are purposes of inflammation? Select all that apply.
c: Neutralize or destroy harmful agents.
Limit harmful agents' spread.
Prepare damaged tissue for repair by clearing dead tissue and bringing nutrients.
Guarantee that no collagen or scar will form.
Prove that the original injury was caused by infection.
qs.e: Inflammation starts healing by controlling the harmful agent and preparing the tissue for repair. It does not establish infection, and repair can include collagen deposition and scarring.

qs.q: Redness, heat, swelling, and pain are four cardinal signs of inflammation. What is the fifth?
qs.e: The five cardinal signs are redness, heat, swelling, pain, and impaired function. The notes connect fluid leakage with swelling, pain, and loss of function.

qs.q: Which are listed chemical mediators of inflammation released from mast cells and immune cells? Select all that apply.
c: Histamine and prostaglandins.
Leukotrienes.
Plasma proteases and platelet-activating factor.
Other cytokines.
ANA and anti-CCP as the listed primary mediator group.
qs.e: The notes attribute most inflammatory mechanisms to release of these chemical mediators. ANA and anti-CCP are listed as autoantibody tests, not as this mediator group.

qs.q: Which sequence and sign explanation correctly describe the vascular response to injury?
c: Sustained vasoconstriction stops blood delivery and directly produces warmth.
Vasodilation occurs without any permeability change, so no fluid enters tissue.
Capillaries become less permeable, and tissue fluid returns immediately to blood.
Brief vasoconstriction is followed by vasodilation and increased permeability; increased blood delivery causes redness and warmth, while leakage causes swelling, pain, and impaired function.
qs.e: The vascular response briefly constricts and then dilates vessels while allowing fluid into tissue. Increased delivery brings blood, oxygen, fuel, and antibody to the area.

qs.q: Which white cells are the first to arrive in the injured area according to lecture?
qs.e: The cellular response involves white cells moving into the injured area, with neutrophils arriving first. Monocytes and macrophages also arrive and can present antigen.

qs.q: Which findings and effects belong to the cytokine-driven acute-phase response?
c: Fever, increased white cells, and skeletal muscle protein breakdown; fever can impair pathogens and improve some white-cell activity.
Fever alone, with a required positive culture.
Reduced white cells, increased muscle protein storage, and guaranteed infection.
Only local redness, without any systemic effects.
qs.e: The acute-phase response includes fever, more white cells, and skeletal muscle catabolism, meaning muscle protein breakdown. Fever can be useful because many pathogens cannot tolerate the heat and some white cells function better.

qs.q: Which set correctly matches exudate descriptions?
c: Serous–pus; sero-sanguineous–clear yellow; purulent–watery blood.
Serous–watery blood; sero-sanguineous–pus; purulent–clear yellow.
Serous–clear, light yellow; sero-sanguineous–watery blood; purulent–pus.
Serous–clear, light yellow; sero-sanguineous–pus; purulent–watery blood.
qs.e: Serous exudate is clear and light yellow, sero-sanguineous is watery blood, and purulent is pus. These descriptions distinguish the listed forms of exudate.

qs.q: Which consequences of abnormal inflammation or impaired immunity are described in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Prolonged inflammation can get out of control.
Chronic irritation can cause metaplasia.
Persistent inflammation can cause loss of function and deformity, as in rheumatoid arthritis.
Impaired immunity can prevent agent neutralization, containment, and preparation for repair.
Impaired immunity guarantees faster repair and better containment.
qs.e: Excessive or persistent inflammation can damage tissue and function. Too little effective immune activity produces the opposite problem: the agent remains uncontrolled and repair is not properly set up.

qs.q: A patient has a fever the day after surgery and later develops a scar. Which interpretation is supported by the notes?
c: The fever automatically proves infection, and scarring proves autoimmunity.
The fever may be an acute-phase response to tissue injury, and the scar can result from collagen deposition during repair.
Both findings rule out an inflammatory response.
The fever proves a type I allergy, and scars form only after hypersensitivity.
qs.e: A postoperative fever is not automatically infection; tissue injury can trigger the acute-phase response. The notes also name scarring from collagen deposition as a cost of inflammatory repair.

qs.q: Which statement correctly applies the ABCD hypersensitivity memory aid?
c: I–Delayed; II–Complex; III–Allergies; IV–antiBodies.
All four types are immediate antibody responses.
I–Allergies; II–antiBodies; III–immune Complex/complement; IV–Delayed, with all four mediated by T cells.
I–Allergies; II–antiBodies; III–immune Complex/complement; IV–Delayed, with I–III on the antibody/immediate side and IV mediated by T cells.
qs.e: The slide's ABCD aid separates the antibody-mediated types I–III from delayed, T-cell-mediated type IV. The notes describe I–III as the immediate/B-cell side.

qs.q: What initiates a type I hypersensitivity reaction?
c: An allergen binds IgE already on mast cells or basophils, causing degranulation and mediator release.
IgG binds acetylcholine receptors and directly prevents muscle contraction.
Immune complexes deposit and activate complement.
T cells directly kill tissue without antibody involvement.
qs.e: Type I is the IgE/immediate reaction. Allergen binding to cell-bound IgE causes mast cells or basophils to release inflammatory mediators.

qs.q: Which examples are classified as type I hypersensitivity in lecture? Select all that apply.
c: Allergic rhinitis or hay fever.
Asthma.
Urticaria or hives, and atopic dermatitis or eczema.
Anaphylaxis.
Poison ivy contact dermatitis.
qs.e: The class groups hay fever, asthma, hives, eczema, and anaphylaxis under type I IgE hypersensitivity. Poison ivy contact dermatitis is the type IV example.

qs.q: What term is defined in the type I extras as face swelling?
qs.e: The notes define angioedema as face swelling. They list it among the additional type I hypersensitivity concepts.

qs.q: Which description explains anaphylactic shock in lecture?
c: Localized T-cell killing raises blood pressure.
Autoantibodies destroy only pancreatic cells.
System-wide degranulation causes blood pressure to fall.
A positive ANA causes red cells to settle faster.
qs.e: Anaphylaxis involves system-wide degranulation. The resulting fall in blood pressure is described as anaphylactic shock.

qs.q: Which combination correctly identifies type I predisposition and the treatment categories listed in lecture?
c: No prior exposure or genetic contribution; antimicrobials only.
Prior sensitizing exposure and genetic makeup; antihistamines, anti-inflammatories, and corticosteroids.
High red-cell count alone; plasmapheresis as the only listed treatment.
Positive urine culture; insulin and cultures.
qs.e: Prior exposure may sensitize a person through inhalation, swallowing, injection, or skin contact, and genetic makeup also predisposes. The listed treatment categories are antihistamines, anti-inflammatories, and corticosteroids.

qs.q: Which mechanism defines type II hypersensitivity?
c: IgE on mast cells binds allergens.
T cells release cytokines without antibodies.
Deposited immune complexes cause damage only through subsequent inflammation.
IgG or IgM binds a cell or tissue antigen, and the antigen-antibody reaction itself damages the target.
qs.e: Type II is antibody-mediated/cytotoxic hypersensitivity involving IgG or IgM. The notes emphasize that the antigen-antibody reaction itself, rather than inflammation after complex deposition, damages the target.

qs.q: Which pair consists of type II examples, with the listed mechanism correctly explained?
c: Blood transfusion reaction and myasthenia gravis; antibodies against acetylcholine receptors prevent muscle contraction in myasthenia gravis.
SLE and poison ivy; both involve IgE on mast cells.
Asthma and eczema; both are caused by T cells attacking pancreatic cells.
Type 1 diabetes and transplant rejection; both require IgM against acetylcholine receptors.
qs.e: Blood transfusion reactions and myasthenia gravis are the notes' type II examples. Myasthenia gravis involves antibodies against acetylcholine receptors, interfering with muscle contraction.

qs.q: What distinguishes type III tissue damage from type II tissue damage?
c: Type III has no antibodies, whereas type II uses T cells.
Type III involves IgE degranulation, whereas type II involves complement only.
Type III damage comes from inflammation after immune-complex deposition and complement activation; type II damage comes from the antigen-antibody reaction itself.
Type III protects tissues from inflammation, whereas type II always affects only the skin.
qs.e: The harmful step differs: direct antigen-antibody reaction in type II versus subsequent complement-driven inflammation in type III. SLE is the listed type III example.

qs.q: Which mechanism defines type IV hypersensitivity?
c: IgE-dependent degranulation of basophils.
Delayed T-cell responses that kill directly or release tissue-damaging cytokines, without antibodies.
IgG or IgM binding directly damages a target.
Antibody complexes deposit and activate complement.
qs.e: Type IV is delayed and T-cell-mediated. T cells either kill directly or release cytokines that damage tissue; antibody is not involved.

qs.q: Which are listed examples of type IV hypersensitivity? Select all that apply.
c: Poison ivy contact dermatitis.
Type 1 diabetes, with T cells attacking pancreatic cells.
Transplant rejection.
SLE.
Blood transfusion reaction.
qs.e: The notes list contact dermatitis, type 1 diabetes, and transplant rejection as type IV examples. SLE is type III, and blood transfusion reaction is type II.

qs.q: AIDS belongs to which broad immune-disorder category rather than autoimmunity?
qs.e: Immunodeficiency is failure to attack a real threat, whereas autoimmunity attacks self. Allergy is a type of hypersensitivity, not a separate fourth immune system.

qs.q: Which problem–assessment–treatment combination correctly describes immunodeficiency in the class sorting table?
c: Self-tissue damage–autoantibodies–immunosuppressants.
Unnecessary inflammation–allergy testing–antihistamines.
Infection–ANA–corticosteroids only.
Infection–cultures and WBC count–antimicrobials.
qs.e: The class table links immunodeficiency with infection, checked using cultures and WBC count and treated with antimicrobials. A WBC rise alone still does not prove infection because it can occur in the acute-phase response.

qs.q: Which problem–assessment–treatment combination correctly describes hypersensitivity in the sorting table?
c: Allergic reaction and unnecessary inflammation–allergy testing–antihistamines and/or anti-inflammatory drugs.
Infection–cultures–antimicrobials.
Self-tissue damage–autoantibodies–antimicrobials only.
Failure to respond to threats–HLA testing–NSAIDs only.
qs.e: The table connects hypersensitivity with unnecessary inflammation and allergic reactions. It lists allergy testing and treatment with antihistamines and/or anti-inflammatory drugs.

qs.q: Which combination correctly describes autoimmunity and the limits of inflammatory markers?
c: Infection–cultures–antimicrobials; elevated ESR uniquely identifies autoimmunity.
Allergy–allergy testing–antihistamines; elevated CRP uniquely identifies allergy.
Self-tissue damage–autoantibodies–anti-inflammatory drugs and immunosuppressants; ESR or CRP can rise in all three disorder categories.
Self-tissue damage–urine cultures–antimicrobials; inflammatory markers never rise.
qs.e: Autoimmunity is checked with autoantibody tests and treated with anti-inflammatory drugs and immunosuppressants in the sorting table. Immunodeficiency, hypersensitivity, and autoimmunity can all raise inflammatory markers, so ESR or CRP alone cannot sort them.

qs.q: Which finding is the most reliable sign of infection in the class practice item?
c: Increased ESR.
Positive urine culture.
Increased WBC count.
Positive ANA.
qs.e: The practice item identifies a positive urine culture as the most reliable listed infection finding. ESR indicates inflammation, WBC can rise in the acute-phase response, and ANA points toward autoimmunity.

qs.q: Which are listed functions of the immune system? Select all that apply.
c: Provide immunity
Distinguish self from nonself
Mediate inflammation
Perform cancer surveillance
Activate immune cells against all self-antigens
qs.e: The notes list immunity, self/nonself recognition, inflammation, and cancer surveillance as immune functions. Self-tolerance normally prevents responses against a person's own antigens.

qs.q: What term means the absence of an immune response directed against a person's own antigens?
qs.e: Self-tolerance allows the immune system to distinguish self from nonself without normally attacking self-antigens.

qs.q: Which mechanisms normally maintain self-tolerance? Select all that apply.
c: Suppressor T cells inhibit self-reactive immune cells
Self-reactive T and B cells are eliminated during maturation
T-cell activation requires foreign antigen complexed to an appropriate MHC molecule
All self-antigens are permanently hidden from lymphocytes
Helper T cells activate without antigen presentation
qs.e: The notes identify suppression, elimination during maturation, and the MHC presentation requirement as safeguards. These mechanisms help prevent inappropriate responses against self.

qs.q: What is the role of cell-surface major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules?
c: Produce antibodies against DNA
Display antigens for inspection by T cells
Destroy all extracellular antigens directly
Release inflammatory mediators from basophils
qs.e: MHC molecules display antigens for T-cell inspection, assisting in identification of foreign antigens.

qs.q: Which description best matches the distribution of Class I MHC molecules?
c: Only on macrophages
Only on basophils
On nearly all nucleated cells, mostly cells not capable of phagocytosis
Only on cells containing extracellular antigens
qs.e: The study guide places Class I MHC on nearly all nucleated cells. It notes that these are mostly cells not capable of phagocytosis.

qs.q: Which are listed examples of antigens presented by Class I MHC? Select all that apply.
c: Normal self-antigens
Viruses that have gained access into cells
Abnormal proteins produced by cell mutations
Exclusively extracellular antigens obtained by macrophage phagocytosis
Only allergens bound to IgE
qs.e: Class I MHC primarily presents intracellular antigens. Listed examples include normal self-antigens, intracellular viruses, and abnormal cell proteins.

qs.q: Which CD-designated T cells recognize foreign antigens only when complexed to Class I MHC?
qs.e: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells require foreign antigen presentation by Class I MHC.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes Class II MHC?
c: It primarily presents intracellular antigens to CD8+ cells
It is found mainly on macrophages/APCs and presents extracellular-source antigens obtained by phagocytosis
It activates helper T cells without displaying an antigen
It is an antibody deposited in damaged tissues
qs.e: Class II MHC is found mainly on macrophages/APCs, which obtain foreign antigens by phagocytosis. It presents antigens from extracellular sources.

qs.q: Which CD-designated T cells require foreign antigen displayed by Class II MHC for activation?
qs.e: CD4+ helper T cells recognize foreign antigens complexed to Class II MHC. Without this presentation, helper T cells do not activate.

qs.q: Why is requiring the appropriate antigen–MHC presentation before T-cell activation important?
c: It helps maintain self-tolerance
It ensures all self-reactive cells become activated
It prevents all inflammatory responses
It replaces the need to distinguish self from nonself
qs.e: The notes explicitly include the MHC presentation requirement among mechanisms maintaining self-tolerance. It is a safeguard against inappropriate immune activation.

qs.q: What is the term for the reaction of tissue to injury, regardless of cause?
qs.e: Inflammation is defined as the tissue reaction to injury regardless of its cause. Its purpose includes beginning the healing process.

qs.q: How does inflammation help begin healing? Select all that apply.
c: Neutralizes or destroys harmful agents
Limits the spread of harmful agents
Removes dead tissue to prepare for repair
Helps transport nutrients to prepare for repair
Prevents all movement of fluid and WBCs into injured tissue
qs.e: Inflammation helps control harmful agents and prepares damaged tissue for repair. Dead-tissue removal and nutrient transport are listed examples of this preparation.

qs.q: Which set contains all five cardinal signs of inflammation listed in lecture?
c: Fever, increased WBCs, muscle catabolism, heat, pain
Redness, heat, swelling, pain, impaired function
Redness, fever, infection, swelling, autoantibodies
Heat, muscle catabolism, pain, infection, impaired function
qs.e: The inflammatory-response diagram lists redness, heat, swelling, pain, and impaired function. Fever, increased WBCs, and muscle catabolism are listed separately as systemic acute-phase effects.

qs.q: Which are listed chemical mediators of inflammation? Select all that apply.
c: Histamine and prostaglandins
Leukotrienes
Plasma proteases and platelet-activating factor
Other cytokines
Class I and Class II MHC molecules
qs.e: The notes list all four mediator groups and state that these chemicals are released by mast cells, immune cells, and other sources. MHC molecules are described as antigen-display molecules.

qs.q: Which sequence correctly describes the vascular response to injury?
c: Sustained vasoconstriction → decreased permeability → fluid remains in vessels
Vasodilation → permanent vasoconstriction → WBC destruction
Momentary vasoconstriction → vasodilation → increased capillary permeability → fluid escapes into tissues
Immune-complex deposition → decreased permeability → tissue repair
qs.e: The vascular response begins with brief local vasoconstriction, followed by vasodilation and increased capillary permeability. Fluid then escapes into tissues.

qs.q: The cellular response to inflammation involves movement of which cells into the injured area?
qs.e: The notes distinguish WBC movement into the injured area as the cellular response. Vessel dilation and permeability changes are the vascular response.

qs.q: Which are systemic acute-phase effects related to cytokine release? Select all that apply.
c: Fever
Increased WBC count
Skeletal muscle catabolism
Elimination of all self-reactive antibodies
Decreased capillary permeability
qs.e: Cytokine release produces systemic acute-phase effects including fever, increased WBCs, and skeletal muscle catabolism.

qs.q: A breakdown in immune self-tolerance underlies which major immune disorder category?
qs.e: Autoimmunity involves loss of tolerance toward self-antigens. The slides associate it with damage to self tissue.

qs.q: Which are proposed explanations for breakdown of self-tolerance? Select all that apply.
c: Abnormal self-antigen structure
Faulty T-cell receptor/MHC-complex interaction
Disordered immune surveillance
Antigenic mimicry or release of sequestered antigens
Normal elimination of self-reactive T and B cells
qs.e: The first four choices include all five theories listed in lecture. Normal elimination of self-reactive cells maintains tolerance rather than disrupting it.

qs.q: A foreign antigen resembles a self-antigen so closely that antibodies against it also react with self. What is this mechanism called?
qs.e: Antigenic mimicry describes antibody cross-reaction with self because a foreign antigen closely resembles a self-antigen.

qs.q: Why might tissue injury that releases a sequestered self-antigen provoke autoimmunity?
c: The antigen may not have contacted lymphocytes during early development
All self-antigens normally activate CD8+ cells without MHC
Released self-antigens always become IgE
Injury eliminates all antigen-antibody complexes
qs.e: Sequestered self-antigens may not come into direct contact with lymphocytes during early development. Their later release, such as after injury, may cause autoimmune reactions.

qs.q: Which factors are listed as predisposing to autoimmunity? Select all that apply.
c: Genetic factors
Virus or microorganism trigger events
Chemical exposure or release of sequestered self-antigens
Gender/hormonal factors, with greater frequency in women
High RBC count as an established predisposing factor
qs.e: The notes identify genetics, trigger events, and gender/hormones as predisposing factors. Autoimmunity is described as more common in women.

qs.q: Which client has the strongest listed risk profile for autoimmune disease?
c: A female whose mother has SLE
A female with a high RBC count
A male with a smoking history
An elderly male
qs.e: Female sex and a family history of SLE align with the listed gender/hormonal and genetic risk factors. The other profiles do not combine those stated risk factors.

qs.q: Using the notes' theories, why might infection with group A, beta-hemolytic streptococcus predispose someone to autoimmune disease?
c: Infection guarantees elimination of all self-reactive cells
Antibodies against a similar foreign antigen could also react with self-antigens
Microorganisms permanently prevent immune-complex formation
Infection makes MHC presentation unnecessary for normal tolerance
qs.e: Antigenic mimicry offers a possible explanation: antibodies against a foreign antigen may react with a resembling self-antigen. The notes also identify microorganisms as potential autoimmune triggers.

qs.q: Which description of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) matches the notes?
c: Antibodies develop only against external allergens
Antibodies develop against many self-antigens, including nuclear DNA and RNA
Only direct T-cell cytotoxicity occurs, without antibodies
It results from failure to produce any immune response
qs.e: SLE involves antibodies against many types of self-antigens. The notes specifically include the nuclear antigens DNA and RNA.

qs.q: Which sequence explains the vicious cycle of tissue damage in SLE?
c: Cell damage → DNA release → anti-DNA antibodies and complexes → tissue deposition → complement activation → inflammation and more damage
DNA release → IgE binding to basophils → permanent self-tolerance
Cell damage → suppression of complement → removal of all autoantibodies
Extracellular antigen → Class II display → no immune response anywhere
qs.e: Antibodies react with DNA from damaged cells anywhere in the body, forming complexes that deposit in tissues. Complement activation and inflammation then cause further damage and immune reactions.

qs.q: What name is given to the antibodies against DNA described in the SLE pathway?
qs.e: The notes describe formation of anti-DNA antibodies following release of DNA from damaged cells. These antibodies participate in immune-complex formation.

qs.q: Which definition best matches a hypersensitivity disorder?
c: A normal response against every self-antigen
A pathological immune response following sensitization to antigens that would not affect most people
The absence of any inflammatory response to injury
An inability to display any intracellular proteins
qs.e: Hypersensitivity is an inappropriate pathological response after sensitization. The triggering antigens would not affect most people.

qs.q: Which exposure routes can produce sensitization to a triggering antigen? Select all that apply.
c: Inhalation
Ingestion
Injection
Skin contact
Genetic inheritance as a route of antigen exposure
qs.e: The notes list inhalation, ingestion, injection, and skin contact as exposure routes. Genetic makeup is a separate predisposing factor, not an exposure route.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly applies the ABCD memory trick for hypersensitivity types I–IV?
c: I—Allergies; II—antiBodies; III—immune Complex/Complement; IV—Delayed
I—Delayed; II—Allergies; III—antiBodies; IV—Complement
I—Complement; II—Delayed; III—Allergies; IV—antiBodies
I—antiBodies; II—Complement; III—Delayed; IV—Allergies
qs.e: The slides use Allergies, antiBodies, immune Complex/Complement, and Delayed to recall types I, II, III, and IV respectively.

qs.q: Which comparison of hypersensitivity mediators is correct?
c: Types I–III are antibody-mediated; type IV is T-cell-mediated
All four types are IgE-mediated
Types I and IV are antibody-mediated; types II and III are T-cell-mediated
All four types require direct T-cell cytotoxicity
qs.e: The notes explicitly group types I, II, and III as antibody-mediated. Type IV is T-cell-mediated, also called cellular hypersensitivity.

qs.q: What initiates the mediator release of type I, or immediate, hypersensitivity?
c: IgG binding to DNA deposited in tissues
Allergen binding to allergen-specific IgE on mast cells or basophils
CD8+ cells recognizing Class I MHC on every normal cell
Complement binding directly to all extracellular antigens
qs.e: Allergen binding to IgE on mast cells or basophils triggers release of inflammatory chemical mediators. This is the IgE-mediated, immediate hypersensitivity mechanism.

qs.q: Which are listed examples of type I hypersensitivity? Select all that apply.
c: Allergic rhinitis (hay fever) and asthma
Urticaria
Atopic dermatitis (eczema)
Anaphylaxis
Blood transfusion reactions
qs.e: Allergic rhinitis, asthma, urticaria, atopic dermatitis, and anaphylaxis are listed type I disorders. Blood transfusion reactions are listed under type II.

qs.q: Which mechanism characterizes type II antibody-mediated/cytotoxic hypersensitivity?
c: IgG or IgM interacts with a cell/tissue antigen, and the reaction itself damages the target cell
IgE-bound mast cells release mediators after allergen binding
Deposited complexes cause damage only through subsequent inflammation
T cells cause injury without antibody mediation
qs.e: Type II involves IgG or IgM interacting with cell or tissue antigens. The notes emphasize damage from the antigen-antibody reaction itself.

qs.q: Blood transfusion reactions are listed as examples of which hypersensitivity type?
c: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV
qs.e: The notes place blood transfusion reactions under type II, the antibody-mediated/cytotoxic category.

qs.q: Which statement best distinguishes type III from type II hypersensitivity?
c: Type III is mediated by IgE on basophils
Type III damage results from inflammation after immune-complex deposition and complement activation, rather than the antigen-antibody reaction itself
Type III is exclusively direct T-cell killing
Type III does not involve antibodies
qs.e: Type III complexes deposit in tissues and activate complement, causing inflammatory damage. In type II, the notes attribute target-cell damage to the antigen-antibody reaction itself.

qs.q: Which hypersensitivity type is exemplified by SLE in lecture?
qs.e: SLE is the listed type III example. Its tissue-deposited antigen-antibody complexes activate complement and inflammation.

qs.q: How do T cells cause tissue injury in type IV hypersensitivity?
c: Only by producing IgE
By directly acting cytotoxically or releasing cytokines that cause tissue damage
Only by forming circulating anti-DNA antibodies
By blocking every inflammatory mediator
qs.e: Type IV injury can occur through direct T-cell cytotoxicity or through cytokines released by T cells. Unlike types I–III, it is not antibody-mediated.

qs.q: Which pair is listed as examples of type IV hypersensitivity?
c: Hay fever and anaphylaxis
Blood transfusion reactions and SLE
Contact dermatitis, such as poison ivy, and diabetes mellitus
Asthma and urticaria
qs.e: The source lists contact dermatitis and diabetes mellitus under type IV. It does not specify a diabetes subtype in this chunk.

qs.q: Which mapping correctly distinguishes the major problems associated with immune disorders?
c: Immunodeficiency—infection; hypersensitivity—allergic reactions and unnecessary inflammation; autoimmunity—self-tissue damage
Immunodeficiency—self-tissue damage; hypersensitivity—absence of inflammation; autoimmunity—only infection
Immunodeficiency—allergies; hypersensitivity—cancer surveillance; autoimmunity—normal tolerance
All three categories mean the same thing
qs.e: The slides distinguish infection risk with immunodeficiency, unnecessary allergic inflammation with hypersensitivity, and self-tissue injury with autoimmunity.

qs.q: Which diagnostic plan matches the three immune disorder categories?
c: Immunodeficiency—allergy testing; hypersensitivity—autoantibodies; autoimmunity—urine culture only
Immunodeficiency—cultures and WBC count; hypersensitivity—allergy testing; autoimmunity—autoantibodies
Immunodeficiency—ANA only; hypersensitivity—RBC count; autoimmunity—allergy testing
Use only inflammatory markers to distinguish all three
qs.e: The slides recommend cultures and WBC count for infection associated with immunodeficiency, allergy testing for hypersensitivity, and autoantibody testing for autoimmunity.

qs.q: Which listed laboratory finding most reliably indicates infection rather than nonspecific inflammation or autoimmunity?
c: Increased ESR
Increased WBC count
Positive ANA
Positive urine culture
qs.e: A positive urine culture is the most direct infection-related finding among these choices. The slides note that inflammatory markers can rise in all three disorder categories and associate autoantibody testing with autoimmunity.

qs.q: What is the key limitation of using elevated inflammatory markers to distinguish immunodeficiency-associated infection, hypersensitivity, and autoimmunity?
c: Only autoimmunity can increase them
Only hypersensitivity can increase them
All three can cause them to increase
They establish the specific triggering antigen
qs.e: The slides explicitly state that all three categories can increase inflammatory markers. An elevation alone therefore does not distinguish these categories.

qs.q: Which medication-category pairings match the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Immunodeficiency-associated infection—antimicrobials
Hypersensitivity/allergic reactions—antihistamines and/or anti-inflammatory drugs
Autoimmunity—anti-inflammatory drugs
Autoimmunity—immunosuppressants
Allergic reactions—antimicrobials as the listed primary medication category
qs.e: The slides pair antimicrobials with infection, antihistamines and/or anti-inflammatory drugs with hypersensitivity, and anti-inflammatory drugs plus immunosuppressants with autoimmunity.

qs.q: When planning interventions for a hypersensitivity disorder, what direction does the study-guide table provide?
c: Use the same intervention for every hypersensitivity type
Choose interventions specific to the individual disorder
Treat every disorder as a blood transfusion reaction
Avoid distinguishing the underlying mechanism
qs.e: The hypersensitivity table states that interventions are specific to individual disorders. This chunk does not supply a detailed intervention plan for each example.

qs.q: Which hypersensitivity type is associated with blood transfusion reactions in lecture?
c: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV
qs.e: The notes list blood transfusion reactions as an example of Type II hypersensitivity.

qs.q: Which hypersensitivity type is associated with SLE in lecture?
c: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV
qs.e: The notes identify SLE as an example of Type III hypersensitivity.

qs.q: A student is classifying contact dermatitis caused by poison ivy. Which type matches the notes?
c: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV
qs.e: The notes place contact dermatitis, including poison ivy, under Type IV hypersensitivity.

qs.q: Which hypersensitivity type is paired with diabetes mellitus in this chunk?
c: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV
qs.e: The notes list diabetes mellitus under Type IV. This chunk does not specify a diabetes subtype.

qs.q: How does the source describe assessment findings for these disorders?
c: Identical for all hypersensitivity types
Specific to individual disorders
Limited to a butterfly rash
Always the same as a transfusion reaction
qs.e: The assessment statement says findings are specific to individual disorders. It does not supply a universal assessment pattern.

qs.q: Which label does the vocabulary list assign to Type I?
c: IgE-mediated disorder
Antibody-mediated/cytotoxic disorder
Immune complex-mediated disorder
T cell-mediated disorder
qs.e: The vocabulary list explicitly labels Type I as an IgE-mediated disorder.

qs.q: Which label does the vocabulary list assign to Type II?
c: T cell-mediated disorder
Immune complex-mediated disorder
Antibody-mediated/cytotoxic disorder
IgE-mediated disorder
qs.e: Type II is listed as an antibody-mediated/cytotoxic disorder. Both descriptors appear in lecture.

qs.q: Which label does the vocabulary list assign to Type III?
c: Antibody-mediated/cytotoxic disorder
IgE-mediated disorder
T cell-mediated disorder
Immune complex-mediated disorder
qs.e: Type III is identified as an immune complex-mediated disorder.

qs.q: Which label does the vocabulary list assign to Type IV?
c: Immune complex-mediated disorder
T cell-mediated disorder
IgE-mediated disorder
Antibody-mediated/cytotoxic disorder
qs.e: The vocabulary list labels Type IV as a T cell-mediated disorder.

qs.q: Which term is paired with allergic rhinitis in the vocabulary list?
c: Eczema
Hives
Hay fever
Malar rash
qs.e: The list presents allergic rhinitis/hay fever as a paired entry.

qs.q: Which term is paired with atopic dermatitis in the vocabulary list?
c: Eczema
Hay fever
Angioedema
Urticaria
qs.e: Atopic dermatitis/eczema is the pairing given in the list.

qs.q: Which term is paired with butterfly rash?
c: Exudate
Malar rash
Hives
Eczema
qs.e: The vocabulary list pairs butterfly rash with malar rash.

qs.q: Which term is paired with urticaria?
c: Hay fever
Malar rash
Hives
Angioedema
qs.e: The listed entry is urticaria/hives.

qs.q: Which term is paired with antigen-antibody complex?
c: Autoantibody
Immune complex
Fibrinogen
Mast cells
qs.e: The list gives antigen-antibody complex/immune complex as one entry.

qs.q: What does MHC stand for in the vocabulary list?
c: Major histocompatibility complex
Malar histocompatibility complex
Major hypersensitivity complex
Mast histocompatibility complex
qs.e: MHC is expanded as major histocompatibility complex in lecture.

qs.q: Which classes are explicitly included with MHC in the vocabulary list?
c: Class I only
Class II only
Class III and Class IV
