cards.def: Control center of the cell. Contains DNA, which provides instructions for synthesis of essential proteins and genetic information passed down through generations. Makes RNA to transmit those instructions to the cytoplasm for protein production.
Held in the nucleus; provides instructions for the synthesis of essential proteins and carries the genetic information passed down through generations.
Made by the nucleus; transmits instructions from DNA to the cytoplasm (where protein synthesis takes place) and facilitates protein production.
Sites of protein synthesis. Impaired ribosomes mean synthesis of defective proteins or decreased protein synthesis.

A tube system that transports substances throughout the cell and houses ribosomes and the enzyme systems that carry out the cell's metabolic functions. If it fails, substances may not be transported appropriately within the cell.
Transform food energy into ATP, which is used to power cell activities. Aerobic metabolism happens here. Failure means the cell cannot generate enough energy to maintain function.
The form in which cell energy is stored. When the cell needs it, ATP is broken down and energy is released to power cell activities.
"Bags of enzymes" that digest worn-out cell parts and foreign material such as bacteria that have gotten into the cell. Failure leads to accumulation of worn-out parts and foreign material.
Similar to lysosomes; hold enzymes that detoxify substances and help control free radicals — highly unstable compounds that can damage cytoplasm.
Modifies what the ribosomes made, packages it into secretory granules or vesicles, and directs it where it is supposed to go. Hormones and lysosomal enzymes depend on this step.

Holds the cell together; barrier against foreign organisms and toxic molecules. Contains carrier proteins and ion channels for transport, receptors for hormones, antigens that label the cell self or nonself, and maintains and transmits membrane potentials.
An autoimmune disease in which antibodies are made against the receptor, so the chemical message does not land on the target cell.
Channels in nerve and muscle that let small ions and molecules pass straight from cell to cell, so an action potential spreads fast through that tissue.
Requires oxygen; occurs in the mitochondria. The efficient path for energy production.
No oxygen; occurs in the cytoplasm. Less efficient, produces lactic acid. Matters when oxygen delivery is low.
No energy required; follows a chemical or electrical gradient from high to low, trying to even out. Includes diffusion and osmosis.
Particles move down the concentration gradient. Which substance diffuses depends on cell membrane permeability. The goal is equilibrium.

Water moves down its gradient through a semi-permeable membrane until solute concentration is equal on both sides. Usually more K+ inside, more Na+ outside; K+ can diffuse out, Na+ cannot get in, so water moves instead.
Energy (ATP) required; used when a substance has to move against the concentration gradient. The only transport method that spends ATP and goes uphill.
An active transport mechanism that keeps sodium higher outside the cell and potassium higher inside. Restores ionic balance during repolarization and requires ATP.
The cell engulfs material, forms a vesicle, and brings it in. Includes pinocytosis (fluid and dissolved particles) and phagocytosis (microorganisms, damaged cells, and other particles).
A type of endocytosis in which the cell takes in fluid and dissolved particles.
A type of endocytosis in which the cell engulfs microorganisms, damaged cells, and other particles, which are then killed or broken down.
The reverse of endocytosis. A secretory granule fuses with the membrane and opens outside, releasing hormones the cell made and dumping debris.
More sodium outside the cell draws water out; the cell shrinks. Opposite of pump-failure swelling.
All body cells are electrically polarized; at rest the inside is more negative than the outside. Potassium diffuses out leaving mostly negatively charged ions inside.
A stimulus makes the membrane more permeable to sodium. Sodium rushes in, down its gradient, and the inside is no longer more negative — that is the action potential.

Two steps: first the membrane returns to its original permeability (less open to sodium, more open to potassium), then the sodium-potassium pump moves sodium back out and potassium back in. Requires ATP from aerobic metabolism.
The electrical event produced by depolarization; current-carrying ions pass through gap junctions and the impulse spreads through muscle or nerve.

Highly unstable atoms that react with key molecules. They damage membranes and proteins, inactivate enzymes, and damage DNA. Byproducts of normal metabolism and inflammation; outside sources include tobacco smoke, pollutants, pesticides, radiation.

Inadequate oxygen to the cell; a power failure that leads to inadequate energy, switch to anaerobic metabolism (lactic acid, lower pH), pump failure (cell swells), lysosomal leak (self-digestion), and can end in cell death.
Result of the switch to anaerobic metabolism during hypoxia: lactic acid accumulates and pH drops. Membranes get damaged and intracellular enzymes (CK, LD, troponin) leak out.
Enzymes in the lysosome do not work properly, so worn-out cell parts and foreign material accumulate. Example named: Tay-Sachs.
A packaging problem: lysosomal enzymes are never delivered into the lysosome, so digestion cannot occur.
The cell goes back to a smaller size and a lower level of function. Oxygen and energy needs fall, so survival is more likely.
Bigger cell with more functional parts, so it can meet a higher work demand.
More cells, not bigger cells.
One cell type changes to another that can survive the adverse condition. Usually follows chronic irritation or inflammation.
Deranged growth; cells vary in size, shape, and appearance. Usually follows chronic irritation or inflammation. The one that looks abnormal.
Cell death; the injury is irreversible. Follows reversible injury if the cell cannot recover.
The basic unit of a living organism; composed of nucleus, cytoplasmic organelles, and cell membrane.
Inner organs of the cell; include ribosomes, ER, mitochondria, lysosomes, peroxisomes, and Golgi complex.
Modifies substances synthesized by ribosomes, packages them into secretory granules/vesicles, and directs them to where they are supposed to go.
Keeps the cell together; acts as a protective barrier against foreign organisms and toxic molecules; contains transport proteins, receptors, and antigens; maintains/transmits membrane potentials.

Proteins in the cell membrane that assist in transport of substances in/out of the cell through the membrane (source lists carrier proteins and ion channels together and gives no further distinction between them).
Molecules on the cell membrane that label cells as self or nonself.
Cells use oxygen and the food we eat to produce the energy needed to function; energy is stored as ATP and released when needed.
Movement of molecules/ions across the cell membrane with no expenditure of energy; occurs related to chemical or electrical gradients.
Molecules that interact with receptor proteins of other cells and trigger desired physiologic effects (one of two methods of cellular communication).
Failure of sodium-potassium pump and energy-dependent transport causes more Na and water to enter cells, leading to swelling.
Cell injury that the cell can recover from if the damaging stimulus is removed.
Occurs when cell injury is irreversible.
Byproduct of the switch to anaerobic metabolism during hypoxia/ATP depletion; lowers pH and leads to damage to cell membranes with leakage of intracellular enzymes out of the cell.
Two methods: (1) chemical messengers that interact with receptor proteins of other cells and trigger the desired physiologic effect, and (2) gap junctions in nerve and muscle cells.
Oxygen is necessary for a cell to repolarize because aerobic metabolism in the mitochondria produces the ATP needed to power the sodium-potassium pump that restores the resting membrane potential.

Power failure within the cell leading to a switch to anaerobic metabolism, lactic acid production, drop in pH, damage to cell membranes with leakage of intracellular enzymes, failure of the sodium-potassium pump, cellular swelling, and entry of calcium causing abnormal enzyme activation and cell damage.

Factors that cause cell injury: physical agents (mechanical forces, temperature extremes, electricity), radiation, chemicals (drugs, environmental toxins such as lead and tobacco smoke), biologic agents (microorganisms, parasites), nutritional imbalances (excesses such as obesity/atherosclerosis and deficiencies such as iron-deficiency anemia), genetic derangements, and autoimmune disorders.
Occurs if cell injury is irreversible.
Substances on the cell membrane that label cells as self or nonself; if self-antigens are damaged, autoimmune diseases may result.
Abnormal alteration in normal cellular function (components, metabolism, membrane movement, or communication) that leads to nursing problems.

Patient problems that result from pathological change in cell function; identified for each alteration (nucleus, ribosomes, ER, mitochondria, lysosomes, Golgi complex, cell membrane, metabolism, movement across membrane, communications).
Structure labeled within the nucleus of the composite cell diagram.
Structure labeled inside the nucleus in the composite cell diagram.
Endoplasmic reticulum region identified on electron micrograph with the nucleus.
Organelle featured as "Mighty Chondrion"; site of the mitochondrial matrix where aerobic pathways occur.
Organelle depicted as eating material ("I'mma lysosome and I'mma eat chu! NOM NOM").
Cell structure named as a key term for this class.
The post office of the cell.
Vesicles that carry proteins from the Golgi apparatus in the cell.
Structure labeled in the composite cell diagram.
Structure labeled in the composite cell diagram.
Carbohydrate and protein receptor sites shown on the outer surface of the cell membrane.
Component of the cell membrane shown between water-soluble heads and water-insoluble tails.
Location shown for the anaerobic pathway of cellular respiration.
Location shown for the aerobic pathway of cellular respiration.
Making energy.
Pathway that occurs in the presence of oxygen: Krebs cycle and electron transport chain, in the mitochondrial matrix.
Pathway that occurs in the absence of oxygen: fermentation (alcohol or lactic acid), in the cytosol.
Substance that splits into the anaerobic or aerobic pathway of cellular respiration.
Anaerobic process occurring in the absence of oxygen, producing alcohol or lactic acid.
Part of the aerobic pathway occurring in the presence of oxygen.
Part of the aerobic pathway occurring in the presence of oxygen.
Example of a lysosomal storage disease.
Difference in concentration; particles move down it from higher to lower concentration to reach equilibrium.
Membrane whose permeability is the deciding factor in whether particles move (diffusion) or water moves (osmosis).
Goal of passive movement.
Usually more K+ inside of cell, more Na+ outside of cell (due to activity of the sodium-potassium pump); K+ diffuses out, Na+ can't go in, so water moves instead.
Releases the energy that drives the sodium-potassium pump.
Methods used for communication between cells (textbook Figure 3-31).
State of the cell at rest, maintained by the ion distribution.
Negatively charged ions present in large numbers inside the cell alongside K+.
Usually more K+ inside of cell, more Na+ outside of cell (due to activity of sodium-potassium pump).
K+ diffuses out, Na+ can't go in -> left with mostly anions inside cell.
Lots of anions present as well inside the cell (Slide 56); when K+ diffuses out and Na+ can't go in, the cell is left with mostly anions inside.
Something changes permeability of the membrane so that Na+ can go into the cell, allowing an action potential to be generated.
Pump maintains more K+ inside and Na+ outside; K+ diffuses out leaving anions inside; depolarization and repolarization then repeat the cycle.
Key mechanisms of cell injury include free radicals and hypoxia.
Agents illustrated alongside healthy atoms and free radicals in cell injury diagrams.

Inadequate energy branches into two pathways that both end in cell death: (1) anaerobic metabolism -> lactic acid production -> metabolic acidosis -> cell death; (2) metabolic failure -> cell death. (Metabolic failure comes from inadequate energy, not from acidosis.)
Follows inadequate energy supply; leads to cell death.
End result of metabolic failure / metabolic acidosis from inadequate oxygen.
A lab marker (with LD and troponin) used in cell injury/assessment.
A lab marker (with CK and troponin) used in cell injury/assessment.
A lab marker (with CK and LD) used in cell injury/assessment.
Three categories of cellular responses: cellular adaptation, reversible injury, and cell death.
One of the cellular responses (with reversible injury and cell death); includes atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, metaplasia, dysplasia.
Enlargement of the left ventricle, an example of hypertrophy.
Example of hyperplasia: enlarged prostate compresses the urethra compared to normal.
Normal columnar epithelium is replaced by squamous epithelium (basement membrane intact).
Diagram: normal cell → hypertrophy, hyperplasia, dysplasia, cancer.
The ongoing process by which dead cells are replaced by new cells, even in healthy people. It has TWO steps: proliferation and differentiation.
The first step of cellular replication: cells increase in number (they proliferate).
The second step of cellular replication: newly formed cells become different from each other — they specialize and develop unique capabilities.
Division of somatic (regular body) cells producing 2 daughter cells, each with 46 chromosomes (23 PAIRS) — the same as the parent. Everything except germ cells reproduces by mitosis.
Division of germ cells (egg or sperm) producing gametes only. Each new cell has 23 chromosomes — NOT 23 pairs — so that egg + sperm = 46 (23 pairs) in the zygote.
Regular body cells; they reproduce by mitosis and make all other cells in the body.
Cells that produce gametes (egg or sperm) by meiosis. NOT 'derm cells' — a misstatement corrected by the instructor.
Egg and sperm cells; the ONLY cells produced by meiosis. Each carries 23 chromosomes so the zygote has 46.
The cell formed when egg + sperm combine; it has 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) because each germ cell brought 23.

The PRIMARY influence on proliferation and differentiation: each cell type is genetically pre-programmed for how often it should divide (e.g., liver cells ~ once every 1–2 years; GI epithelial cells 2+ times a day). Which genes are switched ON vs OFF determines proliferation rate and level of differentiation.

Cells proliferate until they contact many other cells and feel crowded, then proliferation slows (e.g., wound edges meet → stop). Cancer cells LOSE this inhibition and do not care if they get crowded.

Secondary influences (primary = genetic programming). FOR PROLIFERATION: amount of growth factor, hormones, and nutrients available; events such as blood loss or tissue injury. FOR DIFFERENTIATION: growth factors, nutrients, how much oxygen is present, and whether cells get crowded.
The process the cell goes through as it proliferates; the lecture counts FOUR main phases (G1, S, G2, M). G0 is resting/outside the cycle and is NOT counted.
Getting ready: the cell makes more proteins, RNA, and organelles, because one parent must fully supply TWO daughter cells.
The cell synthesizes/replicates DNA so the parent has enough for two cells. Errors here → some genetic disorders.
Pretty much a repeat of G1; similar preparation for division.
The cell actually splits into two. If chromosomes are not divided equally between daughters → chromosomal disorders.
Outside the cell cycle: the cell is not preparing to divide and is not dividing. 'Resting' means resting from replication only — the cell is still alive (makes ATP, etc.).
Cell-cycle specific drugs that prevent DNA from being replicated, often by interfering with enzymes needed for that process.
Cell-cycle specific drugs that keep the cancer cell from actually dividing into two.

Often give more than one drug at a time (e.g., one S-phase + one M-phase) to wipe out more cancer cells than one drug alone; drugs must also be given long enough for all cancer cells to cycle through that phase.

Nerve, skeletal muscle, brain cells: unique jobs (e.g., conduct action potentials) but MUCH less able to reproduce — brain cells reproduce at a much slower rate. They make only their own specialized type.
Mid-level cells such as skin and liver cells: less specialized than nerve/muscle, but much MORE capable of reproducing (skin cells reproduce often) and produce only cells just like themselves.

e.g., bone-marrow stem cells: few specialized capabilities but can enter the cell cycle and produce LARGE numbers of new cells, usually MORE THAN ONE kind (bone-marrow stem cell → RBCs, platelets, and all WBCs).

Tissue growth that exceeds that of normal, is not appropriate, serves no useful purpose, in fact hurts the host, and yet is continuing. BOTH replication steps are messed up: abnormal proliferation AND abnormal differentiation.
A change in a person's genes. Mutations change the genetic programming → abnormal proliferation + abnormal differentiation = cancer.
Something that can cause cancer; examples listed: radiation (including sun), tobacco smoke, asbestos, toxic chemicals. These generate free radicals.
Generated by carcinogens; they steal electrons from cell parts and cause cell damage. If they steal electrons from genes/DNA → genetic mutation → predisposition to cancer.

Often 5 to 30 years between carcinogen exposure and cancer diagnosis, making it hard to track the original risk factor (e.g., ~30-year lag from smoking to lung cancer in the instructor's family example).
Only specific viruses are linked to specific cancers (a cold or flu does NOT increase risk): HPV → cervical cancer; Hepatitis B & C → liver cancer; Epstein–Barr virus → certain lymphomas.

Viruses must enter a host cell and use its machinery to replicate; viral DNA is incorporated into the host cell's DNA (combination DNA), which IS a genetic mutation that can cause abnormal proliferation and differentiation.

Cancer cells are probably developing in everybody's body all the time; the immune system should recognize and eliminate them before they establish. If it is not working correctly (AIDS, immunosuppressive drugs, aging), cancer incidence rises.
A cancer-causing mutation in a GERM cell (egg or sperm) is inherited by the child and increases cancer risk. A mutation in a somatic (body) cell is NOT passed to kids.

Higher percentage of cells actively in the cell cycle, fewer in G0, loss of cell density–dependent inhibition, and failure to die on schedule → uncontrolled cell growth that crowds out and starves normal cells of blood/O2/nutrients.

Cancer cells do not specialize properly, so they cannot perform the normal tissue function (e.g., liver cancer cell ≠ normal liver function → liver failure). Expect dysfunction of whatever organ developed the cancer.
Normal cells like to stick together; cancer cells LOSE cohesiveness, break apart, and wander via blood or lymph to start cancers elsewhere — the reverse of normal tissue behavior.
The spread of cancer cells through blood or lymph to other parts of the body where they start new cancers; results from lost cell-to-cell cohesiveness.

A substance made by cancer cells that promotes growth of NEW blood vessels, allowing a tumor to keep increasing its blood supply (O2 + nutrients) and keep growing past the size its original vessels could support.
Hormones produced NOT by regulated endocrine glands but by cancer cells in an abnormal location. Because cancer cells are not controlled by negative feedback, they overproduce → hormone imbalance.
Result when something goes wrong in M phase and chromosomes are not divided equally between the daughter cells.
Result when something goes wrong in S phase and DNA is replicated incorrectly.
In an abnormal location (same word as ectopic pregnancy: embryo not in the uterus, e.g., in the fallopian tube).
Endocrine glands are regulated by negative feedback so they do not overproduce. Cancer cells are NOT regulated by any feedback and ignore how much hormone is already present.

cards.term: Lung cancer – hormone production (ACTH, ADH, PTH)
cards.def: Classic example of ectopic hormones: many lung cancers produce hormones just like ACTH, antidiuretic hormone (ADH), or parathyroid hormone (PTH) → unregulated overproduction.
Substances made by cancer cells that damage tissue; damaged tissue often does not heal normally, so a sore that does not heal is a warning sign of cancer (e.g., skin cancers).
Abnormal antigens on the cell membranes of poorly differentiated cancer cells. Used as clinical markers to MONITOR progression or EVALUATE treatment success — NOT to diagnose and NOT to screen.
Marker found on the cell membrane of some prostate-cancer cells. Measured in blood to monitor progression, evaluate treatment, or detect recurrence — never for diagnosis or screening.
Marker found in certain GI cancers (colon, gastric, pancreatic) and certain breast cancers. Used to monitor progression/evaluate treatment/detect recurrence, not to diagnose or screen.

cards.term: Why markers are NOT for diagnosis/screening
cards.def: Markers are not reliable for that purpose; some antigens appear in non-cancerous conditions, and sometimes they do not appear until cancers are fairly advanced — and we want to find cancer before it is advanced.

After biopsy diagnosis, measure PSA and start a drug: PSA still high/switch drugs; PSA dropping/drug working; after remission draw periodically (e.g., every 6 months); PSA rising years later/possible recurrence — bring him in.
Weight loss / wasting away seen in advanced-cancer patients. Caused by nutrient theft and by cytokine-induced anorexia. DO NOT mix up with anorexia (loss of appetite).
Cancer cells steal blood supply and nutrients from surrounding normal cells; the cancer grows while the patient gets skinny.
A substance white blood cells make to help them do their job. Released by the immune system trying to kill cancer cells.
Side effect of cytokines released against cancer: anorexia (loss of appetite) → patient is not hungry → weight loss.
Loss of appetite — related to but NOT the same as cachexia (the weight loss/wasting).
Tumor presses on nerve endings; tumor presses on blood vessels cutting off blood flow so tissue is short of blood/O2; enzymes/toxins damage tissue; possibly release of chemical mediators of pain.

One of the more challenging nursing issues; adequate control may require enough medication that the patient becomes sedated, and end-stage patients do not want to sleep away remaining time with family.
Lower than normal RBCs or hemoglobin.
Anorexia→poor nutrition→iron/B-vitamin deficiency; toxins damage tissue→bleeding; tumors erode into blood vessels→blood loss; metastasis to bone marrow; chemo/radiation suppress marrow.
Not cancerous; ONLY proliferation is abnormal while differentiation is totally normal. Grows by expansion, usually has a fibrous capsule, does not metastasize or cause systemic effects.
Cancerous; BOTH proliferation and differentiation are abnormal. Grows by expansion and spreads by metastasis, infiltrates surrounding tissue, has NO capsule.
Benign tumors are very frequently surrounded by a fibrous capsule that contains them; malignant tumors have NO capsule and send out tentacles into normal tissue.
Benign tumors do NOT make VEGF, ectopic hormones, or damaging enzymes/toxins, and do not cause anemia or cachexia; problems are local, around the tumor.
Certain benign brain tumors can still kill because of location: when too big they squash brain tissue and interfere with regulation of breathing, heart rate, or blood pressure.

Remove the cancer → remove its harmful effects on nearby tissue. Limit: hard to be sure every cell is out; leftover cells multiply and cancer returns, so surgery is almost always combined with radiation and/or chemo.

Generates free radicals that either kill the cancer cell outright or damage it so it cannot replicate. Downside: nearby normal cells can also be radiated; most affected are the most rapidly proliferating cells.

Many drugs work in a specific cell-cycle phase to block what should happen there (enzymes, DNA, protein, or splitting into two). Usually PO or IV so effects are not limited to cancer cells → almost always side effects.
Radiation and toxic drugs are on the list of things that can CAUSE cancer; treating cancer with them can predispose to a different cancer later, but without treatment the patient dies.
A drug that modifies/changes some biologic response in the body — mostly immune responses — making the immune system more effective at getting rid of cancer.
A drug that modulates/changes the immune system; basically the same idea as a biologic response modifier.
A man-made (cloned) antibody designed to target a specific substance causing a disease; once you know the culprit substance, design an antibody to get rid of it.
Man-made versions of cytokines (substances WBCs make to help them do their jobs); another way to change immune response and hopefully make it more effective.
Complex molecule that stores genetic information, made of chains of nucleotides; nitrogenous bases (A, C, G, T) carry the genetic information/form the genetic code.
Building block of DNA chains; each contains one of four possible nitrogenous bases (A, C, G, T).
Which nitrogenous bases appear (A, C, G, T), in what order, and in what quantity.
DNA is translated into RNA; RNA carries the genetic code out into the cytoplasm so ribosomes can use it to make proteins.
The code is read in groups of THREE = a triplet code; each triplet is a codon and represents ONE specific amino acid.
The codons put together = instructions for one particular protein. Genes hooked end to end make one big DNA molecule. (Some big proteins need more than one gene.)
A DNA molecule wound really tight around a little protein core; contains many, many genes.
Most body cells have 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs: one chromosome of each pair from mom, one from dad.
22 of the 23 chromosome pairs; alike whether you are male or female.
The 23rd pair; determines male or female — males XY, females XX. A karyotype with XY is a male genotype.
The chromosome picture/genotype; e.g., XY = male genotype.

1) Regulate protein synthesis → control cell function (proteins carry out most cellular functions). 2) Determine inheritance patterns — physical, biochemical and physiologic traits, and predisposition to diseases such as cancer.

Bases = letters; codon (3 bases = 1 amino acid) = word; gene (instructions for one protein) = sentence; chromosome (tightly wound DNA, many genes) = paragraph/story; 46 chromosomes = the whole book for one person.
Basic inheritance patterns first proposed by Mendel and published around 1865 (about the time of the Civil War); still taught essentially as he proposed them.
The two members of a gene pair (one from mom, one from dad).
The more influential gene in the pair; it is expressed in EITHER a homozygous OR a heterozygous pairing (e.g., brown eyes if one brown + one blue gene).
The other gene of the pair; expresses itself ONLY in a homozygous pairing — only if no dominant gene is present (e.g., blue eyes needs two recessive genes).
Both genes of the allele pair the same — both dominant (AA) or both recessive (aa); uppercase = dominant, lowercase = recessive.
One dominant + one recessive gene in the pair (Aa).
A heterozygous person who can pass on a gene/disease but does not have symptoms themselves (e.g., brown-eyed person carrying a blue-eye gene).

Result of genetic mutations/a change in a person's genes, occurring during meiosis when DNA replication is inaccurate; in this lecture these are mutations in a GERM cell so they can be passed to the next generation.
A mistake in DNA replication (e.g., during meiosis) so DNA is not replicated accurately; sometimes due to radiation, toxic chemicals or environment, often a spontaneous 'metabolic accident.'
Mistake/mutation in ONE gene in a germ cell, then passed on; because a gene codes for a specific protein, that protein will be missing or defective/non-working.
Disorders involving the bigger chunk of genetic material (chromosomes = many genes), so they usually mean a BIGGER NUMBER of kinds of problems — not necessarily more serious, just more problems.
Mistakes in more than one gene; inheritance is more complicated. This class only covers single-gene disorders (only one gene among all genes in all chromosomes is wrong).

Single-gene disorders follow Mendelian patterns closely. Three primary patterns, determined by (1) whether the defective gene is on a sex chromosome or an autosome, and (2) whether it carries a dominant or recessive trait.
Defective gene is on a sex chromosome (usually the X), not an autosome. Less common than autosomal disorders because there are 22 pairs of autosomes vs only 1 pair of sex chromosomes.
Defective gene is on an autosome (a non-sex chromosome). A random gene mistake is more likely on an autosome because there are 22 pairs of autosomes vs 1 pair of sex chromosomes.
A trait that is expressed even when only one copy of the defective gene is present. Referred to as uppercase A in notation.
A trait that is expressed only when no dominant/normal gene is present (i.e., two copies needed). Referred to as lowercase a in notation.

cards.term: X-linked: why males have the disease
cards.def: Males have only one X. If that X is defective there is no second X with a normal gene to override it → male HAS the disease. Females with two X's are usually carriers.
Most common X-linked disorder. Defective gene = instructions for Factor VIII (factor 8), a clotting factor. Causes trouble with bleeding — bruising, bleeding into muscles and joints.
A clotting factor. The defective gene in hemophilia A provides instructions for Factor VIII; without functioning Factor VIII there is trouble with bleeding.

Defective gene on an autosome AND carries a dominant trait → it will be expressed. Only ONE defective gene is enough for symptoms. There are NO carriers — if you have the defective gene you have the disease. Notation: Aa (or AA) = disease, aa = normal.

Autosomal dominant disorder. Defective gene has part of the instructions for making connective tissue. Symptoms span multiple systems: long thin arms/legs/fingers, chest and spinal deformities (scoliosis), retinal detachment, lens dislocation, heart valve prolapse, aneurysm tendency.

Defective gene on an autosome carrying a recessive trait. To HAVE the disease you need two recessive defective genes (aa) — a defective gene from BOTH parents. Carriers (Aa) have no symptoms but can pass the defective gene.

Autosomal recessive disorder. Defective gene = instructions for hemoglobin; only ONE amino acid is coded incorrectly, all others are correct. Under certain conditions defective hemoglobin makes RBCs sickle-shaped, causing clots, occlusion, pain, and anemia from RBC destruction.
Having one defective gene (carrier state) for sickle cell. The person does not have sickle cell anemia but can pass the defective gene to children.
Hemo = blood/hemoglobin; lysis = breaking apart. Anemic because the body is breaking down its own RBCs — as in sickle cell disease where sickled RBCs are destroyed extra, causing anemia.

Used in genetic counseling to visualize a couple's risk of a child with a single-gene disorder or a carrier child. Draw boxes, put parent genes on the sides, fill in all possible combinations, and calculate risk.
Sex-linked → risk calculated out of 2 (only the two possible kids of that sex). Autosomal → risk calculated out of 4. Getting the denominator wrong is the fastest way to miss the question.
An affected dad cannot give the disease to his sons (they get his Y, not his X). He gives his defective X to ALL daughters, who become carriers if mom is normal.
During meiosis a piece may break off a chromosome and get lost. All the genes on that lost piece are missing → problems.
The normal process — chromosomes divided equally between two daughter cells during meiosis, so each germ cell gets ONE copy of each chromosome.

Disjunction did NOT happen. Parent gives ONE daughter cell BOTH copies of a chromosome and the other daughter cell gets NONE. Causes wrong chromosome numbers in zygotes when those daughter cells combine with other germ cells.
Zygote has only ONE copy of a chromosome (supposed to have two). Mono = one. Defects are usually severe and often 'incompatible with life' — fetus usually cannot survive and is miscarried.

Zygote has THREE copies of a chromosome (supposed to have two). Tri = three. The number indicates which chromosome has the extra copy (e.g., trisomy 18, 13, 22). Most common: trisomy 21 = Down syndrome.

Most common trisomy. Karyotype shows all chromosomes paired except chromosome 21, which has three copies. Children have characteristic facial features, some degree of mental retardation, and possible congenital heart/GI defects — a constellation of abnormalities, not one protein problem.
Proliferation and differentiation. Primary control of both = genetic programming (which genes are on/off).
G1 (makes proteins, RNA, organelles), S (DNA synthesis), G2 (like G1 — more preparation), M (mitosis/split). G0 = rest FROM replication, outside the cycle, but the cell still makes ATP.
Rest from replication — the cell is outside the cell cycle but still makes ATP. Cancer has more cells in cycle and fewer in G0.
Sun radiation, tobacco, asbestos, toxic chemicals → free radicals → DNA electron theft → mutation. Latency period is 5–30 years before disease appears.
5–30 years between exposure to carcinogens and development of cancer. Mutation occurs at exposure; disease manifests much later.
Cancers arise often; the immune system should clear them. When immune function is reduced (AIDS, immunosuppressants) cancer risk increases.
Cells like skin and liver cells that reproduce well but only make their own type. Differentiated progenitor cells have limited lineage capacity.
Cells (e.g., bone marrow) that can make many lineages — RBCs, platelets, all WBCs. Found in marrow; broader capacity than progenitor cells.
S-phase errors → gene disorders (mutations during DNA synthesis). M-phase unequal split → chromosomal disorders (nondisjunction during cell division).
23 (from one germ cell) + 23 (from the other) = 46 / 23 pairs. Germ cells start with 23 so the zygote is not overloaded.
Brain cells reproduce slowly (not zero). Progenitor cells (skin, liver) reproduce well but only make their own type. Stem cells (marrow) make many lineages.
Viral DNA into host DNA = mutation. HPV–cervical; HBV/HCV–liver; EBV–lymphoma. Viruses need host machinery to replicate; bacteria do not.
Chemotherapy drugs are often specific to cell-cycle phases (S or M). This is why combo drugs and long courses are used — to target cells at different points in the cycle.
Mitosis = somatic/body cells, 46 chromosomes. Meiosis = germ cells, 23 chromosomes (not 23 pairs).
Also called cell density-dependent inhibition; a normal regulatory mechanism of mitosis where cells stop dividing when crowded.
Abnormal proliferation (growth exceeds normal, no useful purpose, harms host) plus abnormal differentiation; result of mutations in regulatory genes. Not one disease; continues indefinitely.
The only mutations that are hereditary; a mutated gene may be inherited through the germ cell line. Example: highly hereditary breast cancer → preventive mastectomy.
Crowds out normal cells, steals blood/O2/nutrients; uncontrolled cell growth and infiltration into surrounding tissues.
Organ fails at its job; loss of cohesiveness → metastasis via blood or lymph; may produce VEGF, ectopic hormones, enzymes/toxins, abnormal antigens.
Abnormal biochemical product; promotes new vessel growth so tumor can grow past blood-supply limit.
Used to monitor, judge treatment, and watch for recurrence — NOT to diagnose or screen. CEA: colon, gastric, pancreatic, some breast cancers.

Abnormal proliferation only (normal differentiation); often enclosed in a fibrous capsule, expansion/local problems only, no VEGF/hormones/toxins/cachexia/anemia typically, rarely fatal except by location (e.g., brain).
Both abnormal proliferation and abnormal differentiation; infiltrates and metastasizes, no capsule, causes systemic effects (cachexia, anemia, ectopic hormones).

Surgery is almost always combined with radiation and/or chemo because leftover cells regrow. Radiation uses free radicals to kill or stop replication; hits fastest-dividing cells hardest. Treatment irony: radiation and chemo are themselves carcinogens but used because alternative is death.

Consists of chains of nucleotides containing 1 of 4 possible bases: A, C, G, T. Bases arranged in a triplet code; after transcription into RNA the triplet is called a codon. Each codon codes for a specific amino acid.
Triplet of bases in RNA (after transcription from DNA); each codon is a code for one specific amino acid.
Homozygous: alleles are the same. Heterozygous: alleles are different. Recessive traits expressed only in homozygous pairings; dominant traits expressed in either.

Error in DNA replication → change in genetic code; a germ-cell mutation is a 'metabolic accident.' Single-gene disorders: one protein missing/bad; no universal signs/symptoms or treatment; cannot yet fix the mutation.

Defective gene on a sex chromosome (usually X), usually recessive. Males affected (one X), females usually carriers (two X). Y too small (>1000 fewer genes). Example: Hemophilia A = Factor VIII deficiency → bleeds into muscle/joint.

Defective gene on an autosome and dominant; one bad gene = disease, no carriers. Example: Marfan syndrome — connective tissue disorder with long limbs/fingers, chest/spine deformity, lens dislocation/retinal detachment, valve prolapse, aneurysms.

Defective gene on an autosome and recessive; aa = disease, Aa = carrier, AA = normal. Example: sickle cell anemia — one wrong amino acid in hemoglobin gene → sickled RBCs → clots, pain, hemolytic anemia. Disease vs trait distinction.
Tool for predicting inheritance risk. X-linked: use X/Y and risk out of 2 by sex. Autosomal: use A/a and risk out of 4. Affected X-linked dad + normal mom → 0% affected sons, 100% carrier daughters.

Chromosome 21 has 3 copies instead of 2; causes characteristic face, intellectual disability, congenital heart defects, GI malformations. Extra chromosome causes many problems even if each gene is 'spelled' correctly.
Treat symptoms and support quality of life; cannot fix the chromosome error. Revisited in pediatrics.
Exposure to carcinogens (drugs, radiation, cigarette smoke), cancer-causing viruses (HPV, EBV, HBV), immunologic defects, heredity (germ-line mutation).

Anemia (from nutrition deficit, bleeding from toxins or vessel erosion, marrow mets, or marrow suppression from chemo/radiation); pain (nerves, ischemia from vessel compression, tissue damage, possible pain-mediator release); cachexia (wasting — tumor steals nutrients + cytokine-induced anorexia). Note: abnormal antigens are a change of abnormal differentiation, not a generalized effect.
Newer cancer drugs including monoclonal antibodies and synthetic cytokines; work by modifying the immune response.
Genes determine inheritance patterns transmitted through gametes; zygote receives chromosomes from each parent to make a paired set (2 genes per trait = alleles). Mendel published ~1865.
The arrangement of DNA bases in groups of three. After transcription into RNA, the triplet is called a codon. Each codon is a code for a specific amino acid.
The allele in a pair more likely to be expressed. Dominant traits are expressed in either a homozygous or heterozygous pairing.
The allele less likely to be expressed. Recessive traits are expressed only in homozygous pairings.
Error during meiosis causing a change in chromosome structure or number. Predisposing factors include exposure to chemicals, radiation, viral infections.

Defective gene located on a sex chromosome (usually the X). Most have a recessive inheritance pattern. Females are usually carriers; males usually have the disease because they have only 1 X chromosome.
Example of an autosomal dominant disorder—a connective tissue disorder.
DNA directs protein synthesis through the gene instructions for synthesizing specific proteins.
Genes determine inheritance patterns transmitted through gametes following Mendel's laws. The zygote receives chromosomes from each parent to make a paired set.
Production of hormones by a tissue that does not normally produce that hormone; an example of a chemical product of abnormal cells.
Antigens produced by abnormal cells that can trigger generalized effects in the body.
Systemic effects caused by a neoplasm, such as weight loss, ectopic hormone production, and abnormal antigens.
Tumors that are more likely to be encapsulated, grow more slowly, and do not metastasize. Example of a disorder in the growth/function framework.
Tumors more likely to metastasize compared to benign tumors; may also cause generalized effects such as weight loss.
The spread of malignant tumor cells to other parts of the body—a key difference between malignant and benign tumors.

Generates free radicals that can damage the cancer cell and interfere with its replication. Still accepted despite damage to normal cells because cancer cells divide more rapidly and are more vulnerable.
The CAUSE of the disease. PF → disease → s/s (signs and symptoms). Examples include exposure to chemicals, radiation, viral infections.
The RESULT of the disease, arising after the predisposing factor causes the disease.
Body cells (except gametes) containing 23 pairs of chromosomes. A single gene disorder usually occurs when there is a genetic mutation in a germ cell, not a somatic cell.
The cell type in which a genetic mutation usually occurs to produce a single gene disorder (as opposed to a somatic cell).
The process by which the DNA triplet code is converted into RNA, at which point the triplet is called a codon.
How the body makes blood cells; the three cell lines (erythrocytes, leukocytes, thrombocytes) all originate from bone marrow stem cells.
Red blood cells; carry oxygen to tissues via hemoglobin containing iron. One of the three products of bone marrow.
White blood cells; defend against infection and foreign material. One of the three products of bone marrow.
Platelets (PLTs); responsible for primary hemostasis — forming the platelet plug. One of the three products of bone marrow.
The process by which all three blood cell lines develop from hematopoietic stem cells in red bone marrow through levels of differentiation until mature circulating cells are produced.
Pluripotent stem cells in red bone marrow that give rise to all three blood cell lines through differentiation.
A growth factor produced by the kidney that stimulates bone marrow to make RBCs; primary stimulus is hypoxia. Synthetic versions are given clinically for anemias.
A growth factor that stimulates neutrophil production; given clinically when neutrophil counts are too low.

The production of red blood cells; the primary stimulus is hypoxia (low O₂ at tissues) → kidney produces EPO → bone marrow makes RBCs → increased O₂-carrying capacity. Production is on the order of 200 × 10⁹ RBCs per day.
Not enough oxygen at the tissues; the primary stimulus for erythropoiesis and a major predisposing factor for polycythemia.
Slightly immature RBCs released from the marrow; at any one time about 1% of circulating RBCs are reticulocytes. Developmental path: hemocytoblast → proerythroblast → … → reticulocyte → erythrocyte.
An index of bone marrow activity. Low retic = marrow not producing RBCs fast enough (nutrition missing or marrow problem). High retic = marrow is producing faster (most common trigger: blood loss).
The iron-containing molecule inside RBCs that binds and transports oxygen. Iron inside hemoglobin is what allows O₂ carriage.

RBC surface antigens (A, B, both, or none) group blood. Type A has A antigen and anti-B antibody; Type B has B antigen and anti-A; Type AB has both antigens and no antibodies; Type O has neither antigen and both antibodies. ABO antibodies appear spontaneously by 3–6 months of age.
RBC bursting when a surface antigen meets its matching antibody in the wrong-type transfusion.

Named for the rhesus monkey (1940). Many antigens (C, D, E); D is most reactive and used for Rh typing. Rh+ has the D antigen; Rh− does not. Rh− people make anti-D ONLY if exposed to Rh-positive blood.

Too many red blood cells. Causes: (1) bone marrow disorder (e.g., polycythemia vera) or (2) chronic hypoxia (smoking, COPD, high altitude) → chronic EPO overproduction. Effects: increased blood viscosity (thicker blood, clot risk) and increased blood volume (stresses heart/vessels).
A type of blood cancer where the bone marrow itself overproduces RBCs (and often other cell lines).
Lower than normal RBCs or hemoglobin so tissues get less O₂. Symptoms: fatigue, weakness, dizziness, pallor, rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, chest pain, headache, leg pain, insomnia.

(1) Nutritional deficiencies (iron, B12, B9); (2) Bone marrow failure (aplastic anemia); (3) Blood loss (GI bleed, trauma, postop hemorrhage); (4) Excessive/premature destruction or hemolysis (sickle cell, toxins, burns, mechanical valves, autoimmune).
Iron deficiency anemia; RBCs are small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic) because they lack hemoglobin/iron. MCV and MCHC are both DOWN.
CBC index measuring the SIZE of the RBC. DOWN in microcytic hypochromic iron-deficiency anemia; the cell is smaller so volume is lower.
CBC index measuring how much hemoglobin is packed in each RBC. DOWN in microcytic hypochromic iron-deficiency anemia (less Hb → lower concentration).
Caused by B12 or B9 deficiency; RBCs come out LARGE (macrocytic) and often megaloblastic (big, immature-looking) because these vitamins are needed for DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing marrow cells.
Vitamin B12; needed for DNA synthesis in marrow cells and for normal myelin (nerve sheath). Deficiency causes macrocytic anemia plus neuro changes. Also called cobalamin.

Vitamin B9; needed for DNA synthesis in marrow cells. Deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and, in pregnancy, neural-tube defects (spina bifida). Does NOT cause the neuro changes seen with B12 deficiency.

Made by parietal cells in the gastric mucosa; required for B12 absorption from gut into blood. Protects B12 from digestive enzymes. Lost via chronic gastritis, gastric surgery (cancer or weight-loss), or certain drugs.
Anemia caused specifically by insufficient intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed. This name is used ONLY when IF is the reason B12 is missing (not from diet or ileal disease).
Numbness, tingling, odd sensations; a neuro change associated with B12 deficiency due to impaired myelin.
Coordination problems; a neuro change associated with B12 deficiency due to impaired myelin.

Neural-tube defect from B9 (folate) deficiency in pregnancy; vertebrae do not close in the back. Severity ranges: bony defect only → meninges/nerves protruding → actual cord protruding (risk of paralysis).
Cracked, inflamed corners of the mouth; a clinical clue that can accompany B-vitamin deficiency anemias.
Bone marrow failure — marrow not producing the cell lines; red cells (and often WBCs and platelets) drop. Causes: radiation, toxic drugs/chemicals, marrow cancer.

Acute blood-loss anemia; cells look normal in size and color because whole blood was lost (MCV and MCHC stay normal). Chronic slow GI bleed can later become iron-deficient (microcytic hypochromic) once iron stores are spent.
Low circulating blood volume (hypo=low, vol=volume, -emia=blood). Especially dangerous with large loss in a short time; leads to compensatory tachycardia before hypotension.
BP has dropped to the point that major organs cannot be adequately perfused and begin to fail; can progress to multi-organ failure and death. Tachycardia precedes hypotension.
Excessive or premature RBC destruction. Causes: sickle cell, toxins/bacterial toxins, severe burns, artificial heart valves (mechanical trauma to RBCs), autoimmune attack on RBCs.
Breakdown product of hemoglobin released during hemolysis; excess bilirubin causes jaundice (yellowing) and is dumped into the bile/liver pathway.

The process of how bleeding stops; the study guide lists five stages: (1) vessel spasm/vasoconstriction, (2) platelet plug (primary hemostasis), (3) fibrin clot (secondary hemostasis), (4) clot holds while vessel heals, (5) clot degradation by plasmin.
Platelets stick to the injured vessel wall and to each other (aided by prostaglandins such as thromboxane A2) to plug the hole; the plug is unstable and can be knocked loose by flow.
The coagulation cascade lays fibrin over the platelet plug to stabilize it so it stays in place; the cascade end-product is fibrin, not the platelet itself.
Plasmin breaks down the fibrin clot once the vessel has healed; a check-and-balance so clots are not left indefinitely.

Produced by the LIVER (not platelets); they drive the coagulation cascade to form the fibrin clot that stabilizes the platelet plug. Do NOT confuse with platelets (which are marrow-derived and make the plug).
Activated by injury to the blood vessel wall (e.g., atherosclerosis can injure the vessel without injuring surrounding tissue).
Activated by injury to tissues (cut, trauma) via tissue factor.
Clotting pathway activated by injury to the BLOOD VESSEL. Atherosclerosis can injure the vessel without injuring surrounding tissue, so the two paths are not totally redundant.

cards.def: Clotting pathway activated by injury to TISSUES (cut, trauma) via tissue factor. Both pathways start on different factors, then JOIN; end result of either path is a fibrin clot.
cards.src: Doc: Class 3 source text, Intrinsic vs extrinsic cascade section

cards.def: Clotting factors circulate in INACTIVE form and sequentially activate the next one. Blood also has anticoagulant/anti-clotting factors so you only clot where needed.
cards.src: Doc: Class 3 source text, Intrinsic vs extrinsic cascade section

cards.def: Too few platelets. Bleeding occurs because a stable plug cannot be built. Predisposing factors: bone marrow depression, splenomegaly, autoimmune destruction.
Pinpoint bleeds in the skin. Seen when platelet plugs cannot form.
Nosebleed. A sign of platelet plug failure (thrombocytopenia).
Enlarged spleen sequesters more platelets (they hang in the spleen up to ~8 hours) and over-clears old/defective cells including platelets.
Removal of the spleen. Used when autoimmune destruction or splenomegaly is sequestering/eating platelets.

Plasma exchange — machine like dialysis separates blood, returns cells with synthetic plasma, and discards patient plasma containing attacking antibodies. Two or three rounds can put some patients into remission.
Drugs that quiet the immune attack on platelets (or other cells) in autoimmune destruction.
Drugs that prevent platelets from clumping into a plug. Patients bleed longer and bruise more; used intentionally to prevent arterial clots causing ischemic stroke, TIA, angina, ACS, PAD, MI.
Prototype antiplatelet. Stops platelet clumping → bleed longer, bruise more. Mini-dose/baby aspirin once daily is for antiplatelet effect, not analgesia. Risks: GI bleed, hemorrhagic stroke.
Antiplatelet class (clopidogrel/Plavix, prasugrel/Effient, ticlopidine/Ticlid) used for ACS, stent, stroke, PAD. Ticlid also causes thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, TTP.
Dipyridamole (Persantine) after valve replacement with warfarin; cilostazol (Pletal) for claudication. Shared adverse effect is bleeding.
Potent antiplatelet class (ReoPro, Integrilin, Aggrastat). Adverse effects include GI, urinary, and retroperitoneal bleeding.
A clot that formed where it is located.
A clot that has traveled from where it formed.
Events from clots (thrombus or embolus): MI, ischemic stroke, PE, DVT. Result of too many clotting factors / too much clotting.
The liver MAKES clotting factors. A sick liver produces not enough factors and may not make bile (needed for vitamin K absorption).

Many clotting factors need vitamin K to be made in a WORKING form. Causes: low dietary intake, inability to absorb (fat-soluble needs bile), broad-spectrum antibiotics wiping out gut bacteria that help make vit K.
Hereditary clotting-factor disorder; classic example was Factor VIII deficiency. Factors are produced in insufficient amounts or non-functional forms.
Clotting factors used up faster than replaced. Lead-in to DIC; consumption leaves nothing to stop a bleed.

Widespread clotting inside vessels all over the body. NOT a primary disease — a complication of severe infection, trauma, or advanced cancer (ICU patients). Microthrombi occlude flow → organ failure AND factors are consumed → hemorrhage. Paradox: abnormal clotting AND abnormal bleeding at the same time.
Polymorphonuclear leukocyte. Granulocyte phagocyte — first-line eater of bacteria/foreign material. Lysosomal enzymes digest what it engulfs. Mature = segs; immature = bands.
Segs = MATURE neutrophils (segmented nucleus). Bands = IMMATURE neutrophils (horseshoe/band nucleus). CBC splits neutrophils into these two groups.
More bands than usual on a CBC. Most common cause: infection or inflammation. Marrow speeds neutrophil production so immature cells spill out; also called neutrophilia.
A granulocyte, grouped with neutrophils and eosinophils. Allergy/histamine role is the usual pairing.
Granulocyte whose primary job is fighting parasites (too big to phagocytose) using granule enzymes. Also piles up in allergy/asthma. Some enzymes pro-inflammatory, some anti-inflammatory.
Monocytes are phagocytes in BLOOD. When they leave the vessel into tissue they become macrophages or dendritic cells.
B lymphocytes mature in Bone marrow → antibody producers (humoral immunity). T lymphocytes mature in Thymus → cell-mediated immunity. NK (natural killer) cells = innate immunity.
Too few leukocytes (WBCs in general). General term for WBC deficiency.

Too few neutrophils. High concern because neutrophils are the most plentiful WBC and first phagocytes on scene. Causes: marrow problems, autoimmune destruction, splenomegaly, increased consumption into infected tissue.
Too few granulocytes. Often used interchangeably with neutropenia.
Neutrophil count < 200 (normal ~3,000–7,000). Neutrophils so low it is almost like having none; essentially without granulocytes.
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor — a synthetic growth factor given to push the marrow to make more neutrophils (used in neutropenia).

Cancer of the blood/WBC line. Cells don't function properly (blasts), crowd out normal cells (anemia + thrombocytopenia + neutropenia), can metastasize/infiltrate organs, cause anorexia/cachexia and pain.
Very immature white-cell precursors. Acute leukemias are blast-heavy and poorly differentiated.
Acute: sudden onset, many blasts, poorly differentiated, sick fast. Chronic: more mature-appearing cells, slower course (still cancer).
Aspiration = withdraw fluid; biopsy = bigger needle, actual chunks of marrow. Usual site: iliac crest. Goal: see cell differentiation, stage the leukemia, name the specific type.
Collection from patient or donor → lab processing/purification → cryopreservation (freeze) → high-dose chemo/radiation to wipe marrow → thawed cells reinfused. Allogeneic = donor cells.
Gut bacteria help make vitamin K. BSA wipes them out → less vit K → worse clotting. BSA hits the bacterial K source, not the marrow.
Resistance to disease by defending against pathogenic organisms.
Recognition of foreign molecules and getting rid of them. Works because almost every cell has surface antigens with unique molecular shapes.
A tool to defend against harmful agents and start healing—not just a bad feeling.
The immune system is supposed to recognize and clear abnormal cells that arise all the time.
A marker on a cell membrane used to decide self vs non-self. Antigens are not automatically bad; a self antigen is left alone, a foreign antigen is targeted.
What the immune system MAKES to get rid of an antigen it has decided is foreign.
The name for the unique molecular shapes on surface antigens that white cells have learned to identify as self or foreign.
Normal body markers on cell surfaces.
An antigen not belonging to self; targeted by the immune system.
White blood cells plus the substances they make: antibodies and cytokines.
Bone marrow and thymus—where immune cells are produced or mature. Failure impairs immunity a lot, especially bone marrow.

Spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, appendix, and patches in GI/respiratory/reproductive tracts. Trap antigens and promote their interaction with mature immune cells; clean foreign material out of lymph before it returns to blood.
GI patches named in the handout; part of the secondary lymph structures.
Mucosal tissue in respiratory, GI, and reproductive systems that traps antigens and promotes their interaction with mature immune cells.
Natural/native/nonspecific immunity present at birth. Jumps in right away against anything foreign; holds pathogens until adaptive kicks in.
Specific/acquired immunity acquired later. Learns the particular pathogens you meet; slower to start but more effective because it is aimed at one antigen.
Mainly neutrophils and monocyte-macrophages that engulf and digest foreign particles, tumor cells, and virus-infected cells; also act as antigen-presenting cells (APCs).
Phagocytic white cells that process foreign antigen and display it on their membrane so a T cell can see it; that display activates adaptive immunity.
The only lymphocyte in innate immunity. Kill tumor cells and virus-infected cells by releasing toxins or enzymes, not by phagocytosis. Attack anything foreign.

Hormone-like proteins released by certain white cells that act on other white cells to regulate the immune response. Examples: interferons, interleukins, tumor necrosis factor, colony-stimulating factor.

A cascade of about 20 plasma proteins sitting in blood in inactive form; each factor activates the next. Complements the work of phagocytes and antibodies in clearing pathogens; ends with inflammation. ⚠ Conflict: her lecture/handout says about 20 plasma proteins; the full Patho study sheet says 10. Go with her lecture (~20) unless she says otherwise.
Mast cells and basophils release granules holding mediators of inflammation (histamine, leukotrienes, bradykinin). Degranulation = inflammation.
A chemical signal that calls white cells to the area that needs them.
Bursts pathogens or abnormal cells, including cells that have become cancerous.
Coats antigen-antibody complexes with complement pieces so phagocytes can grab them. Antibody gives a handle; complement makes the handle even easier to pull in.
Adaptive lymphocytes targeting microbes INSIDE cells—usually viruses. Cannot enter the cell, so they kill the infected cell. Each is programmed for ONE specific foreign antigen.
Adaptive lymphocytes targeting microbes OUTSIDE cells—usually bacteria—by making antibodies. Antibodies cannot go inside cells, so this branch is for extracellular targets.
The master switch. Once an APC shows it its programmed antigen, it releases cytokines that activate other T cells and B cells. Wipe out helper T and adaptive immunity does not turn on.
Kills tumor cells and virus-infected cells by releasing toxins and enzymes. Adaptive, so must be activated by helper T first; targets one specific foreign antigen.
Slows or stops the immune response once the pathogen is gone and suppresses self-reactive white cells that would attack normal self, helping prevent autoimmune disease.
Hangs around a long time and remembers a pathogen so a second exposure is recognized fast enough to mobilize before you get sick.
A specialized B cell that makes antibodies. Antibodies bind surface antigens and act like handles so phagocytes can grab encapsulated bacteria.
Hangs around after infection; on re-exposure it quickly drives proliferation of plasma cells so a large antibody burst happens before you get sick.
Most plentiful antibody class; the only one that crosses the placenta, giving newborns most of their protection for the first few months.
Secretory IgA found in tears, saliva, GI and respiratory secretions; protects mucous membranes, which are portals of entry.
First antibody to appear; suggests current or recent infection. Does not hang around.
On the B-cell membrane like a monitor; stimulates proliferation. Not usually free in blood.
Mediates allergic reactions and defends against parasites.
Your immune system generated it. Long-lasting but takes days to weeks after first exposure. Examples: getting sick and making antibodies, or getting a vaccine (antigen).

Your immune system did nothing and just received it from another source. Short-term only; antibodies break down and cannot be replaced. Examples: mom's antibodies crossing the placenta, gamma globulin injection.
One or more branches of the immune system are not working. Expected problems: persistent/hard-to-treat infections and higher cancer incidence because cancer surveillance fails.
Born with it; an inherited gene defect or mutation leads to defective white cells that cannot do the job.
Acquired later from infection (AIDS), cancer (leukemia), immunosuppressive drugs, or another organ failure that hits immunity.
Missing an activating factor means the body cannot generate inflammation, so one defense tool is gone. Missing an inhibiting factor means inflammation cannot be slowed once it starts.
Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome — an immunodeficiency disorder, NOT an autoimmune disorder. Diagnosis switches when helper T count drops below 200 or an AIDS-defining illness develops.
A retrovirus that selectively attacks the immune system, mainly helper T cells. Lose helper T and you lose all adaptive immunity and innate immunity works less efficiently.
Has RNA only, not DNA. Most viruses have one or the other, not both.
The enzyme that changes viral RNA into viral DNA during HIV replication.

Enters a host cell (usually helper T), viral RNA becomes viral DNA via reverse transcriptase, viral DNA is inserted into host DNA, host makes more virus, helper T breaks apart releasing new HIV to infect other helper T cells.
Infection by an organism that does not bother people with a normal immune system.

Not mainly transfusion — U.S. blood has been screened since the mid-1980s (about 1 in 2 million transfusions). Real route is shared needles among IV drug users; healthcare needle sticks are rare but have transmitted it.
Semen and vaginal secretions. Not casual contact: not a handshake, toilet seat, or shared glass.
Usually NOT in utero — placenta is a good barrier. Usually exposure to mom's blood in labor and delivery, or breastfeeding; depends on mom's viral load.

Infected, no immunodeficiency symptoms yet. Virus is there, immune system keeps viral levels low; the cell serves as a reservoir for the virus. Can last up to 10 years or more; dangerous because they can still transmit.
CD4 below 200, OR an AIDS-defining illness. Normal helper T frame is about 600 to 1,200.
About 600 to 1,200. AIDS threshold is below 200.

Time between infection and seroconversion (blood test flips from negative to positive). Textbook: 1 to 3 months with cheaper screening tests; blood bank tests shorten it to about 2 or 3 weeks. Use standard precautions on everybody.
The blood test flips from negative to positive after infection.
Enzyme immunoassay / enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay — common screen. Not HIV-specific (also used for CMV). Has false positives, so a positive must be confirmed.
Follow-up if EIA is positive. More expensive, more specific. Positive = HIV infection; negative = the EIA was a false positive.
CDC AIDS surveillance case definition list, mostly opportunistic infections and cancers. Infections become more numerous, more severe, and harder to treat.
The most common AIDS pneumonia, caused by the fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii. Old name Pneumocystis carinii is the animal form.
Opportunistic cousin of TB — same genus, different species, TB-like symptoms, not as hardy, so it hits impaired immunity.
Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis; also occurs in AIDS but is NOT opportunistic.

A vascular malignancy — cancer of cells lining some smaller blood vessels. Raised reddish-purple skin lesions, often trunk or head and neck; can be on internal organs and then cause organ dysfunction.
HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder. Maybe half of AIDS patients; most have no symptoms or only mild ones, and only a small percent progress to dementia.
Weight loss that happens WITHOUT an opportunistic infection or cancer that could explain it. In parts of Africa with a lot of AIDS it is called slim disease.
Oral lesion in AIDS caused by Epstein-Barr virus.
Monocytes/macrophages and neutrophils.
Also known as helper T cells; the master switch of adaptive immunity.
The only innate lymphocyte. Kills with toxins, not phagocytosis; does not need helper T and is not antigen-specific.

The absence of an immune response directed against a person's own antigens. Maintained by suppressor/regulatory T cells, elimination of self-reactive T and B cells during maturation, and the MHC activation gate.
Suppress self-reactive immune cells and turn the response off, maintaining self-tolerance.
Molecules located on the cell surface that display antigens for inspection by T cells. T cells do not activate unless the foreign antigen is complexed to the right MHC molecule.

Found on nearly all nucleated cells (mostly cells not capable of phagocytosis); displays intracellular antigens — normal self antigens, viruses, and abnormal proteins from mutation. Interacts with CD8 cytotoxic T cells.

Found mainly on macrophages/APCs (which obtain foreign antigens by phagocytosis); displays extracellular antigens. Interacts with CD4 helper T cells — if an antigen is not displayed by Class II, no helper-T activation occurs.
Can only recognize a foreign antigen if it is complexed to a Class I MHC molecule (intracellular display). Class I gates the cytotoxic T cell.
Can only recognize foreign antigen if complexed to a Class II MHC molecule. No Class II display means no activation of the helper T cell.

The human name for MHC genes; the type checked for a transplant match via DNA/HLA testing. It takes about 128 genes to code one MHC molecule, with 50–650 alleles, which is why a transplant match is hard.
Pathological change: breakdown of self-tolerance in which the immune system attacks the person's own tissues.
A foreign antigen looks so much like a self antigen that antibody made against it also hits self tissue. Example: group A beta-hemolytic strep antigens resemble heart and kidney tissue.
Self antigens that never met lymphocytes during early development; injury later releases them and the system treats them as foreign.
The attack stays on one tissue or organ.
The same mechanism hits many organs. SLE is the systemic example.
An autoantibody test; a positive ANA points at autoimmunity, not at infection. Other autoantibody tests include anti-DNA, anti-CCP, antiphospholipid, and rheumatoid factor.

CRP and fibrinogen are acute-phase proteins the liver makes when cytokines signal inflammation; ESR is how fast red cells settle (faster when those proteins are up). All three indicate inflammation, not a specific disease.

Drugs used to treat autoimmunity: immunosuppressive drugs, monoclonal antibodies, and corticosteroids. (Per the class sort table, hypersensitivity is managed with antihistamines and/or anti-inflammatory drugs, not immunomodulators.)
Filtering antibodies out of plasma; a vocabulary/intervention item listed under treatment of autoimmune disease.
Synthetic cortisol used as immunomodulators/anti-inflammatories; they carry a lot of side effects.
Antibodies against many self antigens including nuclear antigens such as DNA and RNA. A type III hypersensitivity; it remits and flares, and diagnosis is made after other causes are ruled out.

Cell damage releases DNA → anti-DNA antibodies form → they meet DNA from damaged cells anywhere → antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissues, activate complement, cause inflammation and more cell damage, and the cycle repeats.
A characteristic facial rash of SLE; the disorder also causes bruising, lupus arthritis, and involvement of kidney (renal failure), heart, eyes, lungs, GI, and blood cells.
The reaction of tissue to injury, regardless of cause. Purpose is to begin healing: neutralize or destroy the harmful agent, limit its spread, and prepare damaged tissue for repair.
Redness, heat, swelling, pain, and impaired (lost) function. More blood, oxygen, fuel, and antibody in the area causes redness and warmth; the fluid leak causes swelling, pain, and lost function.
Mostly histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, plasma proteases, platelet-activating factor, and other cytokines, released from mast cells and immune cells.
Brief/momentary vasoconstriction followed by vasodilation; capillary permeability rises and fluid escapes into the tissue.
From cytokines: fever, more white cells, and skeletal muscle catabolism (breaking down muscle protein). Fever is useful because many pathogens cannot take the heat and some white cells work better.
The first cells to arrive in an injured area during inflammation; monocytes and macrophages also arrive and can present antigen.
Fluid that escapes into tissue during inflammation. Serous: clear, light yellow. Sero-sanguineous: watery blood. Purulent: pus.
Chronic irritation from unchecked inflammation can cause metaplasia (abnormal change of cell type); loss of function and deformity can also result, e.g., rheumatoid arthritis.
Unnecessary inflammation / an allergic reaction — the immune system aims at the wrong thing or aims too hard. Types I–III are antibody-mediated (immediate); type IV is T-cell (delayed).

Allergen binds IgE already on mast cells or basophils; they degranulate and dump inflammatory mediators. Examples: allergic rhinitis (hay fever), asthma, urticaria (hives), atopic dermatitis (eczema), anaphylaxis.
IgG or IgM binds a cell or tissue antigen; the antigen-antibody reaction itself damages the target. Examples: blood transfusion reaction, myasthenia gravis (antibody against acetylcholine receptors).
Antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissue, turn on complement, and inflammation does the damage — not the binding itself. Example: SLE.
T cells kill directly or release cytokines that damage tissue; no antibody involved. Examples: contact dermatitis (poison ivy), type 1 diabetes (T cells on pancreatic cells), transplant rejection.
System-wide mast-cell/basophil degranulation; blood pressure falls, producing anaphylactic shock. Treated with antihistamines, anti-inflammatories, and corticosteroids.
Face swelling associated with a type I hypersensitivity reaction.
Type II hypersensitivity in which antibody against acetylcholine receptors prevents muscle from contracting.
Allergies (IgE), antiBodies (cytotoxic), immune Complex (complement), Delayed (T cell) — the four types of hypersensitivity.
The system fails to attack a real threat, producing infection. Checked with cultures and WBC count; treated with antimicrobials. The most reliable sign of infection is a positive urine culture.
A cost of inflammation when repair occurs by laying down collagen.
Redness, heat, swelling, pain, and impaired function — the five hallmark signs (S/S) of inflammation.

Histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, plasma proteases, platelet-activating factor, and other cytokines released from mast cells, immune cells, etc. Mechanism of inflammation is mostly r/t release of these.
Momentary vasoconstriction in the area, followed by vasodilation → increased capillary permeability → fluid escapes into tissues.
Movement of WBCs into area of injury.
Antibodies formed against DNA released from damaged cells; react with DNA from damaged cells anywhere in body, forming antigen-antibody complexes that deposit in tissues.

Major Histocompatibility Complex molecules located on cell surface whose role is to display antigens for inspection by T cells, assisting in identification of foreign antigens. Two classes: Class I and Class II.

Found on nearly all nucleated cells. Display mostly antigens from intracellular sources (normal self antigens, viruses, abnormal cell proteins). CD8+ (cytotoxic) T cells only recognize foreign antigens if complexed to Class I MHC.

Found mainly on macrophages (APCs). Display mostly antigens from extracellular sources. CD4+ (helper) T cells only recognize foreign antigens if complexed to Class II MHC. No helper T cell activation if antigen not displayed by Class II MHC.
Suppress activity of self-reactive immune cells; one mechanism of maintaining self-tolerance.
T cells that interact with Class II MHC molecules; can only recognize foreign antigen if complexed to Class II MHC molecule.
T cells that interact with Class I MHC molecules; can only recognize a foreign antigen if it is complexed to a Class I MHC molecule.

Pathological immune response, following sensitization, to antigens that would not affect most people. Classified into four types (I–IV). Types I, II, and III are antibody-mediated; Type IV is T cell-mediated.

IgE-mediated or immediate hypersensitivity: allergen binds to allergen-specific IgE on mast cells/basophils → release of chemical mediators of inflammation. Memory trick: Allergies. Examples: allergic rhinitis, asthma, urticaria, atopic dermatitis, anaphylaxis.

Antibody-mediated/cytotoxic disorder: interaction of IgG/IgM with cell/tissue antigen → reaction causes damage to target cell. Damage caused by antigen-antibody reaction itself. Example: blood transfusion reactions. Memory trick: antiBodies.

Immune complex-mediated disorder: antigen-antibody complexes deposited in tissues → activation of complement → tissue damage r/t inflammation. Damage caused by inflammation, not by antigen-antibody reaction itself. Example: SLE. Memory trick: immune Complex (Complement).

T cell-mediated/cellular disorder: T cells either directly cytotoxic, or release cytokines that cause tissue damage. Examples: contact dermatitis (poison ivy), diabetes mellitus. Memory trick: Delayed.
A triggering antigen that causes allergic reactions; exposure through inhalation, ingestion, injection, or skin contact. In Type I, allergen binds to allergen-specific IgE on mast cells/basophils.
A common Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity disorder.
A common Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity disorder involving allergic airway inflammation.
A Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity disorder affecting the skin.
A Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity disorder (hives).
A Type IV (T cell-mediated) hypersensitivity disorder, e.g., reaction to poison ivy.
Also called immune complex. Formed when antibodies bind to antigens; in Type III hypersensitivity these complexes deposit in tissues → activation of complement → tissue damage r/t inflammation.
An autoantibody directed against nuclear components; checked in autoimmunity workup. A positive ANA is associated with autoimmune disease.
An antibody directed against self-antigens; checked for in diagnosis of autoimmune disorders.
Impaired immune system function leading to infection. Diagnosed by checking cultures and WBC count; treated with antimicrobials.

A facial rash pattern listed on the Immune Part 2 vocabulary list, grouped with the SLE/autoimmunity terms. Note: the source text lists the term but does not define it or explicitly state its association with SLE.

Predisposing factors for autoimmune disease including a virus or microorganism, chemical exposure, or release of 'sequestered' self-antigens. Genetic factors and gender/hormones (more common in women) also contribute.
A cascade of proteins activated by antigen-antibody complexes in tissues, causing inflammation and more cell damage.
Cells that release chemical mediators (histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, etc.) upon activation; bind allergen-specific IgE in Type I hypersensitivity reactions.
Medications used to treat hypersensitivity/allergic reactions causing unnecessary inflammation.
Medications used to treat autoimmunity (damage to self tissue), often along with anti-inflammatory drugs.
An autoantibody directed against DNA; an antibody against self tissue. Listed among autoantibodies seen in autoimmunity.
A complex formed when antigen binds antibody (an immune complex). Deposits of these complexes drive Type III immune complex-mediated disorders.
A characteristic facial (malar) rash listed as a finding of systemic lupus erythematosus.
An inflammatory marker listed with inflammation/inflammatory findings. Rises with inflammation.
A metabolic process listed with inflammation; the breakdown phase of metabolism.
The release of granule contents (mediators) from mast cells. Occurs in immediate hypersensitivity reactions.
A hypersensitivity reaction that develops later, i.e., the Type IV T cell-mediated disorder.
A lab measure of red blood cell settling that increases with inflammation; listed as an inflammatory finding.
A clotting/inflammatory protein listed with inflammation; increases during the inflammatory response.
A hypersensitivity reaction occurring right after exposure, i.e., the Type I IgE-mediated disorder.

cards.term: Major histocompatibility complex/MHC (Class I and Class II)
cards.def: Self-antigen markers on cells that direct immune recognition; MHC Class I and Class II molecules. Involved in self-tolerance and immune activation.
Immune cells or antibodies that react against the body's own tissues. Related to autoimmunity and autoantibody production.
The initial exposure that primes the immune system to an allergen, producing antibodies/sensitized cells. A first step in hypersensitivity reactions.
Antigens hidden/separated from the immune system (e.g., in an enclosed area), which may be recognized as foreign if released.
Immediate hypersensitivity mediated by IgE. Examples: allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis, urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis.
Hypersensitivity in which antibody binds antigens on cell surfaces, causing cytotoxic damage. Example: blood transfusion reactions.
Hypersensitivity caused by deposited antigen-antibody (immune) complexes. Example: SLE.
Delayed hypersensitivity mediated by T cells (not antibody). Examples: contact dermatitis (like poison ivy), diabetes mellitus.
A skin manifestation of allergic/immediate hypersensitivity listed under Type I disorders.
The classic example of a Type II antibody-mediated/cytotoxic disorder.
An example of a Type IV T cell-mediated (delayed) disorder caused by skin contact with an allergen such as poison ivy.
Listed as an example of a Type IV T cell-mediated disorder.
Findings are specific to individual disorders; assessment varies by the particular hypersensitivity/autoimmune condition.
